comments.body:
Thanks for raising this. It's unfortunately a very tricky one to deal with directly in a clean and widely-supportable manner, so there might not be a great out-of-the-box option. It's a reasonable use case, but also an uncommon-enough one that it wouldn't be enough to drive a big change across the ecosystem, which is what message template syntax and semantic changes tend to entail.

Since the problem is fundamentally a rendering issue, though, the first place I'd look for a workable solution is _Serilog.Expressions_, which is a Swiss Army knife for hacking in modifications to rendering of all sorts. You can plug in custom functions (https://github.com/serilog/serilog-expressions/?tab=readme-ov-file#implementing-user-defined-functions) that get full access to the underlying `LogEvent` and its message template, including the raw text, and you can parameterize them either via the call syntax in your output template, or at configuration time when you plug them in.

It might not be a simple matter to get _Expressions_ wired in between Serilog and your sink of choice, but worth taking a look at, anyway.

Hi @slepmog,

`@p['some name']` is only required (in expression templates) if a property has a non-identifier name in its path. You can refer to structured object sub-properties in expression templates using regular dotted syntax, e.g. `ThatObject.ImportantProperty`.

Expression templates (per logger) are different from message templates (per event). Message templates are super-simple and drive capturing the data as well as formatting it. Expression templates are much more sophisticated, but only usable for formatting.

HTH!

Not really a solution, but probably worth mentioning if you don't know about it ... 

In some project we are currently using [`Elastic.CommonSchema.Serilog`](https://github.com/elastic/ecs-dotnet/tree/main/src/Elastic.CommonSchema.Serilog) ... what it does is that we write logs however we want in the app ... but "some" property names are recognized [and get mapped to the corresponding "standard" in the ECS Schema](Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties) ... and the ECS schema, while not identical, is [fairly close to OTel Semantic Conventions](https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/ecs/ecs-otel-alignment-details).

What we end up doing is that: 
- in "generic" logging enrichment portions (think "Middleware that enriches from incoming HTTP requests") we use ECS standard properties, for instance using constants exposed in [`Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties`](https://github.com/elastic/ecs-dotnet/blob/main/src/Elastic.CommonSchema/LogTemplateProperties.Generated.cs) ... 

code looks like : 

```cs
   _logger.ForContext(Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties.UserId, "userId").Information(....);

  // or 
  
  `_diagnosticContext.Set(Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties.UserId, "userId")
```

- in specific logging, if we have access to data that seem to match ECS reference, we enrich the context with properties from  `Elastic.CommonSchema.LogTemplateProperties` , using `LogContext` or "contextual loggers"


The caveat is that the ECS Serilog library does the mapping from those "well known properties" to the expected naming in the JSON Logs as part of Formatting, i.e. when "spitting out" the logs, not where they are written.

Hi @nblumhardt,

I may need to reopen this issue after further consideration. While the enricher approach works well in synchronous scenarios, there's a challenge with async logging pipelines where `Activity.Current` becomes null when the log event is actually processed.

For example:

```csharp
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .Enrich.With(new ActivitySamplingFlagsEnricher())
    .WriteTo.AsyncChannel(a => a.Console(new RenderedCompactJsonFormatter()))
    .CreateLogger();
```

In this async configuration, the enricher captures the activity during log call initiation, but the actual log processing happens on a different thread where the activity context is lost. This is similar to why traceId and spanId are designed to be captured and stored in the log context rather than relying on the process context.

Perhaps we need a more fundamental solution that captures these values (including IsAllDataRequested) at the moment of logging and preserves them through the async pipeline, similar to how trace identifiers are handled. Would love to hear your thoughts on this.

Hi @debuggedme - in that configuration, the `IsAllDataRequested` flag will be collected/attached to the log event at the same point the trace and span id are collected (synchronously, at the `Write` call). I might be misunderstanding, but it sounds like the enricher approach still does what you need, here.

comments.body:
Hi!

Serilog's built-in `IBatchedLogEventSink` support does support this functionality, and includes test suite entries that cover it.

Although _Serilog.Sinks.AwsCloudWatch_ is uses recent APIs, it [has dependencies on old versions](https://www.nuget.org/packages/serilog.sinks.awscloudwatch) of the packages involved (probably to maximise backwards compatibility). NuGet's default package installation algorithm resolves dependencies to the minimum, rather than maximum, version that can support the other packages in your solution.

To make sure your app actually uses the latest functionality, your best bets are:

 * Add an explicit reference to version 5.0.0 of _Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching_, or
 * Update _Serilog.Sinks.AwsCloudWatch_ to remove the _Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching_ dependency, using the built-in _Serilog_ package's batching features directly.

Hope this helps,

Nick

Hey Nick, thanks so much for this package and for taking the time to respond.

Your explanation makes sense and I'm adding `Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching` as a top-level dependency so I can specifically install the latest version, but I still have a question about how to actually use the `PeriodicBatchingSink.EmitAsync()` from the consumer-side of things.

I'm assuming that what left unsaid in your response is that a call to `logger.Dispose()` will automatically emit the batched log events after upgrading to `PeriodicBatching` 5.x?

Do you mind clarifying when/where the call to `EmitAsync()` is being made? `CloudWatchLogSink` instantiates a `PeriodicBatchingSink` with an inner `PeriodicBatchingSinkImplementationCallback` implementing `IBatchedLogEventSink`, but neither `PeriodicBatchingSink` doesn't call `EmitBatch()`/`EmitBatchAsync()` in its `Dispose()` implementation and the other nuget's `PeriodicBatchingSinkImplementationCallback` isn't even disposable. I see that a `DisposingAggregateSink` gets created from the `CreateSink` call, but that's not aware of `IBatchedLogEventSink` (so far as I can tell).

Separately, as the `PeriodicBatchingSink` instance is private (via composition) to `CloudWatchLogSink` (and `CloudWatchLogSink` doesn't implement `IBatchedLogEventSink` itself), I think the other part of my question about flushing all sinks *without* disposing the logger is still not possible? Even if/when `CloudWatchLogSink` skips the intermediary `PeriodicBatching` crate and directly using the batching APIs in newer serilog versions, Serilog doesn't really provide access to a logger instance's sinks (because they're treated as immutable) so there's no convenient way to call `EmitBatchAsync()` externally without bypassing the easy-to-use static `LoggerConfiguration` extension methods and creating your own instance of `XxxSink` then storing it *somewhere* so you can manually call `EmitBatchAsync()` (or its native serilog alternative?) when and where needed?

I really appreciate your help and patience, sorry for asking all these questions but despite using Serilog for probably over a decade this is the first time I've had to dive into its internals.

Thanks for your reply, Mahmoud.

Just to answer your second question, which I skipped earlier - there's no API for manually flushing a batched sink in Serilog, as things stand. It's been considered a few times in the past but hasn't seemed worth the added complexity, for the scenarios it would cover.

The latest `Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching` package is a fairly complex compatibility shim to keep the ecosystem working, but there's probably not much point digging into its internals here. For a maintained sink like the CloudWatch one, switching over to use the newer Serilog functionality directly will be a better bet for the long haul.

The new batching sink is this one:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Sinks/Batching/BatchingSink.cs

Its dispose methods signal to the background task that shutdown is required, and then wait on the background task to complete:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Sinks/Batching/BatchingSink.cs#L263

The task itself, after observing cancellation, works its way through the remainder of the queue:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Sinks/Batching/BatchingSink.cs#L169

Hi! Thanks for the note 👍 

This is somewhat by design; Serilog isn't a general-purpose serializer, and arbitrary objects shouldn't be captured using `@` or `destructureObjects`. The internals of the capturing process are optimized for throughput, and otherwise merely aim to survive accidental serialization of unintended things.

A proposal to add efficient circular dependency handling in a non-breaking way would definitely be welcome, but otherwise, it's unlikely any changes will be made in this area.

Unfortunately I don't have a proposal and don't have the capacity to put one forth.  If I were to go down that path, I'd likely look at how Microsoft does it in System.Text.Json since it's likely to be highly optimized for speed and efficiency already when trying to determine if the loops exist.

Thanks for your reply. If someone coming across this in future is keen to explore options further that would still be great, but closing right now as it's not a design goal for Serilog to efficiently handle arbitrary/circular object graphs. Cheers!

Hi John! Quite a bit to digest there, so just a couple of quick thoughts/answers, others with more Aspire experience might jump in :-)

* For Seq, whether you send events via the Serilog sink or OTEL, I'd recommend using an API key. Allocating different API keys to each unique app and service, per environment, means that you can use Seq's Data > Ingestion page to see how much data is coming from each source, and to filter/restrict it in case of log flooding or noise.
* If you want to see traces in Seq, you'll either need to point an OTLP exporter at it, or wire up SerilogTracing to route activities through the Seq sink.
* OpenTelemetry includes a metrics signal, which neither Serilog nor Seq collect.

HTH,
Nick

Hey @nblumhardt,

Thank you so much for your response. It been a while since we last spoke, and I appreciate you taking the time to address our setup.

Based on your suggestions, I'll make the following adjustments and have a few follow-up questions:

1. API Keys for Seq:

We will implement unique API keys for each app and service per environment. This sounds like an excellent way to manage and monitor our data ingestion. Is there a best practice for managing these keys in an Aspire environment, particularly for local development?

2. Traces in Seq:

We'll explore both options you mentioned. For our use case, which would you recommend:
   a) Pointing an OTLP exporter at Seq, AND
   b) Wiring up SerilogTracing to route activities through the Seq sink?

Are there pros and cons to each approach in an Aspire context? We want to avoid duplication in Seq or the Aspire Console I guess and we tend to lean toward SerilogTracing but would this be reported to the Aspire Console as well ? 

3. OpenTelemetry Metrics:

Thanks for clarifying that about metrics. Given that neither Serilog nor Seq collect these, what would you recommend as a complementary solution for metrics collection that would integrate well with our Serilog/Seq/Aspire stack? Is there anything on the roadmap for Serilog / Seq that would support this ?

4. Aspire Integration:

Since you mentioned others might have more Aspire experience, are there any Aspire-specific considerations we should keep in mind when implementing these changes, particularly regarding the Service Defaults setup? I feel like we have to have our feet in both camps but I'd rather be all in with Serilog and Seq without deliberately breaking or ignoring the Aspire Console functionality unless I really had too.

Again, thank you for your guidance. Your insights have always helped shape our observations and logging strategy.

Best regards,

John

Thanks for the reply, John! Here's my impressions -

On 1, I'd consider logging locally during development and not worrying about an API key at all. `Aspire.Hosting.Seq` can help with spinning up a local Seq container, or you can just log to a local Seq instance and all should be good. If you're writing to a shared development server, then I think this is a case where I wouldn't worry too much about API keys either. The main benefits are in the production context.

For 2, either or both should work. I like the SerilogTracing API considerably more than bare System.Diagnostics.Activity, so I'd lean towards trying to get it in there. There's still the option to go with bare System.Diagnostics.Activity and let traces flow to Seq through the OpenTelemetry SDK and an OTLP exporter if you hit any awkward integration points.

Metrics (3) brings Prometheus to mind, though I haven't used it in a production setting. InfluxDB + Grafana is the combination I have most experience with and enjoyed a lot, but that was many years ago.

Today, internally, we use Seq + an experimental feature flag to ingest OTLP metrics into Seq, and we have some automation which produces dashboards based on metric definitions. It's great to use for our purposes, but we haven't publicised this because the underlying event storage is too inefficient to be competitive for heavy metrics workloads. Our roadmap has native metrics support right at the top, https://datalust.co/roadmap - but given the imminent release of clustering and our expectation that a lot of resources will go into it over the next few months, it's more likely that native OTLP metrics is a 2026 project for us.

On 4, hoping others will chime in, looking forward to learning more about this myself.

Sorry about the slow reply, the week got away on me! Have a good weekend.

comments.body: @justinmchase `JsonFormatter` indeed does not respect any STJ stuff - https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Formatting/Json/JsonFormatter.cs#L23. This is by design. You can implement your own formatter and pass it as argument into `Console` method.

I ended up doing this but I'm not going to lie, it's a lot to implement just to get one thing to serialize right. There are so many extension points missing, it's really hard to believe it's by design.

Hi! This is not by precisely design, unfortunately you were thrown off by:

```csharp
logger.LogInformation("Example {e}", new Example(7, 11));
```

To serialize an object into the log you need to prefix the placeholder property name with `@`:

```csharp
logger.LogInformation("Example {@e}", new Example(7, 11));
```

From that point, serialization is handled by Serilog's `IDestructuringPolicy` implementations, e.g. a custom `IDestructuringPolicy`, `Destructure.ByTransforming`, _Destructurama.JsonNet_ for NSJ, or [this one](https://gist.github.com/nblumhardt/8aea89e86663829170d08aa573bd0f49) for STJ.

HTH; if you need more info, Stack Overflow's `serilog` tag will be the quickest place to get questions answered around these APIs. Cheers!

Fundamentally, fields in structured logs have names (see overview in https://serilog.net/), which is important for lots of sinks. The other thing in play is that the format string is upward compatible from .NET format strings (e.g. `{0}` etc will work).

The next thing you could potentially run into is that `Log.Information("{} is {}", "a", "b")` involves two names. Someone that knows more of the details will be along in due course, but it seems to me that the change you're suggesting is not an obvious bug with an obvious easy fix that doesn't have any cons.

comments.body:
Thanks for dropping us a line!

When a format specifier appears in a message template (or format string), it's an argument to `IFormattable.ToString(string, IFormatProvider)` on the value being formatted.

`l` isn't a valid format specifier for enums or `DateTime`s, so these types' `IFormattable` implementations throw when `ToString()` is called with this value.

If you replace the `ILogger.Information()` calls with `Console.WriteLine()`, you'll see the exception; Serilog makes a guarantee not to throw exceptions from `ILogger` methods, so the exception in our case is written to the `SelfLog` output instead. You can check this by calling `SelfLog.Enable(Console.Error)`.

Serilog's no-exception guarantee doesn't go any further than that, though. When the exception is hit, logging for that message stops, and Serilog (the console sink in this case) just moves on. We're keen not to clutter the code up trying to handle cases of invalid usage like this, so I don't think this behavior should change.

Switching your code to not use the format specifier, or to use a format specifier that's valid for the target type being logged, will sort this out.

Thanks again for the report, though :+1:  - hope this helps.

The `HttpRequestId` property (or `@TraceId`) can be used to correlate events raised during the request and navigate across to see the larger end-request message with the interesting info. If you haven't spotted it previously, `RequestLoggingOptions.EnrichDiagnosticContext` is the API to check out.

#2090 should get rid of those `HashSet` allocations, it'd be nice to see what other possibilities show up via the profile - keen to keep pushing improvements though :+1:

comments.body:
Hi @alekdavisintel! Thanks for dropping by.

This is a bit of any annoying limitation in how the default message template rendering works. #2011 touches on it, but it's not looking likely to make it into v4 at this stage.

Fortunately, you appear to be using `Serilog.Expressions`, which provides some better options for doing what you're after (and doesn't need `:l` and `:j` etc. - they're the built-in defaults).

In a nutshell, your expression template will look like:

```
[{@t:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.ffffff zzz}] [{@l:u3}] [{MachineName}] [{ProcessId}:{ThreadId}] [{CorrelationId}] [{ClientIp}] [{UserName}] [{ApplicationId}] [{SourceContext}] [{ActionName}] [{MethodName}] {EscapeNewlines(@m)}
```


The change is the `EscapeNewlines(@m)` call; this will be a user-defined formatting function you add when setting up the logger:

```csharp
    .WriteTo.Console(new ExpressionTemplate(
        "the template from above",
        nameResolver: new StaticMemberNameResolver(typeof(EscapingFunctions)))
```

Its definition:

```csharp
public static class MyFunctions
{
    public static LogEventPropertyValue? EscapeNewlines(
        StringComparison comparison,
        LogEventPropertyValue? maybeMessage)
    {
        if (maybeMessage is ScalarValue sv && sv.Value is string s)
            return new ScalarValue(s
                .Replace("\r", "\\r")
                .Replace("\n", "\\n"));

        return null;
    }
}
```

See also: https://github.com/serilog/serilog-expressions/?tab=readme-ov-file#implementing-user-defined-functions

Not tested so you may need to tweak some of this, but should be pretty close. Keen to hear how it goes!

Hi @alekdavisintel,

Currently you need to do:

```csharp

{
    public static NameResolver NameResolver { get; } = new StaticMemberNameResolver(typeof(MyFunctions));

    // As before
```

And:

```json
          "formatter": {
            "type": "Serilog.Templates.ExpressionTemplate, Serilog.Expressions",
            "template": "[{@t:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.ffffff zzz}] [{@l:u3}] [{MachineName}] [{ProcessId}:{ThreadId}] [{CorrelationId}] [{ClientIp}] [{UserName}] [{ApplicationId}] [{SourceContext}] [{ActionName}] [{MethodName}] {EscapedMessage:lj}\n{#if @x is not null}[{@t:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.ffffff zzz}] [{@l:u3}] [{MachineName}] [{ProcessId}:{ThreadId}] [{CorrelationId}] [{ClientIp}] [{UserName}] [{ApplicationId}] [{SourceContext}] [{ActionName}] [{MethodName}] {EscapedException:lj}\n{#end}",
            "nameResolver": "MyNamespace.MyFunctions::NameResolver, MyAssembly"
          }
```

Untested, so may need some tweaking. [Original feature PR](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-configuration/issues/287).

comments.body:
When you set up Serilog, you'll somewhere be doing an `AddSerilog()` or `UseSerilog()` call to wire it into MEL, and/or setting `Log.Logger` to an `ILogger` instance.

You may be able to get what you're after by wrapping this root logger in your own custom type, which would need to implement `ILogger`, `IDisposable`, and `IAsyncDisposable`.

All methods would forward to the wrapped logger, except `IsEnabled(LogEventLevel)`, which would perform some custom check based on an `AsyncLocal`, and `ForContext()`, which would use the same logic as `IsEnabled()` to detect that the current request/activity/whatever is a sampled one, and in those cases, wrap the results of calling `ForContext()` on the inner logger in an additional instance of your wrapper type before returning the result.

Hope this helps!
Nick

Hi @AleyCZ! Semi-related - which IoC container are you using? For Autofac, you can use this https://github.com/nblumhardt/autofac-serilog-integration to have the right contextual logger injected without a generic type involved.

@nblumhardt would be nice to use this as we make everything a primary constructor.
Just allow Serilog.Ilogger<T> in the same way that MEF.Ilogger<T> works.

I find myself often coming back to this issue, and am surprised it is not getting more traction. Do people not want to use primary constructors? Or are they not injecting Serilog.ILogger? Or are they not enriching the logger with the class? How are people using Serilog along with primary constructors?

I'm probably in the minority, but for me, a class's constructor argument list is precious real estate that I don't really want cluttered up with `ILogger<T>`.

Just like we don't thread through allocators, or `TaskScheduler`, or a million other noisy details of the execution environment, I don't usually like threading through loggers. They're a cross-cutting concern, most of the time, so I'm happier using static state and the `Log` class.

`ILogger<T>` also falls apart when a component needs to call a function or construct another component that needs a logger - but with a different `T`.

YMMV, and I do still end up writing code that uses `ILogger`/`ILogger<T>` injection quite a bit, so I'm not against this on principle or anything like that.

FWIW, the `T` part isn't strictly required, it's also possible to have `ILogger` injected with `ForContext()` called behind the scenes, if your IoC container has the hook points to plug it in: https://github.com/nblumhardt/autofac-serilog-integration

I most probalby won't need the redaction sink, but the existance of `LoggerSinkConfiguration.Wrap` is a great hint that looks promising! I just have a fear that it has the same limitation as the enricher, since `logEvent.Properties` in the `Emit` already went through the `PropertyValueConverter` which already stringified it due to the missing `@` (which is exactly my use-case described above). So I assume it will still not allow for enforcing destruction as even when changing the template here, the property is already unusable.

I will still give it a try the next days to ensure my assumptions. The files are generated from ProtocolBuffers, the fields are attributed/marked as hidden. This information is still there in destruction but not after stringification.

As already assumped, this approach is sadly not working since the properties are already processed into a `ScalarValue` loosing all information.

I did some more in-depth debugging and code checks. The issue is that any point the user could hook in (enricher, sinks, ...) is run AFTER the `PropertyValueConverter` already "messed" with the data. So the only possible way is to tamper with the template BEFORE the `MessageTemplateProcessor` (and therefore the default `ILogger`) lays hands on it would be to have an own `ILogger` that wraps the generated `ILogger`. This would need to parse the message template in case any property is of the the wanted type and add the `@` to the property before passing it to the regular `ILogger`. This is a lot of dirty hacking needed for something easily doable (and architecturally intended) to be solved by the `ILogEventPropertyFactory`/`ILogEventPropertyValueFactory` interface (not configurable by the user).

Any one of those changes would allow solving my issue:
* LoggerConfiguration allows to override `Destructuring` per-type passed to `PropertyValueConverter` creation
  * Requires minimal (non-breaking) changes to `PropertyValueConverter` and `LoggerConfiguration`
* LoggerConfiguration allows to override `PropertyValueConverter` with own instance passed to `MessageTemplateProcessor`
  * Requires abstraction of `PropertyValueConverter` since `MessageTemplateProcessor` expects exactly that type which is `internal`
  * Requires minimal (non-breaking) changes to `LoggerConfiguration`
* LoggerConfiguration allows to override `MessageTemplateProcessor` with own instance
  * Requires abstraction of `MessageTemplateProcessor` since `LoggerConfiguration` expects exactly that type which is `internal`
  * Requires minimal (non-breaking) changes to `LoggerConfiguration`

I would vote for option 1 as it's the least intrusive option that would just fit greatly to the architecture that `PropertyValueConverter` already has with minimal changes in complexity. The other two options would mean to make some more stuff `public` that is purely internal logic as of now and increas overall complexity of Serilog which I would avoid.

## Using default behavior (property is `ScalarValue`)
![image](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/assets/940619/d438e30f-093f-45f8-a042-f56573180b2b)

## Using destructure behavior (property is `StructureValue`)
![image](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/assets/940619/f75f1f74-ac40-4b81-9c5e-b7bb545d4922)
I created a PR for option 1 to show that it is aligning with the architecture of Serilog quite well and that it only needs minimal changes.

Hi! Thanks for the follow-up. For comparison, why would you not:

1. Create an `IDestructuringPolicy` implementation for your target types that ignores the "hidden" properties, and,
2. Use redaction to try to catch any accidentally-logged sensitive data that makes it through?

I don't think you can avoid (2) in any scheme, because sensitive information can leak through in pre-formatted strings, exception messages, and so-on.

Consider this:

```csharp
log.Information($"Here is {channel}");
```

There are many variations on this where your custom scalar conversion policy will be circumvented by someone pre-formatting a string.

Redaction is a necessary safety net, and once it's in place, the existing `IDestructuringPolicy` mechanism does exactly what you need.

Let me know if this helps! Thanks for the PR all the same 👍

We already did the destructuring policy, but since it‘s not about exactly one type but hundreds of types, redaction is not possible (only knowing that they use attribution to mark sensitive fields and inherit from a common ProtoBuf type). The logger is injected through DI into multiple assemblies at runtime and the logger at configuration time can not know all types as they are part of the other assemblies.

The PR is only a PoC to convey the idea and I would even need it to work for inherited types and not just one type.

My main problem is, that the `IDestructuringPolicy` is only triggered if the developer is explicitly using @ in the message template. But our framework knows that ever message inheriting from `IMessage`, the ProtoBuf base class, has a custom destructuring that a) ensures the relevant data is in and b) sensitive data is redacted by default. Only if the developer requests stringification using $ the log should use `ToString`.

I can create a MCVE next week to make it more clear. I simplified my initial request to take out some complexity but see now that this lead to confusion. Sorry for that.

I added the MCVE as a separate branch based on the PR to show why it's needed and how it would be used:
[MCVE of destructure fallback](https://github.com/Falco20019/serilog/compare/feature/allow-override-destructuring...Falco20019:serilog:demo/inheritance-override#diff-86f1ea85f8823db5ebf82a426a402d13d27bd9a688919c8a4565aa915176111c)

If you have a better idea on how to solve this issue, I would greatly appreacite to use it instead of needing to change the API.

For context, the `protos/descriptor.proto` is shared and would be in some commonly included place (copied for ease of the example). The `protos/user_credentials.proto` would be specified in another assembly and is not known to the base application. So it's not possible to reference it when defining the logger. The base type `IMessage` is known and would be used for the configuration. The generated logger would be dependency injected into the other assembly containing the generated `UserCredentials` and that would also be the place where the log would happen.

I hope this clarifies a bit my use-case and why redaction is not possible.

I have absolutely no option to modify the `ToString` that's why we need to minimize the risk. We can't circumvent it completely and just have to do our best to have best-possible defaults.

In most cases, we do have another type called `EncryptedData` since we don't use plain-text strings even in memory for sensible data (which marks the data as hidden by default to reduce devs forgetting it). But this is also generated and has the same issue regarding `ToString` (just with the byte array). An `IMessage` can only contain references to other `IMessage` fields or simple data types. That's just how ProtoBuf works.

But there could also be other fields regarded sensitive that are user-defined and not encrypted and those have to be treated as well by the `is_hidden` destruction policy that I added. Right now, we request all developers to make sure to use `@` on log messages. But in my opinion, this will always lead to leaks even if it's part of pull requests to have a second person check that it's done correctly. I would therefore prefer a more secure default, which would by possible to achive when the conversion could be influenced.

I am well aware that there are other possible ways to leak the data (not just through `ToString`), but we have other means in other locations to check for those. Serilog is just one location that might lead to issues the way it's right now for us :)

There was a discussion about this on https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1160 but as you can see, the recommendation is to make sure your logging is taking care of it (which we try right now but there is no easy way to do it with Serilog without message template tampering through an adapter).
@nblumhardt Any more information/input given my last post if you would consider the PR?

Hi! Sorry about the slow turnaround, a bit buried this past week.

I sympathize with where you're stuck, but I think https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/2023#issuecomment-1988038143 is accurate - an optimal solution requires some support in the protobuf implementation for C#.

Given the difficulties with obtaining that, I understand why having some partial fallback support in Serilog would be useful, but what you're proposing is still as fragile as just requiring `@` and a custom destructuring policy. If you can miss one usage of `@` in code review, it's just as easy to miss someone using string interpolation or an explicit `.ToString()` somewhere, which both circumvent the protection you're proposing.

Since there's overhead and complexity involved in adding the feature to Serilog, I don't think it's a good bet, sorry.

> There was a discussion about this on https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1160 but as you can see, the recommendation is to make sure your logging is taking care of it

From what I can tell that thread ends with [a link to a commit adding `debug_redact` support to the proto language](https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/issues/1160#issuecomment-1370085012), so perhaps what you need is on its way? Good luck either way!

I believe https://github.com/serilog/serilog/pull/2024 would also solve my issue described in #1649, where I have no control over the object being logged or the log message template itself. In my case, the logging is coming from a third party library which is not 'structure logging aware', and thus doesn't use `@` anywhere in their log statements, but do pass the full object.
Thanks again for opening this. Closing as not aligned with the current design, but appreciate all the work you put into this and the related PR - thanks @Falco20019!

Thanks for the note. This is a change in ASP.NET Core, rather than Serilog - Serilog has always quoted strings in the default message rendering mode.

I'd love to change this - I don't think it'd be out of the question for a Serilog 4.0 - but for now your best bet is to modify the formatter.

One simple, quick solution is to switch to _Serilog.Expressions_ for JSON formatting:

```csharp
    .WriteTo.Console(new ExpressionTemplate(
        "{ {Timestamp: @t, Level: @l, MessageTemplate: @mt, RenderedMessage: @m, Exception: @x, Properties: @p} }\n"))
```

_Serilog.Expressions_ already uses the nicer message rendering that you're after.

If the code is performance-sensitive at this level, you might instead grab the code for `MessageTemplateRenderer` from:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Rendering/MessageTemplateRenderer.cs

and then embed a modified version of `RenderedCompactJsonFormatter` that uses it (with slightly modified structure and field names) into your project:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog-formatting-compact/blob/dev/src/Serilog.Formatting.Compact/Formatting/Compact/RenderedCompactJsonFormatter.cs

HTH,
Nick

https://github.com/redboxllc/stackdriver-serilog/blob/master/src/Redbox.Serilog.Stackdriver/StackdriverJsonFormatter.cs is only a handful of LoC - your quickest and easiest option would be to grab that file, plus the log level mapping function, and drop it into your app.

```csharp
    ))
    .CreateLogger();
```

Not sure how picky Stackdriver is about levels, you can make a more precise mapping using `if @l = 'Verbose' then 'DEBUG' else ...` etc.

Partially; it's possible to use basic Serilog features today (though the library itself still produces some trim warnings that need suppressing).

```csharp
// Works
Log.Information("Hello, {Name}!", "world");
```

Currently, reflection-based capturing doesn't work:

```csharp
// Does not work
Log.Information("Hello, {@User}!", new { Name = "world" });
```

This could be fixed by adding `[DynamicallyAccessedMembers(DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.PublicProperties)]` to the type parameters on the 1, 2, and 3-argument overloads of the various log methods:

```csharp
    [MessageTemplateFormatMethod("messageTemplate")]
    public static void Information<
        // Add this
        [DynamicallyAccessedMembers(DynamicallyAccessedMemberTypes.PublicProperties)] T
    >(string messageTemplate, T propertyValue)
    {
        Write(LogEventLevel.Information, messageTemplate, propertyValue);
    }
```

With that change, `Hello {@User}!"` works as expected with AOT.

There would still be some caveats:

 * Adding those attributes to `ILogger` would possibly be a breaking change to some degree (needs investigation)
 * Similar generic overloads would be needed for 4+ arguments, up to some reasonable limit (needs investigation, also may be a breaking change depending on the choices made)
 * `ForContext(string, object?, bool)` would need a generic `ForContext<T>(string, T, bool)` variant with annotations
 * It's uncertain whether array arguments or nested properties could be captured (needs investigation)
 * There would always be some scenarios in which the type being captured would be statically unknowable
 * Sinks, enrichers, etc., would need to be reviewed and tested

To move deeper support ahead, someone would need to get immersed in this and put together a fleshed-out proposal.

Unfortunately it's a ship that's sailed; I think our best bet is just to document this in the release notes, and move on.

Since the _s.r.cs.Unsafe_ change, consumers on .NET Core 2.0 and 3.0 will have been locked out of package updates pretty much across the ecosystem, so in practice I don't think people still maintaining code on those frameworks will be very surprised by this, major version bump or not.

(I don't think dropping `netstandard2.0` from the package's TFMs would be a good idea, for the same reason Microsoft probably took this route in the first place: many downstream consumers will still be targeting (only) `netstandard2.0` as a way to reach a wide range supported frameworks, so in order to stop lying about compatibility for obscure and unsupported frameworks, we'd break effective compatibility with all the supported ones.)

I appreciate the heads-up, though. It's nice to have this write-up for anyone who might be searching for an explanation of that error message :+1:

Making the release notes change now.

I totally agree with you that this is going to become increasingly common, and agree the documentation approach is probably the best we can do!

Also agree that dropping netstandard2.0 is probably a non-starter. Interestingly the main reason Microsoft gave for taking the approach is analysers/source generators that _have_ to be netstandard! 

As my post probably makes clear, I mostly find it frustrating that this was hacked into the packages by MS, and means you can't trust anything about supported frameworks on Nuget any more 😞

Follow up on "option 2" from: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/1970#issuecomment-1813118532.

We definitely could conditionally exclude the dependency on _System.Diagnostics.DiagnosticSource_ in the `netstandard2.0` build configuration, and `#if` out the relevant parts of the codebase.

I'd dearly like to avoid that if it's feasible. Serilog just emerged from a long period of slow change in which we accumulated a lot of these, and in 3.0 we managed to clean a good number of them out. I'd like to clean out more: working on code that's full of conditional compilation isn't fun: automated refactorings don't always work, algorithms are hard to follow, and dubious bloat accumulates.

If we end up wanting to ship a 3.1 patch that works on .NET 2.1 and 3.0, I think the way to do it would be:

 1. Create a release branch `release/3.1` from `dev`
 2. Make the changes directly in `release/3.1`
 3. Ship the patch directly from `release/3.1` (modify the build so that release branches are published - don't merge to `main`)
 4. Immediately bump `dev` up to 4.0
 5. Backport any remaining bug fixes to 3.1 as required, until 4.0 ships

It's not an appealing option but there if we absolutely must do it :-)

IMO, it's not worth the hassle. Anyone on 2.1/3.0 is way behind the curve at this point, so I personally think it's ok to chalk this one up to experience, and bear it in mind in any other package updates. At the very least, wait maybe until someone _genuinely_ screams 😄 

I'm just trying to make more people aware of the issue with the MS packages in general tbh, so people consider it when they're adding/bumping dependencies 🙂
Thanks again for the heads-up and all the input 👍

Hi! Thanks for the note, @cargt3.

Memory leaks are _bad_, so we naturally would want to hunt them down. I don't think that's what's happening here, though: it's most likely that by turning `batch` into a massive string, you're causing .NET to increase the size of the heap/LOH, and although garbage will be collected, this isn't immediate nor is it perfect, so the heap won't drop back to its original size in any fixed amount of time.

You didn't mention the versions of Serilog and Serilog.* that you're using, so I tried reproducing with Serilog 3.1.1 and Serilog.Extensions.Logging 8.0.0:

Working set shoots up quickly to 700 MB or so on my machine, despite the string allocations in the loop being only ~60 MB.

I can run this program indefinitely and memory use never increases from there, though.

To investigate this as a leak we'd need some more information on:

1. How memory use behaves when running the test case for a long period of time (e.g. with a load test harness pointing at your /test endpoint), and (if memory steadily increases or the machine OOMs)
2. The state of the heap after running the test for a little while: what types make up the majority of the allocations, and where are they rooted?

Thanks!

That `IsTargetFrameworkCompatible` predicate also looks like a useful technique in general (though the general explicit PropertyGroups per TFM works fine for now)

This is an example from our CI `/project/packages/system.runtime.compilerservices.unsafe/6.0.0/buildTransitive/netcoreapp2.0/System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe.targets(4,5): error : System.Runtime.CompilerServices.Unsafe doesn't support netcoreapp2.1. Consider updating your TargetFramework to netcoreapp3.1 or later.`

I'm really only flagging it because this dropping of TFMs was added in a minor version bump AFAICT, so I would argue is very non-semver 🙈 

If you're not aware of the issue, I wrote about it last year: https://andrewlock.net/stop-lying-about-netstandard-2-support/. The onus is firmly on MS on this one IMO, but library authors don't seem to realise the implications of adding some of these libraries. 

> For what it's worth StackExchange.Redis similarly added a dependency recently and accidentally dropped support, [as described here](https://github.com/StackExchange/StackExchange.Redis/issues/2589#issuecomment-1801901894). 

Just to be clear, I'm not at-all saying you _should_ support .NET Core 2.1 just that "Support" for .NET Standard 2.0 doesn't really get you much IMO. Basically Xamarin and that's it. And it's misleading in NuGet because it looks like you _should_ be able to use it without issues on .NET Core 2.x without issue. So just consider this a heads up 😄

Firstly, thanks for taking the time to note this.

>this dropping of TFMs was added in a minor version bump AFAICT,

No, this is about trimming of specific TFMs when a major bump happens; no such trims have taken place.

On the pending trim list, there's:
- `netstandard2.1`, `net5.0` (both considered to not provide any specific value over supporting `netstandard2.0` and `net6.0`)
- `net7.0` (there's not been any specific benefit identified for providing a specific build for it)

One minor wart is that `Serilog.Sinks.Console` which has just had a `5.0.1` release targets identical TFMs to the core; ideally `net5.0`, `netstandard2.1` and `net7.0` would have been trimmed. (Doing so would have been a good dry run)

@andrewlock Perhaps you might be aware of a good reason not to avoid dropping `netstandard2.1` for a package there are `netstandard2.0` and `net6.0` specific builds?

----

I guess the next question is what someone in your position should be expected to do...

The driving assumption is that given 2.x, 3.x and 5.x are out of support, consumers can either a) use older versions that supported them or b) update to a supported STS/LTS. Is that viable in your case, or do you see another way to resolve the forces?

> No, this is about trimming of specific TFMs when a major bump happens; no such trims have taken place.

Sorry, my comment is a bit of a side-point really, I'll move to a separate issue, I just thought it might be pertinent 😄 

> Perhaps you might be aware of a good reason not to avoid dropping netstandard2.1 for a package there are netstandard2.0 and net6.0 specific builds?

I mean, you can use `Span<T>` in <`net6.0` is the main benefit 🤷‍♂️ But personally I would have favoured `netcoreapp3.1` over `netstandard2.1` in the first place 😄 

> I guess the next question is what someone in your position should be expected to do...
>
> The driving assumption is that given 2.x, 3.x and 5.x are out of support, consumers can either a) use older versions that supported them or b) update to a supported STS/LTS. Is that viable in your case, or do you see another way to resolve the forces?

My case is a special one, because on the Datadog .NET tracer team I'm just _testing_ libraries against a bunch of TFMs. Both of your options are viable and reasonable IMO.

The _problem_ IMO is that the "dropping of support for TFMs" (which _already_ happened when you added System.Diagnostics.DiagnosticSource) should only happen in a major version bump!

>>Perhaps you might be aware of a good reason not to avoid dropping netstandard2.1 for a package there are netstandard2.0 and net6.0 specific builds?

>I mean, you can use Span<T> in <net6.0 is the main benefit 🤷‍♂️ But personally I would have favoured netcoreapp3.1 over netstandard2.1 in the first place 😄

Not talking about the specific APIs that are only available in a given (newer) TFM. I'm wondering if there's a benefit to offering a TFM-specific build independent of whether one would make use of APIs from it, i.e.
- In Serilog core, the `net7.0` build does not do anything different to` net6.0` so it can go
- `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1` also build with identical flags so the plan is to drop `netstandard2.1` specific builds in the next major. I'm asking if you, as someone who has much better appreciation of it all, are aware of a problem that removing it might cause.

>But personally I would have favoured netcoreapp3.1 over netstandard2.1 in the first place 😄

Thankfully I've never had to think about that, and there's no chance of `main` needing to worry about it either!

>The problem IMO is that the "dropping of support for TFMs" (which already happened when you added System.Diagnostics.DiagnosticSource) should only happen in a major version bump!

Yes; I can appreciate that this is the effect. I'm pretty sure this impact was not something that people were conscious of.
The 3.0 release was a cleanup release, and 3.1 is focused on otel integration.

The general philosophy is that the current release (and `main` branch) should focus on supporting as many "current platforms" as practical. The problem is that the assumption that "if you can compile against `netstandard2.0` you cover a lot of consumers" has been proven false.

It would seem that a possible resolution is:
1. put up a notice about the `netstandard2.0` being subject to the "as long as we're not talking .NET core 1.0-3.1" priviso for now...
2. log an issue to `#ifdef` out the `DiagnosticSource` stuff in the `netstandard2.0` (and `netstandard2.1`) builds ; when that's done, the notice can go

Nick (who added the otel integration) will be along in due course and will likely have more complete answers in due course...

👋 I've replied RE the breaking change in #1983 so that we can keep this ticket focused on what our TFM list for vNext will be like. I didn't note the (2) `#ifdef` option over there - thanks @bartelink! - I'll add a note on why I'm not a fan, although it's worth keeping up our sleeves.

> I'm wondering if there's a benefit to offering a TFM-specific build independent of whether one would make use of APIs from it... `netstandard2.0` and `netstandard2.1` also build with identical flags so the plan is to drop netstandard2.1 specific builds in the next major. I'm asking if you, as someone who has much better appreciation of it all, are aware of a problem that removing it might cause.

To my knowledge, there's absolutely no benefit to `netstandard2.1` in this case, and it should be completely non-breaking 🙂 

> It would seem that a possible resolution is:

I agree on both of those, and I think option 1 is the way to go for the sake of everyone's sanity and the longer-term health of the project 😄

We had some discussion in another thread that might cause us to tweak this strategy slightly; quoting @bartelink:

> net6.0 + supported LTS FWs at time of release of any major version, but we trim STS versions, and unsupported LTSes 

I'm just whipping up an initial tiny PR to set dev to 4.0; this ticket could be the next one to follow.

Q. about TFMs in other bits of the infrastructure - I started a PR at https://github.com/serilog/serilog-enrichers-environment/pull/55 a while back with the idea that we could agree on the TFMs for one of the enrichers and then change the others (part of the idea being that having them target things like .NET Standard 1.x seems a waste of time in the main lib doesn't support them any more).
Note sure if those calls should be made based on what Serilog 3 does, or what 4 will do?

In general, the same principles apply
- TFM-specific builds for netstandard2.0, net6.0
- other supported LTS releases can be added, but will be trimmed with every major release of any given component (but see note below about making sure there is a reason for it)
- if core had a net9.0 dep because something new was being used, that does not imply the same is required for any other lib
- similarly, just because core happens to have net8.0 does not mean a new enricher must have a net8.0 build if that's not supported at the time it's being released
- in general, the more TFM specific builds, the more busywork, and it needs to be for a reason. A 3 liner enricher really doesnt need to be compiled 5 times to produce the same IL. Also the more TFM specific builds that are addded and removed over time, the more churn in terms of things that previously resolved to net8.0 suddenly binding to net10.0 or net6.0 etc

The above sort of factors are my reasoning for applying the KISS principle as mentioned in my review comment on core: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/pull/2016#discussion_r1501365476

TL;DR the simplest and most reasonable thing is for core to have netstandard2.0, net6.0 only, and only add anything else when it actually provides a significant benefit. For enrichers and other things, starting off with `net6.0` only is a reasonable default (esp if its not envisaged that people would use them in an environment that only supports netstandard2.0 and/or oyu'd be doing conditional compilation or any other form of shimming)

----

For test assemblies, that's entirely different, you want the min .NET FW, the latest .NET FW, and all supported LTS and STS releases to be covered. For instance, that validates that net14.0, net15.0, net16.0 all function well despite the core assembly only having e.g. netstandard2.0 and net6.0 specific builds.

comments.body:
I think your second statement:

```
Log.Information("Byte array: {@Data}", [| 1uy |])
```

isn't calling the overload of `Information()` that you're expecting - its first arg is a `params` array.

Let me know if this helps :-)

No, that's not it. Here is a modification to the repro that uses multiple values, thereby avoiding that ambiguity. The output is the same as the original example.

```f#
Log.Information("Byte {Kind}: {@Data}", "list", List([ 1uy ]))
Log.Information("Byte {Kind}: {@Data}", "array", [| 1uy |])
```

🤔 hmmmmmm... I think then it will be that byte arrays are processed as scalars (converted to hex strings):

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Capturing/PropertyValueConverter.cs#L68

but other enumerable types (`FSharp.Core.List`?) don't get that special treatment and pass through:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Capturing/PropertyValueConverter.cs#L174

I don't think it's likely to be a bug per se, just the outcome of different types being processed differently - not sure whether/where we'd make any changes to enable a different approach, but if you're able to share some more info about your scenario/preferences it'd be good data to have. Thanks!

> `FSharp.Core.List`?

The repro uses `System.Collections.Generic.List` (typically aliased as `ResizeArray` in F#), though that's irrelevant. The only requirement is that it is not an array.

> if you're able to share some more info about your scenario/preferences it'd be good data to have.

Certainly!

Destructuring _per se_  doesn't help me, so I don't use that. In fact, it would actively hurt me, at least in the first case below.
- A lot of my logging goes to Application Insights, and I really don't want to duplicate big objects between log messages and properties (which significantly increases ingestion costs). In fact, I have a custom wrapper sink for Application Insights that (while preserving the message template itself) replaces the tokens in the message with the rendered values, thereby only sending the final rendered message and the message template to AI, and not any of the message tokens as separate properties.
- A lot of my other logging is done on edge/IoT devices where I log to syslog/logcat but (for data usage reasons) do not transfer the logs out of the device at all (except when there's a problem and I sign into the device to check the logs). Destructuring is pointless here; only the rendered message is shown.

In both of these cases, the only thing that matter to me is the log message. I therefore simply want the rendered log message to be as nicely formatted as possible.

To achieve this, I am serializing most values using custom settings, so they are easy to read. (I used JSON first, but recently switched to YAML because it's even easier to read.)

I use this not only for complex objects, but also single-case discriminated unions ("wrapped primitives"), which are unwrapped using my serialization settings. In general, no matter what I serialize using my "log JSON setting", the output is either better or the same, never worse.

Of course, relative to other performance costs of logging, serialization is a heavy hitter. I used to serialize synchronously and insert the string directly into the log message (`Log.Information("Foo {Bar}", logSerialize myObject)`), but this is wasteful if the log level is not enabled (and in many cases, I logged complex objects at a normally disabled log level). I found out that I could make use of a custom destructuring policy and instead use the destructure operator `@`, which meant that the objects would not be serialized if the log level was not enabled. Also, it's less verbose. So (`Log.Information("Foo {@Bar}", myObject)` would be equivalent to the previous statement, but only serialize if the log level was enabled.

I have not found any other way to accomplish 1) nice custom-formatted complex objects in log messages, and 2) not serializing for disabled log levels.

In terms of this issue, the point is that this destructuring-based approach works wonderfully for everything except byte arrays. Specifically, I'd like to represent them with spaces between the bytes, like `FA 2E C9`, because that makes it easier for me to know "what is byte 5", and easier to paste into other tools we use that accept this format. For byte lists and other byte sequences, it works fine, but the different handling of byte arrays means it didn't work there. This was surprising to me, because there is not just one accepted way to render byte arrays.

Thanks for taking the time to write that! 👍 

I've never been entirely comfortable with our opinionated byte array formatting - the current system came about though because treating byte arrays as lists of bytes was ...... problematic to say the least 😅 ... so something (useful) needed to be done.

Unfortunately, byte arrays are something of an anomaly; most/all "scalar" types Serilog cares about are structs/value objects, which have copy semantics and so can be passed as-is through to the asynchronous side of the logging pipeline, or in the case of `string`, are immutable. Because of this there isn't a great extension point for dealing with byte arrays.

In the past we've considered making `IScalarConversionPolicy` a public/pluggable extension point, along the same lines as `IDestructuringPolicy`, which would potentially sort out your scenario, but it's a nontrival bit of infrastructure to design and maintain without a broadly-relevant set of use cases. This could be something to explore more deeply but probably requires quite a lot of effort.

Depending on how much control you have on the application side, constructing a proxy type such as:

```csharp
record struct ByteArrayProxy(byte[] Bytes);

Log.Information("Some {Data}", new ByteArrayProxy(myBytes));
```

and then targeting it with an `IDestructuringPolicy` would be a possible workaround. (Forgive the C# syntax :-))

Hope this helps.

Thanks for the clarification!

I am indeed wrapping the byte array as a workaround (in the `Some` case of F#'s `option` type, which using my serialization settings is unwrapped).

In any case, what I really want is to be able to control how Serilog formats values of arbitrary types. The fact that I'm using destructuring is just because that's the only way I found. If it would be possible to add a way to let users specify formatting of arbitrary types (e.g., pass `obj` and let the user decide how to transform/stringify it), then that would solve my problem in a less hacky way, would allow me to use destructuring for actual destructuring (if I ever need that), and would also mean I don't have to remember to use `@` everywhere (easy to forget, leading to bad output, and I don't see that before I actually see an example of the relevant log message, which is in some ways the worst kind of error).

The reason to use destructuring or enrichment is that Serilog does capturing on the foreground thread (at the point the event is logged), but formatting on a (potentially) background thread. By the time the data reaches the formatting stage it's already been snapshotted; this is how mutable things like arrays end up logged with the right contents (and race conditions/threading bugs are avoided). HTH!

> Duplicate #1335 - would still love to see a case-insensitive match.

@tillig didn't saw that. thanks for linking.

Somewhat related - serilog/serilog-settings-configuration#386 found that the parser for the log level enum in configuration was inconsistently case-sensitive and case-insensitive, and that got resolved to be case-insensitive everywhere. That makes things just slightly more inconsistent: enum parsing is case-insensitive, but the keys are case-sensitive.
Why can't this be a 'flag' ? Give the developer the option?

Does anyone have comparative perf numbers for performing the level check in case-insensitive vs sensitive mode? I think that's the place we're most likely to hit issues.

I don't think it's a matter of preference, I'd guess (almost?) everyone would be fine with insensitive matches if they performed identically, so keen to steer clear of flags/options at this stage.

v4 is open now, so a good time to look at this if we think it's got a chance :)

Was going to look at this, just coming up with some simple benchmarks, but wanted to verify I'm benchmarking the right thing.

It appears the case-sensitivity comes in when checking if there is a level override for a particular context.

So that means [`Serilog.Core.Logger.ForContext()`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/4bd40f1241057ebeed2062811d4990236be48ba5/src/Serilog/Core/Logger.cs#L140) which calls [`Serilog.Core.LevelOverrideMap.GetEffectiveLevel()` and checks `context.StartsWith()`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/4bd40f1241057ebeed2062811d4990236be48ba5/src/Serilog/Core/LevelOverrideMap.cs#L71). The thing we want to see is if case sensitivity meaningfully impacts the `context.StartsWith()` call.

If I'm not mistaken, that boils down to just determining the difference in perf between

- For systems that don't have `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, [`String.StartsWith(String)`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.startswith?view=net-8.0#system-string-startswith(system-string)) and [`String.StartsWith(String, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.startswith?view=net-8.0#system-string-startswith(system-string-system-stringcomparison))
- For systems that have `ReadOnlySpan<char>`, [`ReadOnlySpan<char>.StartsWith(ReadOnlySpan<char>)`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.memoryextensions.startswith?view=net-8.0#system-memoryextensions-startswith-1(system-readonlyspan((-0))-system-readonlyspan((-0)))) and [`ReadOnlySpan<char>.StartsWith(ReadOnlySpan<char>, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.string.startswith?view=net-8.0#system-string-startswith(system-string-system-stringcomparison))

Does that sound right? Is there some other string comparison or larger path that needs to be benchmarked? Would benchmarks simply comparing those two methods be enough to inform a decision?

Oh, looks like [there's already a nice benchmark set up](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/test/Serilog.PerformanceTests/SourceContextMatchBenchmark.cs) for source context matching, so I can add to that.
Oh, I see why this is. It's the `[SimpleJob(RuntimeMoniker.NetCoreApp21, baseline: true)]` on the `SourceContextMatchBenchmark` job. Might need to update that to run something newer as the baseline.

Rather than stick the `.StartsWith` methods in a tight loop, I just went straight for the `SourceContextMatchBenchmark` because that already had the test for `LevelOverrideMap.GetEffectiveLevel` in place. I ran it three times on the `dev` branch.

- Serilog code unmodified - case insensitive search, but not explicitly specified.
- Use `context.StartsWith(str, StringComparison.Ordinal)` - explicitly specify case-sensitivity.
- Use `context.StartsWith(str, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` - explicitly specify case-insensitivity.

| Case Comparison                  | Method                             | Job      | Runtime  |        Mean |     Error |    StdDev |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------- | -------- | ----------: | --------: | --------: |
| Case Sensitive/Default (Current) | Filter_MatchingFromSource          | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 | 1,629.12 ns | 17.992 ns | 16.829 ns |
| Case Sensitive/Default (Current) | Filter_MatchingFromSource          | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 | 1,177.59 ns | 13.127 ns | 12.279 ns |
| Ordinal (Explicit)               | Filter_MatchingFromSource          | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 | 1,554.08 ns | 25.342 ns | 23.705 ns |
| Ordinal (Explicit)               | Filter_MatchingFromSource          | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 | 1,182.60 ns | 13.657 ns | 12.775 ns |
| OrdinalIgnoreCase (Proposed)     | Filter_MatchingFromSource          | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 |  1,627.5 ns |  15.69 ns |  14.68 ns |
| OrdinalIgnoreCase (Proposed)     | Filter_MatchingFromSource          | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 |  1,146.3 ns |  14.48 ns |  13.54 ns |
|                                  |                                    |          |          |             |           |           |
| Case Sensitive/Default (Current) | Logger_ForContext                  | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 |   460.96 ns |  4.398 ns |  4.113 ns |
| Case Sensitive/Default (Current) | Logger_ForContext                  | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 |   313.29 ns |  2.276 ns |  2.129 ns |
| Ordinal (Explicit)               | Logger_ForContext                  | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 |   468.31 ns |  5.497 ns |  5.142 ns |
| Ordinal (Explicit)               | Logger_ForContext                  | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 |   320.15 ns |  4.472 ns |  4.183 ns |
| OrdinalIgnoreCase (Proposed)     | Logger_ForContext                  | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 |    485.5 ns |   4.53 ns |   4.02 ns |
| OrdinalIgnoreCase (Proposed)     | Logger_ForContext                  | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 |    325.0 ns |   2.09 ns |   1.74 ns |
|                                  |                                    |          |          |             |           |           |
| Case Sensitive/Default (Current) | LevelOverrideMap_GetEffectiveLevel | .NET 6.0 | .NET 6.0 |   106.44 ns |  0.851 ns |  0.796 ns |
| Case Sensitive/Default (Current) | LevelOverrideMap_GetEffectiveLevel | .NET 8.0 | .NET 8.0 |    73.03 ns |  0.602 ns |  0.503 ns |

Things to notice:

- I'm on a Mac, so I can't benchmark .NET desktop framework. I also couldn't get `netcoreapp3.1` or lower to work for reasons I can get into at another time. I'll submit a PR to update a few things in the build and explain it there.
- .NET 8 is definitely faster than .NET 6, consistently.
- Explicitly specifying case-sensitivity doesn't change anything.
- Specifying case-insensitivity has a non-zero perf impact, but it's only really obvious the closer you get to `GetEffectiveLevel`, and it's on the order of 20ns. The benchmark runs `GetEffectiveLevel` on nine different contexts, so that's about 2ns per lookup, averaged out.

If my logic is sound, that basically means it's a question of whether case-insensitivity is worth a 2ns hit per level lookup.

My opinion is that it's a pretty negligible hit to make this consistent across config and logging, but it _is_ a microperf (nanoperf?) hit, so that may make a difference.

Let me know if I should still look at benchmarks for just the string methods.

Awesome, thanks for doing this @tillig.

It's a bit tricky to draw precise conclusions from the benchmark because it mixes results from a variety of cases (some where the logger triggers an override immediately - which bails out of the check early - some where it doesn't, or will trigger further down the list).

It thus might be that the ~20ns you mention is attributable to one or two of the cases, and not across the board. Just making a note of this, and thinking we might want to tweak the benchmark in the future, but at first glance the difference isn't enough to rule out the change :+1:

There's also the possibility that we might be able to improve the performance of the level override map with some other tricks, such as computing a pre-filter based on the first character or two from the context name.

E.g. if my overrides are `System....` and `Microsoft....`, Serilog could potentially skip the lookup for any context that doesn't start with `s` or `m`. `Regex` has some optimizations for doing these kinds of things that could be leveraged - we'd probably have to go that far to beat the vectorized string ops that are likely being used behind `StartsWith` and friends 🤔 

I wouldn't suggest trying to roll this into the case-insensitivity PR, but could be worth keeping up our sleeves.

Are the developers here open to this suggestion? And if so, can we help in any way?

Hi @ProximaB and @Corniel,

I've been working on a Go port of Serilog called [mtlog](https://github.com/willibrandon/mtlog) with an accompanying analyzer. While it's for a different language, our [mtlog-analyzer](https://github.com/willibrandon/mtlog/tree/main/cmd/mtlog-analyzer) experience might offer useful insights for a Roslyn analyzer.

**Key features that proved essential:**
- **Automatic fixes** - Property naming conventions, constant extraction, argument count corrections
- **Severity levels** - Errors (breaking), warnings (likely mistakes), suggestions (best practices)  
- **IDE integration** - Real-time validation significantly improves developer experience
- **Flexible suppression** - Kill switch for all diagnostics or suppress individual warnings as needed
- **Gradual adoption** - Configurable checks and severity downgrading for legacy codebases

**Common issues our analyzer catches:**
```go
// ❌ Template/argument mismatch
log.Information("User {UserId} logged in from {IP}", userId)

// ❌ Duplicate properties
log.Information("User {UserId} did {Action} as {UserId}", id, "login", id)

// ⚠️ Repeated string literals → suggests constants
log.ForContext("user_id", 123).Information("Login")
// Quick fix: const userIDKey = "user_id"

// 💡 Complex types without capturing hints
log.Information("User: {User}", user)
// Suggests: {@User} or implementing LogValue()
```

The analyzer has been invaluable for catching template errors at compile time and enforcing consistent logging practices. Happy to share more implementation details if helpful.

The referenced implementation for Roslyn gives you most of that, and I'm am willing to do the implementation. But a nuget package has to be created, documentation pages to be hosted (explaining the rule violations) That is stuff I most likely do not have the rights for.

I can't speak for that, but if there is anything I can do to help with design, or testing, please let me know. I've been diving deep into Serilog related editor integrations lately and these topic are very interesting to me.

Hi all! Sorry about the patchy availability here, I'm taking a short break and only jumping online sporadically. Back to full speed late next week.

This sounds like a problem unique to _Serilog.Settings.Configuration_, to me. Using some kind of static factory method or constructor should enable this without too much additional machinery. It's slightly awkward, but it's also a fairly niche scenario.

The other solution, which I personally prefer, is to just configure the sink in code, and pull the dynamically-varied configuration from your own custom configuration section (probably just a couple of flat values that identify the Graylog endpoint). Simple and reliable :-)

>   if you look at how the graylog sink consumes the options class, it is too late to change properties of the configuration instance.

I 100% understand that and already told about that particular case. Serilog code _may_ expose suggested new APIs to configure sinks in **any** way sink **supports**.

>  is to just configure the sink in code

Or couse, but the more interesting question is about how to provide additional tuning when starting entirely from `ReadFrom.Configuration`. In my practice I have always configured such sinks from code.

Pros and in the same time cons of suggested `ConfigurationReaderOptions.OnSinkCreated` design is that it works only for sinks constructed from that configuration API. But what is more important is that you still have no access to created sink. You can not write such API because configuration project does not create sinks explicitly, it calls extension methods which add sinks, see `ApplySinks` method from configuration repo.

I'm happy leaving this discussion open if it might flush out some workable solution, but I feel like direct access to sinks goes against the grain of the Serilog design, which deliberately hides them so that sinks can be implemented using techniques like wrapping, which would get in the way of this kind of usage.

Take for example the way `Serilog.Sinks.Async`, `Serilog.Sinks.PeriodicBatching`, or `Serilog.Sinks.Map` work - in those cases the actual type of the sink added to the logging pipeline isn't the one you might expect, and there's no single/sensible way to get at an "inner sink" in those cases, since the inner thing might not even be a sink itself (the periodic batching case) or might be created deep inside a separate piece of infrastructure (the map case).

For these reasons I think it's a ship that has sailed. There are definitely other ways Serilog could approach this, with various pros and cons, but because a design has been chosen I think a solution would need to embrace the decisions that have already been made.

Since _Serilog.Settings.Configuration_ is calling those sink creation extension methods, perhaps instead of looking to access the raw sink, an extension point could be created there for resolving parameters to the extension method?

E.g. `OnCollectSinkArgs(string sinkName, IDictionary<string, object?> args)`? (Likely to itself require some design of course :-))

Hope this helps,
Nick
Just for information - I updated proposal in #1930 with the latest changes  from `dev`.

```fsharp
type LogEnricher() =
  interface ILogEventEnricher with
    member this.Enrich(logEvent, propertyFactory) =
      let prop k v =
```

Thanks for raising this. Unfortunately I think what you're observing is the intrinsic behavior of async-local data in .NET; it's not to do with inheritance but rather the way that child tasks inherit async-local data from their parent (there are some not-immediately-intuitive aspects to this, such as the children being arranged in a tree rather than a stack, that complicate things significantly).

The code that's adding the quotes is in [`Serilog/Events/ScalarValue.cs`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/19d8b1a0b947d70adc7539dbb88772e1410bbab6/src/Serilog/Events/ScalarValue.cs#L66-L79), which is not part of the JSON construction (which is over in [`Serilog/Formatting/Json/JsonValueFormatter.cs`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/19d8b1a0b947d70adc7539dbb88772e1410bbab6/src/Serilog/Formatting/Json/JsonValueFormatter.cs#L559), but part of the message rendering.

_Serilog.Expressions_ is the answer to all formatting questions with Serilog :-)

```csharp
using Serilog;
using Serilog.Templates;

Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .WriteTo.Console(new ExpressionTemplate(
        "{ {Timestamp: @t, Message: @m, Level: if @l = 'Information' then undefined() else @l, Exception, Properties: @p} }\n"))
    .CreateLogger();

Log.Information("I am a {thing}, {attributes}.",
    "teapot",
    string.Join(" and ", "short", "stout"));
```

The default (only) rendering for `@m` in the template shown above is `:lj` style.

comments.body:
Hi! This is not a bug but rather that the argument to `log.Information()` is a [message template](https://messagetemplate.org), not a plain string. `{{` and `}}` are the escape sequences in that language for single `{` and `}`.

To do what you want you can:

```csharp
log.Information("{Result}", resultAsString);
```

Or if you want to do structured logging, skip the JSON serialization altogether and:

```csharp
log.Information("{@Result}", res);
```

HTH,
Nick

In our code we use `UseSerilog` for registration extension, and injecting ILogger<T> to classes with DI.
How can I configure the logger to use the suggestion you wrote?

In general with Serilog, you should never be using the string interpolation (`$`) operator
Perhaps `:lj` might be what you're after, see the formatting wiki https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Formatting-Output#formatting-plain-text
>And what was recently changed? We used to log all of our objects with interpolated string and without template - and everything worked fine

Very little chance anything changed - there's massive usage and you hear about stuff instantly if there's anything even subtly different (this rarely happens though; the maintainers of te core are at this a long time and have skin in the game)
I'd say the likelihood is that you've gotten lucky through some coincidences; the first argument has absolutely always been a message template.
To trap this and other issues, https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=Suchiman.SerilogAnalyzer is fantastic too

@omerron This is simply contrary to how it works. It cannot be made to work. Don't do it.
Read https://serilog.net/ (it stresses that first arg is a message template and what flows from that)
While there is low level hacking that can be done with message interpolation (overloads that get IMessageFormat stuff etc) to unmangle things, thats seriously error prone and anyone that goes down that road comes back
Please stop digging and move on ;)

Next step is to close this, do:

    log.Information("This is the result: {@result:lj}", resultAsJson);
   
and put expected vs actual in a StackOverflow question tagged `serilog`, mentioning your sinks and their config - I've not battled this in any so this is simply not the best place for you to figure out the best solution for you

Agree with @bartelink .

@omerron Think of it as SQL injection. You use a data (string that you want to be logged) as not a data but as a "flow control sequence". This string is interpreted in a special way and under certain conditions (data/config dependant) even _may_ call arbitrary malicious code.

@bartelink @sungam3r I am not sure I understand why it doesn't log it correctly.
I just give it a string as parameter, this string happen to contain a serialized JSON in it - why it doesn't log it properly?

The parameter is a `string`, but the format MUST be a message template. Message templates have tokens in them for fields, that open with `{`; those semantics require quoting (by doubling) if you want to use a brace as a literal. Just like for `String.Format` (it has the same semantics, try it).

But seriously, you've been told enough times. Time to read and/or accept.

> why it doesn't log it properly?

Because the nature of JSON's content **inside** that string parameter contradicts with semantics of that parameter which is used as message **template**, i.e. format string. You cannot safely set any value to this parameter from an unknown or uncontrolled source. Once time again - this is **not** plain text to log, this is message **template** to interpret/parse.
thanks

comments.body:
Serilog uses [FullName](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.type.fullname?f1url=%3FappId%3DDev16IDEF1%26l%3DEN-US%26k%3Dk(System.Type.FullName)%3Bk(SolutionItemsProject)%3Bk(DevLang-csharp)%26rd%3Dtrue&view=net-7.0#definition)

> Gets the fully qualified name of the type, including its namespace but not its assembly.

, not [AssemblyQualifiedName](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.type.assemblyqualifiedname?view=net-7.0), see https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/7f1e791c411457eb392a9b4833a5545a90a67ba7/src/Serilog/Core/Logger.cs#L164
I added repro project at https://github.com/yohny/SerilogRefiRepro where the logging issue can be observed

See

https://github.com/reactiveui/refit/blob/246ee8d9989c29092fdaba6821d5b3098a5ccf9e/Refit/UniqueName.cs#L47

and

https://github.com/reactiveui/refit/blob/246ee8d9989c29092fdaba6821d5b3098a5ccf9e/Refit.HttpClientFactory/HttpClientFactoryExtensions.cs#L50

This is refit implementation of http client name. Then this name will be mapped/used as Serilog's `SourceContext` somewhere in internals of `Serilog.Extensions.Logging` package IMO. Note that you inject MEL `ILogger` instead of Serilog's `ILogger`.

@nblumhardt may help more here than I.

Serilog maps MEL's logger name to `SourceContext`. It seems that this isn't always a type name.

In Serilog also, `SourceContext` is just a strign, it's not strictly defined as always being a `FullName` but that's the general default.

You can work around this by implementing an `ILogEventEnricher` that you plug in using `Enrich.With(...)`; in the enricher, you can first retrieve the `SourceContext` property, trim it as required, and then update it back on the `LogEvent`.

Hope this helps!
