I would add new `SelfLog`-like property and some switch to use either old `SelfLog` or the new one (+ optionally deprecate old `SelfLog`).

> I would add new SelfLog-like property and some switch to use either old SelfLog or the new one (+ optionally deprecate old SelfLog).

In my opinion it would be "more breaking" and complicating the solution.
Simply adding log level is also breaking, but fixing it is very simple and obvious - it is just matter of setting appropriate log level for all WriteLine methods - the compiler will not pass missing parameter.

Another quicker and more efficient option might be to just send PRs to the two projects listed in the original report for a conditional "verbose diagnostics" switch - worth serious consideration, since landing changes in two sinks will be much faster and more effective than trying to land changes in the hundreds of others already written.

> landing changes in two sinks will be much faster and more effective than trying to land changes in the hundreds of others already written

And hundreds of already written would still use selflog improperly. This fix would make it clear how to use selflog. And adapting to new requirements would be really easy for those libraries.
SelfLog is only really intended to be switched on when you're diagnosing a problem, so the current usage is probably correct across the board, to be fair.

At risk of branching out the discussion, I'm seeing a need for both Level and more context, such as the exception, the logger type/name and ideally any additional properties the SelfLog writer wants to include. Similar to a standard log event really.

### Why
We notify ourselves on Slack on SelfLog events, so we can be aware of logging issues.

This is currently a bit spammy and additional context would help us filter spam and provide more details for diagnostics:
- There is no context about the class that had problems or the severity of the problem. We need to use regex to filter out messages we can't do anything about.
- There is no exception details, which would help diagnose the sink if it was related to say JSON serialization exception, HTTP request or writing to disk.
- Additional context, for example [Serilog.Sinks.Logz.Io](https://github.com/serilog-contrib/Serilog.Sinks.Logz.Io) sometimes report 403 Bad Request on SelfLog. It would be possible for the sink to include information about the HTTP request and response in this case, if this is not already made available via the exception.


### Example of SelfLog event that could be Info/Warn level

I'm not sure if this is a bug in the sink configuration, or if this is a common scenario that should be Info/Warn level and could be ignored.

We get this log event twice from SelfLog on startup when using [Serilog.Sinks.ApplicationInsights](https://github.com/serilog-contrib/serilog-sinks-applicationinsights).

```
2023-03-28T08:07:23.0821036Z Ignoring added logger provider Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.AspNetCore.Logging.ApplicationInsightsLoggerProvider
2023-03-28T08:07:23.1435203Z Ignoring added logger provider Microsoft.ApplicationInsights.AspNetCore.Logging.ApplicationInsightsLoggerProvider
```

From what I can tell, this sink is trying to add a Microsoft logger provider and `SerilogLoggerFactory` warns about ignoring this, since I assume it would result in duplicate log events when using `UseSerilog()`.

https://github.com/serilog/serilog-aspnetcore/blob/bf4ae072f7472d285c72f9a43f3eb4920e743110/src/Serilog.AspNetCore/AspNetCore/SerilogLoggerFactory.cs#L63-L70

```cs
    /// <summary>
    /// Adds an <see cref="T:Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILoggerProvider" /> to the logging system.
    /// </summary>
    /// <param name="provider">The <see cref="T:Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.ILoggerProvider" />.</param>
    public void AddProvider(ILoggerProvider provider)
    {
        SelfLog.WriteLine("Ignoring added logger provider {0}", provider);
    }
```

### Proposal: New SelfLog.Write methods and new SelfLog.OnEvent callback

The new methods would be opt-in and the old methods backwards compatible.

- Add type `SelfLogEvent`, a simpler variant of `LogEvent` without templating and where property dictionary is `object` instead of `LogEventPropertyValue` to not support rendering of values.
- Add `SelfLog.Write` methods similar to `Serilog.ILogger.Write`, without templating and where properties must be explicitly specified - no ambient context.
  -  `SelfLog.Write(SelfLogEvent)`
  -  `SelfLog.Write(LogEventLevel, string message, Type? source)`
  -  `SelfLog.Write(LogEventLevel, Exception?, string message, Type? source)`
  -  `SelfLog.Write(LogEventLevel, Exception?, string message, Type? source, IDictionary<string, object>?)`
- Add `SelfLog.OnEvent` method with callback that includes the additional properties in a `SelfLogEvent` type.
- `SelfLog.WriteLine` writes to `SelfLog.Write` with `Error` level and `null` for the other values.
- `SelfLog.Write` invokes both `SelfLog.OnEvent` and `SelfLog.Enable` callbacks, backwards compatible.
- Obsolete `SelfLog.WriteLine`, instruct to use new overload
- Obsolete `SelfLog.Enable`, instruct to use new overload


### Related issues

An open PR proposes to include the exception details if a log event fails, but this would not include any exceptions inside the sink itself:
#1651

Good ideas - in the past I've had a desire to be able to flag Async Sink buffer overflows (i.e. notifying when events were being jetissoned) too - we had Async emission to a File sink, and >= error emission to the console (that would egress via k8s/nomad host). The Console sink was assumed to be failsafe, so warnings from other sinks were routed there.

Something like what you outlined ☝️ might allow the Async Sink to emit notifications OOTB which you can then wire to a failsafe sink (vs having to handwire it via the notiification APIs I added, which I trust have very low usage levels system wide). The PeriodicBatching Sink also has relatively similar needs. Any reboot of the Async Sink based on Channels should also be considered in such a design.

@nblumhardt Wouldn't it be just another SelfLog but different way? Just like adding a few new arguments to SelfLog. How will it prevent from misusing SelfLog? In my opinion there should be a single, good solution for selflogging instead of two solutions. This will lead to misunderstanding.

The difference in thinking is might be that to me there _is_ a single good solution for self-logging, it's just not the feature you were originally looking for. SelfLog really is just intended to be turned on when a problem has to be debugged, it's not supposed to be collected and acted on in production scenarios, despite it being possible to do so.

SelfLog isn't just lacking the `level` argument, it's got no actionable semantics at all, except for "here's something you might look at if logging isn't working for you". Exceptions propagate from SelfLog subscribers; there's no system of sinks not susceptible to recursion/stack overflow, etc.

Delivery monitoring and failover is often requested without any mention of SelfLog, but when you dig into both kinds of requests - failing over to secondary sinks, or being alerted when logging fails, and a more complex SelfLog - there's a common thread that's worth exploring.

Hi everyone! For anyone still tracking this, I've spiked out #2018, which introduces:

```csharp
public interface ILoggingFailureListener
{
    void OnLoggingFailed(
        object sender,
        LoggingFailureKind kind,
        string message,
        IReadOnlyCollection<LogEvent>? events,
        Exception? exception);
}
```

I don't think it came out too badly; I think the information provided to listeners will cover just about everything in this thread, including making failures clear and distinct from "information" messages, writing events to fallback sinks, and because failure listeners are configured per-sink, there's no danger of "fallback inception" if the listener wants to forward events on through another Serilog pipeline.

Feedback and ideas welcome!

Thanks for dropping by!

The performance comparison is meaningless unless the custom file logger has equivalent features to Serilog: message template capturing, a concurrent structured logging pipeline with enrichment, etc. etc..

There's definitely still room to beat Serilog's performance using newer .NET features, but there's not much point comparing performance unless you're matching features. Bottleneck finding is always welcome though, so if you do figure out any specific ways Serilog could improve by all means please do let us know :-)

Just in case it helps you to reach your perf goals - you're using the Serilog file logger in blocking mode, you should [let it buffer](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-file/blob/dev/src/Serilog.Sinks.File/FileLoggerConfigurationExtensions.cs#L108) if you're comparing to a buffered implementation. You'll also then need to `CloseAndFlush()` before taking your perf measurements after making that change.

You might need to whittle your test code down to a minimal repro to figure out why you're not seeing all logs despite increasing the buffer size. It's possible there's some problem in the way the async sink works, but there's a lot of code still in your test harness, so it's quite likely once you start simplifying you'll find the problem there. Interested to hear what you find, either way!

Hope this helps,
Nick

Hi @Mohammad-Moussa-Haidar -

There's always going to be a problem if the log source produces events faster than the sink can emit them. When you're logging in a tight loop, that's always going to be the case - it's much faster to allocate events in memory than it is to write them out to disk.

When this happens there are three possible outcomes -

 * You fill up RAM and eventually OOM
 * You drop events
 * You wait for the sink to catch up

Serilog steers you towards the latter two and gives you the choice which you prefer.

(You might have another option which meets your requirements - obtain a much faster disk 🤔)

In normal applications though:

 * The app actually does something, so rarely if ever will generate logs fast enough to saturate disk
 * The most important performance number is the added latency on the application/logging side, which Serilog.Sinks.Async deals with quite well (on the sink side, only throughput really matters in this case)

Not sure if there's much more I can add but hopefully you find a solution to fit your requirements - all the best with it!

Thank you @nblumhardt, I will evaluate the options I have and go with the best. feel free to mark this issue as closed.

Thanks again and best regards,
👍 keep us posted! Thanks @Mohammad-Moussa-Haidar

Hi Juliano! Thanks for the note.

It's all really going to come down to someone actually needing/wanting an OTEL sink enough to do the research and build one, right now. In the past, every relevant log destination (hundreds of them) has ended up with Serilog support that way. OTEL isn't any different - if someone wants it I think they'll build it whether there's an open issue or not :-)

The challenge is that like all standards, OTEL for logging is something of a lowest-common-denominator. For example, given that a Serilog sink already exists for Elasticsearch that understands all the intricacies of Elasticsearch clusters, indexes, etc., it's not likely anyone would choose a generic sink instead. The situation with other services is similar - I think this might only really change when new/exclusively OTEL logging destinations start to appear.

Are you planning to use a server/service for which OTEL would be the best transport, or where no useful Serilog sink currently exists? Or even just super interested in exploring OTEL? If so, that would be a golden opportunity to help shape something up. If you can stand up a GitHub repo and start hacking away on it, I'd be keen to help you identify useful prior art and unblock any issues that you hit. Let me know if so!

For example, given that a Serilog sink already exists for Elasticsearch that understands all the intricacies of Elasticsearch clusters, indexes, etc., it's not likely anyone would choose a generic sink instead. I can only speak for myself here, but I think you are very wrong on this one. There are huge benefits to using a OTEL sink compared to something like Elasticsearch: it keeps your entire codebase vendor-agnostic, while drastically simplifying the setup.

In conjunction with an external collector like the OpenTelemetry Collector Contrib project, you can then centralize your vendor-specific exports in a single place, even if the target monitoring application doesn't currently support the OTEL protocol natively. This collector can also scale independently as needed.

This is actually the current setup we are experimenting with: every application exports telemetry data using OTEL protocol, and we host a collector instance per environment that redirects everything to Datadog.

> Are you planning to use a server/service for which OTEL would be the best transport, or where no useful Serilog sink currently exists? Or even just super interested in exploring OTEL? If so, that would be a golden opportunity to help shape something up. 
If you can stand up a GitHub repo and start hacking away on it, I'd be keen to help you identify useful prior art and unblock any issues that you hit. Let me know if so!

As mentioned above, we are already fully embracing log exports using OTEL. For these projects, we are currently using the native basic `ILogger` implementation. Right now, the lack of a native OTEL sink would prevent us from using Serilog unless we relied on [the ILoggerSink indirection](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Serilog.Sinks.ILogger/). I would probably not be able to justify working on a brand new sink myself since that workaround would probably work.

I still want to explore using Serilog though even if just for the enrichment API.

comments.body:
The message template you supply must be a valid [message template](https://messagetemplates.org).
In 
```
Log.Debug(str);
```
You are passing something that's not a message template.

The solution is to instead do
```
 Log.Debug("{message}", str);
```

https://github.com/Suchiman/SerilogAnalyzer/ provides hints and tips on this and other similar issues

Originally, it was without parameters。

I want print to file like bellow
```
[11:35:52 0HMKCIGTQP9A4:00000003 DBG] {
  "redirecturl": "https://test.com/Code?template={para1}&code={para2}"
}
```

> `Log.Error("[Serilog Error] " + msg);`

should be `Log.Error("[Serilog error] {message}", msg)`, but really it's not a good idea to use Serilog within a SelfLog handler - better to simply do a Console.WriteLine to avoid the potential for that to get stuck in a loop.

At this point, I really think it would be best to move this out to stack overflow and past a link here before closing - right now Nick and I will receive emails regarding responses, and your intent is not obvious to me.

Once again from me though - the first parameter for Log.Information/Debug/Write etc is a message template - it gets parsed and `{` and `}` have meaning. Therefore if you are seeking to feed a string with potential embedded tokens, like you clearly are, you need to pass that as the second arg: `Log.Debug("{message}", stuffThatMightHaveBracesInIt)`

Scanning your info, I don't see what you're trying to suggest overall; Clearly something is causing the outputs you are seeing, but it's really a matter of narrowing down exactly how it arises. If it was solely down to Serilog, you'd be able to show that in a very small repro indeed, but there's no reason to believe it's the direct cause (you'd see others reporting the issue with a clean repro if that was the case.)

There are a few things that can cause this sort of issue - memory corruptions from unmanaged code in the same process, filesystem issues, etc... Unfortunately although Serilog's in that pipeline somewhere, there are many components that could be the source of this.

One thing I'd check out is whether the null characters always start or end on a 4096-byte (page) boundary; this would put the problem closer to the filesystem (flushing issues, buggy virtual/network disk driver, ...).

If the position of the null blocks is entirely random then I'd look more for in-memory causes.

We're extremely interested in finding and fixing bugs in Serilog, but in cases like this where reproduction is difficult and Serilog not clearly the cause, we'll only be able to make progress if you are able to pinpoint the problem at your end, unfortunately.

Nick

title: How to customize file names when writing logs

comments.body:
Howdy!

Serilog's API doesn't use `.*` in namespace prefixes; try:

```csharp
.MinimumLevel.Override("Remora", LogEventLevel.Warning)
```

To completely disable a source:

```csharp
.Filter.ByExcluding(Matching.FromSource("Default"))
```

The `ConfigureLogging()` block won't have any effect on Serilog - this is MEL's configuration entry-point. Serilog and MEL are both full logging frameworks that can each support the _Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions_ `ILogger<T>` API, they don't share code or configuration behind the scenes.

I have modified the code to the following:
```cs
    .UseSerilog((hostingContext, services, loggerConfiguration) => loggerConfiguration
        .MinimumLevel.Information()
        .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(Matching.FromSource("Microsoft"))
        .Enrich.FromLogContext()
        .WriteTo.Logger(lc => lc
            .MinimumLevel.Information()
            .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(Matching.FromSource("Remora"))
            .WriteTo.File(
                DiscordBotSingleton.GetDiscordLogFileName()))
        .WriteTo.Logger(lc => lc
            .MinimumLevel.Information()
            .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(Matching.FromSource("MyBot"))
            .WriteTo.File(
                DiscordBotSingleton.GetDiscordBotLogFileName()))
        .WriteTo.File(
            DiscordBotSingleton.GetMicrosoftLogFileName()))
```

Now Hopefully the Discord.log file will contain only Remora logs, the MyBot.log file containing only logs to my code, while Microsoft.log contains logs to everything under the Microsoft namespace (example being Microsoft.Extensions.Hosting, Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection, etc).
Will `LogEventLevel.None` be implemented?
I do not think it will, but I hope it will though.

title: Add LogEventLevel.None to mirror Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.LogLevel.None.

There's no way for Serilog to accurately interpret MEL's configuration (attempting to do so in simple cases like this one would be misleading). Serilog's configuration system uses the `"Serilog"` section instead.

comments.body: Thanks for the feedback! Probably not something we will be able to make major changes for, but do check out `CreateBootstrapLogger()` in _Serilog.Extensions.Hosting_ - its purpose is to implement a reconfigurable logger that has the properties you're looking for.

On (2), I think you can reorder things very slightly and use:

```csharp
BootstrapLogger.Reload(_ => loggerConfig); 
Serilog.Log.Logger = BootstrapLogger.Freeze();
```

which will eliminate any overhead for loggers created from that point onward.

On (1), in practice, if you set `Log.Logger` on the very first line of `Main()` it's enough to beat most other static initialization including field initializers in other types.

Since `Main()` is usually a tiny method without much of a runtime role to play, I tend to use `Log.X()` without worrying about `ForContext()`, but you might also just assign a local `var logger = Log.ForContext(typeof(Program))` in there somewhere early, and use that.

HTH,
Nick

Yes, that works, thanks a lot for your help!

Log.Logger is not set on the first line of Main because that's done in a common method that's called from the static constructor, but in practice I haven't yet found any types that are not logging because they were initialized too early, so it's probably fine, as you say.

comments.body: Looks like it _eventually_ frees those references, after some time longer than half an hour and shorter than four hours. Is there a way to clear the cache?

Hi @kjkrum ,
This is usually happens when you pass dynamic strings for the message template parameter. 
Instead, use placeholders for dynamic parameters, so the message templates will be static and won't grow unexpectedly:
https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Writing-Log-Events#message-template-recommendations

@skomis-mm I'm already following that practice.

When searching for this issue, I found [this comment](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/1579#issuecomment-843611736) on another issue:

>Serilog wasn't designed around a static instance - short-lived and throwaway loggers are fully supported.

That is not true if the MessageTemplateParser is static and can't be cleared.
Just realized that and facepalmed. Thanks.

On further reflection, I think this should be reopened but possibly changed from a bug to an enhancement request. Even though loggers are intended to be used with templates, and the number of templates may be small, a leak is a leak. A static cache does not fit with the stated design intention of supporting throwaway loggers.

I'd also argue that caching anything by default violates the principle of least surprise. Logging raw strings should not result in templates being cached. The solution could be as simple as not creating and caching a template if there are no params, or automatically using a template that gives the raw strings a name, equivalent to `LogInformation("{raw}", str);`.

@kjkrum the cache size is limited to 1000 templates; do you have an object count of significantly > 1000 for class `MessageTemplate`?

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Pipeline/MessageTemplateCache.cs#L69

In Microsoft.Extensions.Logging, there are also a 1024 cache for `LogValuesFormatter`, but they cache the formatter only if `(values != null && values.Length != 0 && format != null)` [link](https://source.dot.net/#Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions/FormattedLogValues.cs)

I think convert template without property directly to text token make some sense, performance wise, and when person not careful. vs ide also has a analysis rule warn user if template is not a static expression [CA2254](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca2254)

Thanks for the additional input. Just looping back to add some more explanation:

>  The solution could be as simple as not creating and caching a template if there are no params, or automatically using a template that gives the raw strings a name, equivalent to `LogInformation("{raw}", str);`.

Serilog's APIs don't accept raw strings - whatever is passed to `Information()` etc. is a message template, even if it doesn't have any params.

E.g. consider:

```csharp
Log.Information("I know about templates and use {{ to log a literal left brace");
    - > I know about templates and use { to log a literal left brace
```

Hopefully this illustrates why these kinds of changes wouldn't be valid.

SerilogAnalyzer can detect and flag the logging of raw strings at development time - highly recommended if you're in a large codebase that suffers some problems here.

>  a leak is a leak. A static cache does not fit with the stated design intention of supporting throwaway loggers.

The cache is per root `Logger`, not static, just in case you meant literally `static` here.

Even at 1 kB per unique template, if the logging API is misused, we're probably talking about something close to 1 MB, which is unlikely to show up as a performance issue. If the API is used correctly (i.e. with message templates and not strings), the cache might be closer to a few kB for many apps.

If you're seeing more templates in memory than the cache limit implies, it's also possible that your process simply hasn't GC'd yet (.NET will often defer GC for a long time, when memory pressure is low), so that's another avenue to explore. Do let me know if you track this down to any kind of unintended leak, of course! :-)

I'll close this now as I think Serilog's behavior strikes a good balance across many different, and sometimes demanding, usage scenarios. It's always up for reconsideration, but we'd need a really well-researched, complete, high-performance alternative before there's any chance of making changes in this area.

comments.body: Thanks, Thomas; unfortunately the interpolated string handler API doesn't account for parameter names, which substantially reduces the quality of logged events. There are a few past discussion threads in this repo and elsewhere on the different approaches and workarounds attempted so far, but none really satisfactory. If you think we might have missed something new in the .NET 6 functionality let us know, though! 👍

Further down the page about interpolated string handlers is an example of how to deal with format strings.
With a similar approach one could also add property names I imagine.

There's nothing stopping you doing a proof of concept as a set of extension methods, is there?

One thing I'd point out is that if you follow the tutorial, one thing I got from it is that there should not be many cases of the same message template being used at multiple places in a codebase - i.e. after reading it, I've rarely had trouble correlating a location back to a code location.

That's interesting, @kulakovt - I hadn't considered `CallerArgumentExpression`, here.

Worth some more thought. I'm still unsure about how easy it would be to create low-quality structured log events this way, but given the frequent (mis-)use of interpolated strings as logger arguments, there may be some value in it nonetheless.

Couple of things to think about:

 * Any ideas for property names when the hole looks like `{1 + 1}`?
 * Will analyzing property names lead to perf problems?
 * Will constructing message templates with string builders on-the-fly lead to performance problems?

> Any ideas for property names when the hole looks like {1 + 1}?

Now, in case: `logger.LogInformation($"{1 + 1}");`
`AppendFormatted` will receive `value = 2, name = "1 + 1"`. I believe this behavior is simular to Serilog (with manual template parsing). 

> Will analyzing property names lead to perf problems?

This is entirely the work of the compiler. After compilation, all property names will be just a string constants in the assembly. There is no penalty for runtime.

- [Andrew Lock about CallerArgumentExpression](https://andrewlock.net/exploring-dotnet-6-part-11-callerargumentexpression-and-throw-helpers/)

> Will constructing message templates with string builders on-the-fly lead to performance problems?

By the way, [this method](https://github.com/fedarovich/interpolated-logging-demo/blob/master/InterpolatedLoggingDemo/StructuredLoggingInterpolatedStringHandler.cs#L37) uses a new overload
`StringBuilder.Append(ref System.Text.StringBuilder.AppendInterpolatedStringHandler handler)`
This overload also uses the new string interpolation mechanism.

The author of the [origin repository](https://github.com/fedarovich/interpolated-logging-demo) (@fedarovich) wrote an article about this approach. There are some comparisons and benchmarks there:

- [Structured Logging and Interpolated Strings in C# 10](https://habr.com/ru/post/591171/)

>I believe this behavior is simular to Serilog (with manual template parsing).

The point is that in normal real Serilog, you write `Log.Information("The value is {total}", 1 + 1)`, and the json is reliably always `[{"total": 2}]`. There is no "with manual template parsing".

If there isn't a proper workable solution that reliably gives a stable property name even with refactoring, that's a risk as you can't simply throw an exception to say "you passed 2+2, please use the special named syntax `{2+2:total}`" etc. Even if something like Serilog Analyzer was to trap these cases, it's still dangerous. 

What do I mean by dangerous? The fact that bad log entries not obeying the intended structure are silently propagating through the stores. If anyone has searches that rely on the structure, they can get broken. Or, if I am doing random queries that presume the presence of a field called `"total"` in the message, I can go a long way down the rabbit hole before I go on an an angry `git blame` chase ;)

While I personally can't see a clean way around that as it is, I'm not saying it's necessarily impossible - someone may have a good way to manage it, and/or a small tweak or extension to the C# string interpolation facility might provide a way to e.g. hook up a warning if one does not supply a name etc etc

- [String Interpolation in C# 10 and .NET 6](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/string-interpolation-in-c-10-and-net-6/) by Stephen Toub — a lot of under the hood details and  performance optimizations.

@kulakovt I'd have to try but...

The rules match String.Format rules, i.e. `Log.Information("The value is {0}", 1 + 1)` is acceptable and names the field as `"0"`

Also consider that these conventions are also honored by NLog and MS.Extensions.Logging.

So my guess is that the field would be named `"1+1"`, and some search engines would cope well with it whereas others would not, but it is missing the point - nobody would want a message field to be named something other than a meaningful string - it's entire purpose is to be a _name_ used to identify a field for humans and/or humans generating search queries for alerts or dashboards etc.

I have read the article you linked, but the more relevant article in this case is to read the motivation and flow in https://serilog.net to understand why the name of the field being stable is pretty fundamental to structured logging, and no amount of syntactic sugar for the 90% case can outweigh losing trust in the thing being straightforward, consistent and reliable.

Thanks for all the follow-ups!

@kulakovt -

> >  Will analyzing property names lead to perf problems?
>
> This is entirely the work of the compiler. After compilation, all property names will be just a string constants in the assembly. There is no penalty for runtime.

The interpolated string needs to be converted into a message template in order to work with Serilog (and much of the ecosystem). It's not possible to construct a valid message template that has a property named `1 + 1`, so your example of `"The value is {1 + 1}"` would be rejected by Serilog today.

Message templates need to have a fixed syntax that can be parsed by other tools - if the property names could be any C# expression, then the message template grammar would end up being a superset of C#, much like the interpolated strings themselves.

To avoid this, Serilog would need to scan through the text of the expression being passed through, to determine whether it could be used directly in a message template, or would need some kind of escaping or replacement. This is where the perf issues might start to creep in - we'd need some kind of caching to avoid having to do this every time an event is logged. Definitely need some further investigation of this.

> > Will constructing message templates with string builders on-the-fly lead to performance problems?
>
> By the way, this method uses a new overload
> StringBuilder.Append(ref System.Text.StringBuilder.AppendInterpolatedStringHandler handler)
> This overload also uses the new string interpolation mechanism.

When you write a log event like `Log.Information("Hello, {Name}", name)` today, Serilog gets the template `"Hello, {Name}"` as a fully-formed string, that the C# compiler embeds into your program binary. It passes this string down the pipeline as the message template text.

Interpolated string handlers don't see the whole message template in one go; they'd need to build it up from the parts that are incrementally seen by the `Append*()` methods. This could be beneficial in some ways - Serilog has to do the opposite, and pull the template apart into its components by parsing - but we'd again need some caching mechanism to avoid a whole lot of allocation on every logging call.

All fun stuff to explore and figure out!

I do sympathize strongly with @bartelink's point of view regarding the quality of events; structured logs are much more useful when property names are consistent and well-thought-out. But, this still requires knowledge and effort using Serilog today, so perhaps if we dig deeper and see just how good the interpolated string-based approach could be made, we might come up with some net-wins? Worth some thought, anyway :-) ...

(I'm wondering whether we can use some of C#'s other caller member attributes and/or source generators to drive the caching and property naming requirements... 🤔.)

I agree that name consistency is very important for structured logging. On the other hand I've seen so many times how interpolated strings were used instead of structured logging, so I think the suggested approach can be quite useful.

At the moment [my proof of concept](https://github.com/fedarovich/interpolated-logging-demo) does not handle expressions or even method calls. One of my ideas is to use additional `format` parameter in `AppendFormatted`. In this case we can specify the custom name like format (e.g. `LogInformation("{1 + 1:SomeName}"`). I guess it can work quite well together with a custom Roslyn analyzer, but I'm not sure whether it would be easy to create good and efficient analyzer for this use case.

Thanks for dropping by, @fedarovich!

The main problem with `LogInformation("{1 + 1:SomeName}")` is that it's already quite common to use formatting with log messages, e.g. `LogInformation("{1 + 1:x8}")`. It'd be surprising if this printed a decimal number, and captured a property called `x8`.

Format strings are tricky because they're completely free-form and don't have any escape mechanism, but it'd be possible to work around this to some extent by figuring out an _almost format string_ grammar that adds capturing hints (`$`, `@`) and names, while being esoteric enough that it'd be unlikely to collide with realistic format strings in the wild (and would need some way to disambiguate, also).

Imagining we adopted `|` as the end-of-format-start-of-capturing-info character, we might then end up with `LogInformation("{1 + 1:|SomeName}")` and `LogInformation("{1 + 1:x8|SomeName}")`, for example, while a format string with a `|` in it might need doubling `||` to circumvent this mechanism. Support for `@` and `$` would be along the lines of `LogInformation("{1 + 1:|@SomeName}")`.

Or something like that :-)
(Fixed a typo in the last comment after posting, in case you read the initial version via email...)

I totaly agree with important role of property names. My heart bleeds when I imagine that we can approve camelCase rule for property name instead of PascalCase (if the string interpolation approach wins). But I believe that this is not the topic of this issue. Because in the current version of Serilog this is valid code (this will work):

`logger.Information("Hello {1+1}", 1 + 1);`

We have no way to prevent a user from doing this. They can always write the wrong names. It doesn't depend on string interpolation or the "classic" approach. That's why it's a topic for another discussion.

Now [MessageTemplateParser ignores](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Parsing/MessageTemplateParser.cs#L216) this invalid property name. This behavior can also be applied to property names from interpolated strings. Although I would prefer a compilation error.

> I'm wondering whether we can use some of C#'s other caller member attributes and/or source generators to drive the caching and property naming requirements...

Shure, we can solve a lot of issues with source generators. It can:

- stop the build if message have invalid property name or number of parameters
- parse message template during build time and cache it
- enrich message with static information (message id, project name, line number)
- check `LogEventLevel` before real work
- avoid some kind of reflection
- etc

Another great article from Andrew Lock:

- [Improving logging performance with source generators](https://andrewlock.net/exploring-dotnet-6-part-8-improving-logging-performance-with-source-generators/)

But this topic for another discussion :)

> LogInformation("{1 + 1:|@ SomeName}")

Looks too complicated. Maybe people don't need such sophisticated cases? I suppose, in this situation we can recommend them to extract the expression into separate variable (with a nice name). It will be useful for Serilog and code readability too. Otherwise, the current behavior will be applied (don't treat this part as a property name).

Thanks for the reply!

> Because in the current version of Serilog this is valid code (this will work):

It's not valid Serilog usage, though:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/342712/147165950-4f085897-3cde-4c19-b052-53dbb87b9eaa.png)

But the interpolated version that looks similar definitely is valid use of an interpolated string, so it'd be strange to do something other than capture the property somehow, in the interpolation case.

> We have no way to prevent a user from doing this. 

We reject it via the message template parser you've linked - any API can be misused, but we don't want to let invalid data propagate through the logging pipeline.

> we can solve a lot of issues with source generators

We'd need to solve the specific problem of unnecessary work at the call site; Serilog rejected the idea of log events as annotated functions on static classes early on (SLAB pioneered this), I think we'd need to figure out how to keep close to the current API.

> Maybe people don't need such sophisticated cases?

Worth considering --- Serilog is very much about sweating the small stuff, and achieving a predictable and consistent user experience, though. To meet that bar, ideally,

 - all uses of interpolated strings in logger calls would need to capture property values predictably (even if we fell back to indexers rather than names in these cases),
 - interpolated strings would need to behave pretty much identically to how they would with e.g. `Console.WriteLine()`, and
 - there should be some reasonably non-disruptive way to opt into core Serilog features like capturing with `@` or `$`, and assigning names to values.

Failing that, we might create more of a mess by having to give advice like: "use interpolation in these situations; use message templates in these others".

What do you think the chances are of being able to build an out-of-band package that tries out some ideas, by offering extension methods that sit alongside the Serilog API? Seems like it would be a nicer way to experiment with different ideas/patterns, before adopting anything in the core project.

@nblumhardt out-of-band package with extension methods would be good option and for the abstractions like MEL. Unfortunately, overload resolution prefer signature with string interpolation handler only if method defined on the target type which makes the feature less useful.

I would argue that the implementation should be done as an extension to the Microsoft ILogger interface as opposed to a single implementation.  I have an example here which also supports the use of functions to safely resolve parameters. Also to get around the `$"{1 + 1}"` issue you can leverage the "format" field and use that to name the parameter `$"{1 + 1:Calculated}"`. In fact you could argue that it would be better to force the explicit naming of the parameter via the format placeholder because the suggested structured logging convention is to use PascalCase as opposed to camelCase. In most situations the value you want to pass in is going to be a camel cased local variable.

https://gist.github.com/bronumski/8ffbd37b9446794be4acc5a9a810c776

Thanks for sharing ISLE, @fedarovich! I don't think anything's moving forward here in core Serilog just now, but I'm still watching this space keenly.

Closing the ticket as stale, but further comments/suggestions/feedback here is welcome.

@nblumhardt  One could consider to NOT create a message with parameters and rather just output a single string to Serilog. And with StringInterpolatedHandler it can be done in a highly performant way. And **it will work exactly as before**, and way more performant in case the logger is disabled (which is quite likely for trace/debug).

For most of my projects I stay away from parameter bases log messages and the log messages is written with interpolated strings. This is of course not mordern idiomatic logging, but far from all programs requires this kind of setup. I would guess most programs are not backed by a modern log processing system like Prometheus.

comments.body:
After further review, this seems to be due to AsyncLocal context only "flowing downstream" as in this [Stack Overflow post](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49232514/why-does-asynclocalt-return-different-results-when-code-is-refactored-slightly).  In the failing test with AddLogContextPropertiesAwaitAsync() being async, the LogContext.PushProperty happens "downstream" of the calling sync context.  When the calling sync context is picked up again in ContextPropertiesPushedInAsyncMethod_Fails by another thread and then writes the log, the AsyncLocal will not contain the "downstream" change.

Additionally the reason why the first example works is because it's [eliding async and await](https://blog.stephencleary.com/2016/12/eliding-async-await.html) by returning the task without awaiting it and thus is viewed as though it were a regular synchronous method by the context

So that explains why this is happening, but is this desired/expected behavior?  You essentially can't use PushProperty inside async methods and return the disposable for a using statement which will then have the code with logging inside it.
Thanks for the follow-up - yes, this is expected behavior, it's unfortunately one of the ways in which the async/await abstraction leaks a bit.
Ok, thanks for the confirmation...we'll have to rework our code with this in mind.

comments.body: Update:  Same problem occurs using any version of VS Code (Windows or Mac)

Sorry to be a bother but is there any update on this one?  Am I the only one with this issue using VS Code?  Otherwise, I need to swap out my Serilog for another logging tool which I don't want to do.

Guessing it's something to do with the tools for VS Code looking for a particular line of log output to indicate that the app has started. There was a bug raised against this for VS (I think they changed a regex to fix it) but no idea if the same change filtered down to VS Code. Could be a setting/something configurable on that platform. HTH!

To add more color, VS Code monitors the console output to look for a specific regular expression defined in your `launch.json` under `serverReadyAction`, so if you don't write to the Console at all (as it seems to be your case) or if your write to the Console using an output template that doesn't match what's in the regex, then the browser is never launched.

```json
"serverReadyAction": {
  "action": "openExternally",
  "pattern": "\\bNow listening on:\\s+(https?://\\S+)"  <<<<<<<<
}
```

Writing to the Console should be enough for the browser to be launched by VS Code using the default RegEx that comes with the default template nowadays (I know.... Don't shoot the messenger though, complain to the VS Code folks! 😄 ):

```
builder.Host.UseSerilog((ctx, lc) => lc
    .WriteTo.Console());
```

If that doesn't work and the RegEx doesn't match, you can either change the RegEx, or change the output template to match the RegEx (hacky and not my recommendation, but works):

```csharp
builder.Host.UseSerilog((ctx, lc) => lc
    .WriteTo.Console(outputTemplate: "{Level:w4}: {SourceContext}[0] {NewLine}      {Message:lj}{Exception}{NewLine}"));
```
Thanks @augustoproiete !  This did work for me.

comments.body: Seems to be related to #348, however I feel that Serilog should catch/handle this.

Hi @matthiaslischka ,
indeed, reflection on span api is not supported yet, [see](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/main/src/libraries/System.Memory/tests/Span/Reflection.cs).

As a workaround you can specify custom destructure policy like
```csharp
.Destructure.ByTransforming<ReadOnlyMemory<byte>>(x => new { x.IsEmpty, x.Length, Span = x.Span.ToArray() })
```

We probably should handle this type of exception even if `CanRead` is true. @nblumhardt what do you think?
:+1: some kind of `SpanTypesScalarConversionPolicy`, perhaps?

> 👍 some kind of `SpanTypesScalarConversionPolicy`, perhaps?

The problem that ReadOnlyMemory<>/Span<> are generic types. We can't use reflection api to handle them like we do with ValueTuple<> because of `NotSupportedException`, unless specify all kinds of closed types statically (as workaround we can handle subset of them of most commonly used like (ReadOnly)Memory<char|byte>))

Ah, yes - thanks, I see why a policy won't work :-)

We could hook in at https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Capturing/GetablePropertyFinder.cs#L33 and check the property type's generic type definition before yielding properties? (Some pros/cons vs attempting to handle the exception...)

Keen to dig in but short on time just now, so I might be missing more obvious things. Definitely does seem like one to fix, though.

The main con with `GetablePropertyFinder` is opt-in exclusion. We can't be sure if another new type today or in the future won't throw NSE that will result on bad `Serilog` user experience, given fast and short release cycles of .NET. 

Handling `NSE` prevents that. When Reflection API will work  (aforementioned issue is open) on Span/Memory types `Serilog` code will work without modification.

Both can be combined with custom `ByteMemoryScalarConversionPolicy`-like policy if we wan't to support some of them.

comments.body:
Thanks for the note. The #485 workaround is imperfect - `Log.CloseAndFlush()` here won't be closing/flushing the first two loggers.

[`ReloadableLogger` from Serilog.Extensions.Hosting](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-extensions-hosting/blob/dev/src/Serilog.Extensions.Hosting/Extensions/Hosting/ReloadableLogger.cs) is a more recent take on this, which better handles this scenario. Still may be some corner cases to flush out from it, but eventually this should move towards the core Serilog package. It'd be great to hear how it goes for you, if you're able to pull it in and give it a try.

Thanks for the reply.

>  Log.CloseAndFlush() here won't be closing/flushing the first two loggers

Will `Log.CloseAndFlush()` _never_ flush subloggers, or just in this particular configuration?

`WriteTo.Logger(ILogger)` will never close/flush the passed-in sub-logger; there's no way to instruct Serilog to take ownership of the logger, currently.

A `dispose: true` optional argument might help, but in cases like `WriteTo.Logger(someLogger.ForContext<T>(), dispose: true)`, the contextual logger that's passed in won't be meaningfully disposable, anyway.

The `WriteTo.Logger(callback)` overload does close/flush the created logger, since it's fully owned by the parent logging pipeline.

HTH :-)

@kpato Based on the stack trace you provided, the error is happening in the Mongo DB C# driver when Serilog tries to read the values of properties you passed in as arguments.

```
System.InvalidCastException: Unable to cast object of type 'MongoDB.Bson.BsonString' to type 'MongoDB.Bson.BsonDateTime'.
at MongoDB.Bson.BsonValue.get_AsBsonDateTime()
```

I suggest you report this error to the Mongo DB C# driver devs: https://github.com/mongodb/mongo-csharp-driver#questionsbug-reports

The issue is in WithExceptionDetails enricher. 
When you log some of mongo exceptions (e.g. MongoAuthenticationException) it tries to destruct all exception's public properties. The problem is that some of them are values from MongoDB.Bson with many public properties like (AsBoolean, AsBsonArray etc.).
To solve this particular problem please use Serilog.Exceptions.MongoDb or remove WithExceptionDetails enricher.

Howdy! Thanks for the note.

Unfortunately, `Destructure.*` policies only apply when "destructuring" (applying capturing directives `{@...}` or `{$...}`), and not when capturing regular properties via plain `{...}`. You'll find that the behavior is consistent from this angle. It's a bit sad not to be able to apply this across the board, but this was one of the trade-offs that had to be made when implementing the feature.

When using .NET format string syntax `{0}`, only one property is being captured, so it's invalid to include multiple different capturing directives against the same property in the one template.

To get the behavior you are looking for, a custom `ILogEventEnricher` plugged in alongside `ToMaximumStringLength()` should be sufficient.

HTH!

This is the ol' covariant-`params`-array-binding gotcha: when you pass `result` as an array, C# binds that to the single `params object[] args` argument in `LogInformation(template, args)`.

Serilog's own `ILogger` works around this, but the _Microsoft.Extensions.Logging_ `ILogger<T>` does not (pros and cons to both approaches). If you use `Log.Information()` (or inject a Serilog `ILogger` instead), this will work as expected.

@DaleyKD Can you capture two memory dumps (one after your app starts up, and one after a period of time has passed)? This will help identify what objects are not being GCed.

You should be able to do this with Visual Studio: https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/profiling/memory-usage?view=vs-2019#collect-memory-usage-data

I can get the visual representation, but I can't seem to find a way to output it nicely.  Here are some screen caps:
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7206282/118690279-860b5380-b7cd-11eb-8924-2641004d93f9.png)
![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7206282/118690321-93284280-b7cd-11eb-8e8e-82665b325055.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7206282/118691369-a2f45680-b7ce-11eb-888c-23cf6c74254a.png)

Howdy! Serilog wasn't designed around a static instance - short-lived and throwaway loggers are fully supported.

The gotchas that emerge when you create multiple `Logger`s arise from the state held by sinks. E.g. if you create 1000000 SQL server sinks, they'll be creating 1000000 `SqlConnection`s, if you create 1000000 file sinks, they'll be holding onto 1000000 open files, etc. :-)

Sinks also sometimes hold onto exclusive locks, end up registered for callbacks, etc. etc.

Using a single logger is generally the way to avoid having to think about or deal with these kinds of issues, so that's why we frequently recommend it.

For example, in your case you may be able to `PushProperty("TenantId", ...)` onto `LogContext`, and then use `Serilog.Sinks.Map` to manage a pool of SQL Server sinks by mapping tenant ids to connection strings in the mapping function. (Definitely want to set a limit on the number of open sinks when configuring `Map()` in this case, though.

If there is a bug behind this behavior though, it will probably be one of:

 * Your code is not disposing the right root `Logger` returned from `CreateLogger()`
 * You're using an IoC container that tracks `IDisposable` objects, and not using lifetime scopes to clean them up (this is the case in some MEDI configurations)
 * The MSSQL sink is allocating a resource like a connection from a connection pool that isn't fully released on disposal

Getting a count of the objects on the managed heap by type will reveal which of these it is, if it's any of them.

HTH!
 *

comments.body: Hi! `:l` is a format that is interpreted by Serilog for event messages; if you specify any format for a `DateTime` property it'll need to be a valid .NET DateTime format string (`o`, `yyyy-MM-dd`, etc.) HTH!

Hi Nicholas, 
Just to clarify, I was not trying to format a datetime using literal per se. The point I was trying to make was using the literal modifier in any value type e.g. `Log.Information("value:l}={value}", 2, 2) `causes the logger to truncate the output. 

A bit of background on my part would help: I have a library wrapping Serilog providing an interceptor logger and a logging filter (ASP net core) whereby you can specify the serialization type for arguments and return type (being a generic library I support  `omit | destructure | toString | literal | type` ). Obviously when used this interceptor or log filter the arguments of these methods/controllers could be anything, so while unit testing the Serilog output I noticed the log events being concatenated because it doesn't handle value types formatted as  literal well.   

There is an easy workaround by using standard formatter check: `if value.GetType().IsValueType == true `=> use `{value}` instead of `{value:l} ,` so not a big deal but I thought, given the fact the user would choose the serialization type somehow arbitrarily the output truncation is an issue, so the logger should probably ignored the (literal) format rather than cause truncated output.
Ok that explains the behavior... I will restrict the use to string types then. Thanks.

comments.body:
Thanks for getting in touch.

The current thread discussing this is: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/1468

Duplicate of #1436, #1417, #1232, and #682

Thanks for taking a look.
#1417 and #1468 are the other way around. #1436 and #682 are close, but I wanted to change the level per thread, whilst the level switch is global.
As you see, there is a certain group of users that want this functionality. Maybe, there is some way of using the existing class by default, but also allowing for a more flexible, albeit costly approach?

Thanks for the follow-up. Yes, it's definitely an interesting scenario - it's just that `LoggingLevelSwitch` might not be the place to look for an implementation (for perf reasons it'll probably never have virtual or dynamically-dispatched members).

Another possibility - with a few more lines of code - would be to create a wrapper/delegating implementation of `ILogger` (let's call it `OverridableLogger` for want of a better name).

```csharp
Log.Logger = new OverridableLogger(
    new LoggerConfiguration().WriteTo.Console().CreateLogger());
```

This internally would keep an `AsyncLocal<LogEventLevel?> _minimumLevel`, and you'd provide some (probably static) methods for manipulating it in some scope:

```csharp
using (OverridableLogger.OverrideMinimumLevel(LogEventLevel.Debug))
{
    // _logger somehow descended from the root `OverridableLogger`
    _logger.Debug("helo!");
}
```

The implementation of `OverridableLogger` wouldn't have to be particularly complicated, it'd forward most methods to the underlying `ILogger` passed in its constructor, but:

 * careful implementations of `IsEnabled()` and `Write()` would need to check for a local override first, and
 * `ForContext()` would need to wrap the resulting loggers in `OverridableLogger`s too.

Couple of tips:

 * `Dispose()` would need to be implemented, and delegate to the wrapped logger if it implements `IDisposable` itself, and
 * To get an event through the underlying logger even when its level is "too low", you may need to try casting the logger to `ILogEventSink` and calling `Emit()` rather than `Write()`.

Definitely some experimentation involved, but would be really interesting to see and probably make an excellent gist to help others with the same requirements.

HTH!
Please, have a look at https://github.com/serilog/serilog/pull/1550. Sorry, I didn't find a "squash" option.

Thanks for the note; most of the time, if you find something is sealed or internal, it's because we want to limit the surface area for which Serilog has to maintain backwards compatibility.

Thanks for your reply, @marekott; sorry about the slow response.

I think [_Serilog.Expressions_](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-expressions#formatting) is the best answer to all output-related issues like this :-)

The template you need is along the lines of:

```
WriteTo.Console(new ExpressionTemplate(
    "{ {Timestamp: @t, Level: @l, MessageTemplate: @mt, Exception: @x, Properties: RemoveTypeTags(@p)} }\n"))
```

where `RemoveTypeTag()` would be [a user-defined function](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-expressions#implementing-user-defined-functions) and should only need to do the (slightly more expensive) type tag removal if properties have structured values.

(You need to plug in the user-defined function via the `ExpressionTemplate`'s `nameResolver` argument - there's an example at the link above.)

Would be great to hear how this goes! If `RemoveTypeTags()` is widely-enough used, we may be able to build an implementation of it into _Serilog.Expressions_ at some point.

@Jaegermeiste because the assertion of local time <timezone> is made by the administrative role in user space.  the actual UTCDateTime is not knowable (or not revealable) without it being and offset from local time zone.  Even using system time as UTC is still an administrative assertion from user space.  Having the kernel space reveal the actual system time without user assertion would require an execution chain that is culpable of accuracy without a user space assertion.  there would be no responsibility sharing with platform system administration trust root.

To me, this is a very interesting intellectual topic because we are melding (1) geographical domain with (2) time domain.  From my perspective we always do it.  We've always done it. Thinking more deeply, this makes for a complex interface.  

All systems I've worked with have always required an assertion of TimeZone.  Maybe there are reduced-surface area kernels that can run on hardware that are replete of any concept of time zone.  from a threat modeling scenario, asserting the absence of the possibility of timezone in all kernel space would (seem to me) reduce surface area for confusion type attacks and repudiation of +/-23:30 "Real Date" occurrence wiggle room when the TZ was "set wrong".  an execution kernel would have the concept of human time, just not the side-channel of asserting its geographic location.  The datatime would't be running on UTC, but whatever absolute atomic time that its upstream sync gave it.

comments.body: Thanks for the note; this isn't a Serilog core issue but relates to how _Serilog.Exceptions_ is capturing `Data`. Raising this on Stack Overflow and checking out the Serilog.Exceptions issue tracker for previous discussions should help turn up a solution. Good luck with it!

> this isn't a Serilog core issue

To be clear, this happens when I use `JsonFormatter` such as

` ITextFormatter jsonFormatter = new JsonFormatter(renderMessage: true);`

and **it** (*the formatter*) upon a specific error returns invalid json.

So are you saying that  `Serilog.Formatting.Json.JsonFormatter` is not considered a `Serilog` operation? The error does not happen unless I use the above class. Or is the root of the issue the `Exception parser`?

Hi William, thanks for the reply. "Serialization" in Serilog is split into two roles:

 * the "capturing" side (which _Serilog.Exceptions_ implements) controls how .NET types `Exception` are mapped to the more limited, JSON-like internal data model represented with `LogEventPropertyValue`, and
 * the "formatting" side (`JsonFormatter`, here) writes out whatever that model represents in JSON text.

The problem you're hitting is on the capturing side - by the time the event gets to `JsonFormatter` all we have is a structure with key `"System.Object"` and value `null`, which it's faithfully recording in the JSON above.

Capturing is tricky because of problems like circular references, as you've observed; exceptions in .NET are particularly nasty to serialize as JSON, hence _Serilog.Exceptions_ is a substantial project in its own right.

Probably a bit much of a fine distinction unless you're deeply into the Serilog internals - but the code responsible will be in _Serilog.Exceptions_ somewhere, and not this repo.

HTH!

Thanks for the suggestion! It would indeed be cool to offer this, but it's not something planned for the `MessageTemplateTextFormatter` that's bundled in core Serilog right now.

Ideally, we'd build a very similar output templating mechanism, but use https://github.com/serilog/serilog-filters-expressions to evaluate the "holes". This would open up things like `{SomeProperty[0].Item}`, and things like `{ElapsedMilliseconds / 1000}` or `{coalesce(Prop1, Prop2)}`.

I've been hoping to take a shot at this for a while; thanks for the nudge, with some luck I'll find the time to spike it out soon :-)

Work-in-progress is at: https://github.com/nblumhardt/serilog-expressions (see the section on [formatting](https://github.com/nblumhardt/serilog-expressions#formatting)).

There are a few caveats:

 * `OutputTemplate` won't work with console theming
 * Dotting through to sub-properties of `@x` (`Exception`) won't yet work; more generally, we need to choose between:
    - leaning on _Serilog.Exceptions_ for this (`ExceptionDetail.Message`)
    - adding helper functions to retrieve components of it (`ExceptionMessage(@x)`),
    - adding a general mechanism for turning the exception into structured data (`ExceptionDetail(@x).Message`), and
    - special casing exceptions in format strings (like we do for levels), e.g. `{@x:message}`.

For now, using _Serilog.Exceptions_ will be the way to go (still a lot of other fish to fry).

Looks great, thank you!

Just a thought, as a variant to option (3), we could have a more general "deconstruction" method, like `Serialize(@x).Message`. Basically a method that takes a general object (not just exceptions) and turns it into a JavaScript-Like property bag / JSON, which we can then access with accessors (dot notation).

I've just added support for user-defined functions, so `ExceptionMessage(@x)` or `Serialize(@x).Message` can be (fairly easily) plugged in:

https://github.com/nblumhardt/serilog-expressions#implementing-user-defined-functions

This should open up these scenarios and enable some experimentation without committing to a direction prematurely. Would be great to hear how it goes.

Thanks @idubnori - I've removed the confusing line from the wiki.

Dashed names are not accepted in message templates; they _are_ accepted in `ForContext()` but really only because it's too expensive to parse/validate property names every time `ForContext()` or `PushProperty()` is called.

As the note was suggesting, they're not compatible with most Serilog infrastructure, including output templates, which use the same message template syntax.

Wiki is fixed; closing as by-design. Thanks!

@nblumhardt Thank you for the quick!

Can we clarify the prohibited character list that cannot be used in property names for methods such as:

> ForContext()
PushProperty()
Enrich.WithProperty(), LogFromContext, and so on...

Hi @idubnori thanks for the reply.

There are no prohibited characters in the arguments to any of those functions; the limitation you've hit is one of message templates, of which output templates are an example.

Serilog events can have properties with any name, but message templates don't have syntax for describing them, and thus they can't be output using that mechanism.

The syntax for names in message templates (in the linked spec) is best to use wherever possible.

HTH!

That's an awesome idea! :+1: .... disappointed now that I didn't come up with it :sweat_smile: 

Scenario-wise, having support for multiple listeners, dynamically added, would make it easier for code to interact with a `LoggingLevelSwitch` that it doesn't "own".

 We could follow `ChangeToken`'s registration style, and do:

```csharp
IDisposable OnChange(Action<LogEventLevel> listener);
```

where disposing the result would deregister the listener?

Synchronization is interesting; a lock would need to cover both adding/removing listeners, and changing the level, so that listeners always "know" the correct level (interleavings of changing the level and adding listeners shouldn't result in listeners being stale/missing a change).

Last thought ... calling callbacks under a lock is good to avoid; we probably could, here, but not sure it's worth the substantial effort involved. "The callback will be invoked under a lock" might be worth noting in the XDOC for OnChange?

Could reproduce this on windows. From the stack trace the error about [QueueTask](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/master/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Threading/Tasks/ConcurrentExclusiveSchedulerPair.cs#L544):

> // If the scheduler has already had completion requested, no new work is allowed to be scheduled

 `taskSchedulerPair.Complete()` happens before all outstanding tasks are queued.

`TestCancellingBackgroundTasksClearsQueue` test calls this method on shared scheduler via `CancelBackgroundTasks()`. After that `Dispatchers.LaunchAPI(..)` for `Task.Factory.StartNew(..)` path will throw for any subsequent call. 
Any delay to `AddActionToQueue` like `Thread.Sleep(1)`  instead of logging as @nblumhardt pointed will introduce that race error.

Hi Matt, thanks for the notes and PR 👍 

This is a design alternative we considered, but chose not to implement, because of the performance critical role of `LoggingLevelSwitch` in the "logging is off" path.

Creating a worker thread to periodically check the required level and adjust switches accordingly may be the best solution available right now.

Another option would be to create an `ILogger` wrapper for Serilog, forwarding to the default Serilog implementation, that uses custom logic in `IsEnabled(LogEventLevel)`.

@nblumhardt Thanks for taking a look. So if I understand it correctly, you're saving users from implementing a level check that performs poorly? Or are you saying that using an interface affects performance directly?

Hi @mattvaughan - thanks for your reply.

One of the core performance aims of Serilog is that when logging is "off", statements like:

```csharp
_log.Debug("Iteration {N} of {M}", n, m);
```

should be as close to free/zero-cost as possible (imagine `M` is one billion :-)). We jump through some hoops so that there are no allocations, and normally, just an integer comparison for the level check in addition to the call. On an `ILogger` the call itself will still cost one virtual dispatch, which is the main cost.

Using the current level switch (instead of a fixed level), there's an additional volatile read, which is also potentially expensive, but there's a chance this can be removed through some additional changes (`Interlocked.MemoryBarrierProcessWide()` and non-virtual reads).

Making the switch an interface would add one more virtual dispatch to the overhead, which, while it would be entirely reasonable for users who need the functionality, it's hard to justify adding this overhead on every call, and as these things add up, we've historically been very hesitant to let additional slowdowns into the "off" path.

Hope this helps, and sorry my explanation is a bit rushed!

Nick
