title: Bug report

comments.body:
Thanks for the note!

The difference in accepted values is that message templates have [a precise syntax](https://messagetemplates.org/#syntax), while property names, in general, are arbitrary strings. Message templates are deliberately aiming to stay simple and lowest-common-denominator to ensure wide applicability. I'm not keen on extending it because it will hurt portability, and keeping the format this way has so far allowed diverse loggers to stay compatible - the benefit of this outweighs the loss in flexibility, I think.

(The further down this path we go, the more semantics we'd need to spec around things like `Rpc.Error` - is it a single, dotted property name, or a structured property `Rpc` with field `Error`? Would multiple `Rpc.*` properties that appear in one message be merged into a single structured value? Could we do it efficiently? Etc.)

HTH,
Nick

> or a structured property Rpc with field Error

Structuredeness of a property is determined not by its name, but is specified by service characters - `@`, `$`.

> Would multiple Rpc.* properties that appear in one message be merged into a single structured value?

Again, structuredeness of a property is determined not by its name, but is specified by service characters - `@`, `$`.

I see that you are referring to a grammar in which `Name` does not allow dots and other syntactic characters. Whatever the specification is, it exists and it is much more difficult to change it than implementation, in this I agree with you.

Nevertheless, I see that there is `IMessageTemplateParser` interface. `MessageTemplateCache` gets it in ctor but in fact `MessageTemplateCache` is initialized using a specific parser implementation in `MessageTemplateProcessor`:
```c#
 readonly MessageTemplateCache _parser = new MessageTemplateCache(new MessageTemplateParser());
```

I suggest passing another parameter of the type `IMessageTemplateParser` into `MessageTemplateProcessor` constructor and create `MessageTemplateCache` with it. This will require making the `IMessageTemplateParser` public interface and moving out of `Core` namespace (by the way, which one?). `MessageTemplate` is already public so I don’t think there will be problems.

Next, `MessageTemplateProcessor` is created inside `LoggerConfiguration` where one can easily add a new configuration property to set the parser like `LoggerSinkConfiguration WriteTo` does. Thus, backward compatibility will not be violated, and those customers who need to use additional characters (dot, hyphen etc) in the message template will get this opportunity. They explicitly specify this in the provided configuration.

Will you accept such a PR?

Thanks for the follow-up.

Allowing different message template syntaxes to be used would make it difficult for packages built against `ILogger` to reliably interop, without knowledge of the underlying logger configuration in a specific app (another reason why the message template spec has been frozen for a while, now). I think the momentum behind this would need to be huge before we'd add it, currently.

Thanks for the suggestion, though! If you are keen to explore it, it's possible to wrap `ILogger` today, using `IsEnabled(level)` and `Write(evt)`, in a custom logging interface that uses a different syntax. Could be an interesting option for experimentation, anyway.

> Allowing different message template syntaxes to be used would make it difficult for packages built against ILogger to reliably interop, without knowledge of the underlying logger configuration in a specific app (another reason why the message template spec has been frozen for a while, now). I think the momentum behind this would need to be huge before we'd add it, currently.

Formally, you just open one interface. Not necessary to support other syntax.

> If you are keen to explore it, it's possible to wrap ILogger today, using IsEnabled(level) and Write(evt), in a custom logging interface that uses a different syntax. 

I just don't need _custom logging interface_. My task is to add a new behavior to the existing system, which consists of many api already well adapted to each other. `ILogger` interface is among them. I see that this problem is easily solved by the approach described above, while maintaining backward compatibility.

Why are you saying that other packages should know about the special syntax? This is not true. This is the concern of a particular application as in my case. The sinks I use do not have problems with dot and other symbols in names (`Push` works perfectly), and this is what I follow when I want to configure the Serilog in the app composition root. I repeat for clarity - this is the responsibility of the application developer (composition root author).

After all, if the `Push` api works fine for the sinks used by the application, then **there is no reason not to allow the use of the same names in template strings**. Reference to the specification as the lowest common denominator is not appropriate in this case.

I hope I have correctly emphasized my explanation. By no means do I want to violate the design of the project or go against the specifications. The proposed solution simply closes a single gap.

I was inaccurate suggesting a custom logging interface - it could be Serilog's `ILogger` over an alternative message template parser - sorry.

This comes down to a very similar principle to what we're discussing in #1385 - if you can write code to meet the need yourself, on today's Serilog, and the feature isn't one that's widely requested, having it in your own app or an extension library is good: you can get the functionality you need, and Serilog doesn't add another extension point to maintain/test/document.

Sorry to hold things up - at an earlier stage of the project this would be different, but at the present time minimalizing surface area is a high-priority goal. Appreciate all of your effort and input, though!

>  it could be Serilog's ILogger over an alternative message template parser 

How can I use alternative message template parser in the current version of the serilog? Thanks for the right direction in #1385. I solved that problem with a custom destructuring policy.

Apologies for taking some time getting back to this - I need to do some digging around to figure out what the minimal subset of `MessageTemplateProcessor` etc. is that would accomplish this (it's admittedly a bit awkward). Will take another look as soon as I can.
Nope. I continue to use push API and waiting for feedback from @nblumhardt .

@nblumhardt that helps indeed, thanks a lot!

I came to the same idea, but my implementation of it was rather cumbersome, I did the replacement in a class derived from `Serilog.Formatting.Elasticsearch.ExceptionAsObjectJsonFormatter`.
It is sad to see how a seemingly simple task has to be solved in such a roundabout way while allocating a lot of unnecessary objects.

It sounds like the OP found an alternative way to achieve this that would be essentially zero-overhead, for a bit more effort, so I'm not sure we're failing, here. Is there a chance you could use the same trick, either the pipeline/enricher, or a custom sink, @sungam3r ?

It's a non-goal for Serilog to be completely openly extensible. The more common a requirement is, the easier it should be to implement, and really it would be nice for "nothing" to be impossible, but this is an unusual request so I don't think it's necessarily bad if the solution is imperfect.

I think we should close this as by-design, at this point.
What is OP?
Original Poster :-)
Well, so be it.

Hi! Sorry to bother you, @nblumhardt. 

But I had a similar case:
- I use Datadog as the receiver of my logs;
- One log can contain a lot of properties;
- Datadog has its own style guides, and visually nest properties, which names are separated by `.`.

For example, I'm logging some HTTP request failures:
```
logger.Information("Request '{http_request.action_name}' with correlation id = '{http_request.correlation_id}' was failed due to timeout", request.Url, metadata.CorrelationId);
```

In this case, all properties that are prefixed by `http_request.` will be visually nested in Datadog and also it's much easier to understand, where it goes. Also, this syntax can be much easier transferred to any other style. It's a real case, why that `.` limitation hardness support of Datadog.

I understand, why you are worried about compatibility. But why do users of the system cand decide how to format their data?

Thanks for dropping by @AndersonDev. I'm interested in helping to solve this problem, but it's probably not via extending the message template syntax at this stage. Like all languages, message templates need to make some decisions/trade-offs.

Have you considered using a mapping of property names onto DataDog properties, either explicitly or via some convention? An enricher or some other sink wrapper could convert `HttpRequest_ActionName` into `http_request.action_name`, for example.

> but it's probably not via extending the message template syntax at this stage.

Existing message template syntax will not change. In https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/1384#issuecomment-553263396 I suggested to provide ability to set custom parser. No breaking changes to serilog itself.

> Thanks for dropping by @AndersonDev. I'm interested in helping to solve this problem, but it's probably not via extending the message template syntax at this stage. Like all languages, message templates need to make some decisions/trade-offs.
> 
> Have you considered using a mapping of property names onto DataDog properties, either explicitly or via some convention? An enricher or some other sink wrapper could convert `HttpRequest_ActionName` into `http_request.action_name`, for example.

Thanks for your answer. We are using Serilog in 30+ in-house submodules, which are part of the platform. In platform guidelines we trying to keep one rule for naming any keys in any system: snake case with a dot between namespaces. That's a common practice in many languages and systems. For example: `company_name.product_name.my_setting_key`. This helps easily visually identify the product and system, the key is related to. Also, it can correlate with namespaces in C# itself.

Having the same style in structural logging and in receivers helps to identify problems much more quickly.

I thought to use `company_name__product_name__my_setting_key`, but it creates heterogeneity, is harder to correlate, adds needs to use a wrapper which will go over each log, and each property inside. We have 10+ properties with each log, and millions of logs from hundred thousand devices (we have mobile apps).

I'm sure you are trying to keep one approach for all customers, to have uniformity across logging solutions. But as an enterprise, we are using all in-house modules, and have control over all logging. I don't understand, why the dot can bring some issues here, but I haven't all pictures like you.

At this stage, I added the dot to the validation method inside our Serilog submodule copy. Usually, I try to avoid any changes to 3d-party frameworks, but here 5 symbols in code resolve all of our problems. Sometimes solutions are simpler than they look :)

I don't have any propositions at this moment, but if any of my experience with cases can help - I am ready to be helpful.

Thanks for looping back! It sounds like a name mapping might still be the best bet for you. ASP.NET Core's own built-in instrumentation uses PascalCase names for things like `HttpMethod`, so writing a name translation would keep these lined up also. All the best, whichever way you go 👍

Just what to say we are also trying to adhere to the [elastic common schema](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/ecs/current/ecs-field-reference.html) and lack of support for "." in message templates is making this difficult.  

Using a special character (http_request_id) and remapping to . (http.request.id) complicates interpretation everywhere we log properties.

We would also like to have the option to substitute the message parser.  The only other option to get the desired behavior we (actually specifying the proper property names) is to fork Serilog which is a very undesirable option.

I expect the people wanting to adhere to a logging schema will only increase while the cases you talk about the where eco systems do not support "." in property names is unclear.  Are you sure that breaks things?  Can't people in those cases just not log property names with "."s?

Anyway, love Serilog just wanted to add to this petition for some way to support property names with "."s without obfuscating logging calls (remapping).

I'm open to discussing this one some more. But, there's a lot of code out there that relies on parsing message templates within the current constraints that would potentially break. We'd need to pull together a fairly exhaustive list in order to consider this kind of change.

I don't think it's desirable to leave the ecosystem inconsistent, since it's not always possible or desirable to avoid using a new feature, once code reuse, samples, libraries, etc. are in the mix. If Serilog allows names with dots, they should flow through reasonably to everything else plugged into Serilog, or we'll reduce the overall quality of the solution.

In the Serilog org, apart from the Serilog package, there's Serilog.Sinks.Console and Serilog.Formatting.Compact.Reader that would need updates/new builds.

Serilog.Expressions would need a strategy for handling dotted names, since `a.b = 42` expects to find a property `b` on an object `a`, not a single property with name `a.b`, which would currently be `@p['a.b'] = 42`.

We'd need to consider NLog and other implementers of https://messagetemplates.org, if a 2.0 version of the standard with updated syntax is called for. Probably more libraries listed on that website to check in on in that case, too.

There's also SerilogAnalyzer and the Rider/ReSharper plug-in to consider.

A bunch of tools I write and/or use would need updates, plenty around the Seq ecosystem, I suspect there will be many more cases out there.

It's not that any one of these is a dealbreaker; it's just a lot of work to scope out the impacts, and to follow through with all of the downstream updates if something moved ahead, here.

Thanks, Nick, for the thoughtful response.

It is indeed a large undertaking to make "."s an officially supported option but it seems like a first step would be to have an option to toggle on support in the parser and see what breaks.  Alternatively, the ability to replace or extend the parser could accomplish the same goal but is potentially more inconsistent.  Either option should come with a warning that YMMV and it is not officially supported.

Note that there is already apparent inconsistency in that you can add context properties with "."s.  That's our current hack that means we lose out on the intended conciseness of Serilog.

Okay, thanks for the continued feedback (and for kicking this off, all the way back in 2019, @sungam3r).

It's really a deep part of what makes Serilog "Serilog" so I need to spend some time with it myself; my initial thoughts are putting together something behind e.g.:

```csharp
AppContext.SetSwitch("Serilog.Parsing.MessageTemplateParser.AcceptDottedPropertyNames", true);
```

This would apply globally to all message template parser instances created from that point onwards, so setting the switch at start-up would flick the whole process over into the alternative mode (this is important because some Serilog extensions create and use `MessageTemplateParser` instances directly).

The message template parser itself really needs some attention, so whether this turned into a supported feature in the long term or not, we'd have a chance to refactor and improve it.

I'll post here when I have something to report - trying it in a variety of scenarios could be a team project for all of us on this thread 😄
#2063 needs your 👀  :-)

Dots are now accepted by default, as of v4.2.0: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/releases/tag/v4.2.0

Closing this as I don't think there's any further change likely in this direction. Thanks for all of the input everyone, and for the original nudge @sungam3r 👍

comments.body:
Hi, @augustoproiete. I believe its by design. 'SourceContext' is valid in `ForContext` context, otherwise its just a regular property. 
`ForContext(..)` will create static pipeline with minimum level applied upfront for best performance. If you want to dynamically filter by property name, use filters (`.Filter(..)`) instead

Thanks for calling out the inconsistency with this, @augustoproiete :+1: - we could definitely investigate further.

We left things this way in order to avoid string comparisons against `SourceContext` for every event; I don't know how much impact this would have in practice, but I suspect it could be non-trivial and it would be important to measure before we close the loophole.

Comparisons against the level, like your example above demonstrates, are much cheaper, so we do make a check there - and we committed to this behavior before adding overrides, hence the inconsistency, unfortunately.

> Calling ForContext (in my mind) should only populate the SourceContext property for you, not do the filtering.

I'm probably splitting hairs, but it's not quite like this - the goal of level overrides is to avoid constructing disabled events in the first place, hence there's no `SourceContext` property to populate (and no corresponding wasted allocations).

Cheers!

Thanks for the follow-up, @augustoproiete .

Unfortunately, `MinimumLevel.Override()` is not supported at all by sub-loggers. We've updated the XDOC for `MinimumLevel.Override()` to call it out, but it seems we could still do better.

Implementing full support for it would also be great to explore, though I expect it's going to be very challenging :-)
I think this is stale, but let me know if there's still anything likely to move forward here.

comments.body: FYI: I solved my immediate issue by creating two separate loggers, but this still seems like a bug to me.

Thanks for the note, @jceddy 👍 

This is by design - in the end, we had to make a call on which "wins" - the context value or the one from the message.

On the one hand, context values are needed for correlation and tracking down related events, so they may be preferred in some scenarios

On the other hand, replacing properties that appear in the message with ones from the context could lead to the meaning of the message changing/becoming misleading.

Long ago, we had to make a call, and decided to favor properties from the message; it's been a reasonable choice, and changing direction now would cause problems downstream, so we're not likely to change direction here.

You can work around it by creating your own `ILogEventEnricher` and `Push()`ing that onto the `LogContext` instead of the individual property values. Then, in its `Enrich()` method, instead of calling `AddPropertyIfAbsent()`, as the default log context enrichers do, call `AddOrUpdateProperty()` and replace the existing values.

Hope this helps, let me know if you need more info. Thanks again!

I'm a little confused about what you mean by properties that "appear in the message". In my example, the "Source" property does not appear in the message, it is only ever added my an enricher.  
  
Are you really just saying that with the "default" serilog enrichers, the first enricher "wins"? Does that mean I can just switch the order of the enrichers in my logger configuration to get the result I'm shooting for?

Hi! It's not the `+` sign causing the issue here; the argument to `log.Information()` is a message template, and in that syntax, `}` is a special character that must be escaped by doubling: `}}`.

Using a placeholder in the template, and passing the JSON as an argument (or as a captured object) will work better with the way Serilog is set up.

```csharp
log.Information("Here is some JSON: {Json}", json);
```

HTH

the `:` and the `+` likely triggers parsing related to field format specfiers, i.e. `{0:+5}` etc. The chances are there is some edge case issue (the parsing code is bespoke and has been optimized for performance a lot) ; I challenge you to go write the failing test and/or fix ;)

```

true
```

The `IsValidInFormat()` method is a little bit suspect in how specific it is, given the variety of possible format specifiers, but that's tangential :-)

Thanks for the suggestion!

We looked at this option back around the "great package split" of 2.0, and decided against it back then because the transitive closure of dependencies from `ILogger` started to feel semi-arbitrary (things like `LogEventProperty`, `TextToken` etc.; and the `LogContext` implementation caused further non-abstract types to also be pulled in at the consuming side.

If we were determined, we could factor around some of these, but it's more likely to be something we'd do as part of a full API overhaul ("3.0" or "4.0") than a standalone change. Shifting types between packages right now would cause more churn and tooling pain than any potential churn in the types themselves (we've avoided breaking changes in the binary API for several years, now.)

I'd rather close this for now but keep the general idea in mind when/if we embark on some wider changes in the future.

comments.body:
Hi Travis! Yes, this is the place :-)

You're right in that we bend the conventions a bit, here - because namespaces are case-sensitive we're stuck with `{"Namespace": "Microsoft", "Level": "Debug"}`, otherwise.

Not sure what the MEL provider does in this case - they use the same syntax - but I'd guess it's similar.

What do you think?

In MEL it appears they use [a case-insensitive comparison for the category name (namespace)](https://github.com/aspnet/Extensions/blob/f162f1006bf8954f0102af8ff98c04077cf21b04/src/Logging/Logging/src/LoggerRuleSelector.cs#L63).

However, let me drum up a quick unit test to verify this is the case and that I'm not looking at the wrong thing.

Thanks for the analysis. I don't think it'd hurt for us to switch to case-insensitive comparisons in this case; although it would introduce a slight inconsistency with the core Serilog project's `Matching.FromSource(string)` I think we could live with it. Fair to mark it as an enhancement, though :-D

Is this something that would happen here or in core Serilog? It appears it may be core.

- Specifying an override in configuration ends up [calling `Override` on the `LoggerConfiguration.MinimumLevel`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-configuration/blob/71839b807802f7bbfbd95dd5d399ee34ea398d97/src/Serilog.Settings.Configuration/Settings/Configuration/ConfigurationReader.cs#L108).
- Calling `LoggerConfiguration.MinimumLevel.Override` [adds override values to an override dictionary inside `LoggerConfiguration`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/69f8c14b6b8450b150a33e0bb04553a94d26cd23/src/Serilog/LoggerConfiguration.cs#L98).
- Overrides for a logger [get added to a `LevelOverrideMap`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/69f8c14b6b8450b150a33e0bb04553a94d26cd23/src/Serilog/LoggerConfiguration.cs#L189).
- [`LevelOverrideMap` appears to be where the case-sensitive comparison is happening.](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/8ce1bcec9d7a82c4e7990927470d7e3948bfdafe/src/Serilog/Core/LevelOverrideMap.cs#L71)

I think the fix would be in `LevelOverrideMap` unless I'm mistaken. Does that sound right?

Ah, yes of course - I forgot that this is implemented using `LevelOverrideMap`. Hmmm 🤔 - changing it there would have a bit more impact and would need more careful consideration. I'll move this issue over to that repo and revisit when I can 👍

In the event it helps (or not?) I looked at how log4net does it.

[In .NET desktop framework, it's using object equality. In .NET Core/compact it uses the `string` type's `==` override.](https://git-wip-us.apache.org/repos/asf?p=logging-log4net.git;a=blob;f=src/Repository/Hierarchy/LoggerKey.cs;h=ccc566b1b195d87e7e9eca4bfce72854c909673c;hb=refs/heads/master#l118) The object equality is because they're interning strings in .NET desktop framework.

**Anyway, this boils down to log4net being case-sensitive for its logger names.**

That said, log4net is also pretty tightly tied to loggers being based on types - a "logger repository" in there is tied to an assembly and used as a central sort of cache key. You could ostensibly have two different loggers for any given type if there were two different repositories, each based on a different assembly. It's... an interesting and somewhat complex thing.

Thanks for the follow-up. I think log4net was probably the origin of this decision (it was the main influence on conventions in Serilog at the beginning).

This needs some thought - unfortunately it's not a change we can make quickly, but I'll definitely loop back around to this when I have time to think it through properly.
No worries, just trying to help. Let me know if there's anything else I can do.

There is an exotic issue related to Ubuntu-based docker images. Apparently the convention for Ubuntu is to have all the environment variable keys uppercased and without DOTS in names. If I configure docker image and pass key not in upper case or containing dot, apparently Ubuntu simply ignores that environment variable. Could be related to [this](https://unix.stackexchange.com/a/93533). So we are restricted to uppercase characters and underscores in key. 

That lead to an issue if I try to override minimum level with env variable as

this is simply omitted by Ubuntu:

```
SERILOG__MINIMUMLEVEL__OVERRIDE__MyApp.MyService=Verbose
```
and this does not work due to case-sensitive match and replaced DOT:

```
SERILOG__MINIMUMLEVEL__OVERRIDE__MYAPP_MYSERVICE=Verbose
```

We could of course perform case-insensitive match, but that would not help. For `Product.My_Service` and `Product.My.Service` configuration will looks the same -> `PRODUCT_MY_SERVICE`, so normalization will need to be implemented at a moment we test input value, which is of course dirty 😟 

I do not see a nice way to overcome that without changing configuration schema (so that type name is passed in value, not key). But wanted to post it here, so you are aware 😉
I don't think this is a change we are likely to make in the near future; closing as stale, but thanks for raising it nonetheless. (Hope all's well with you @tillig 👋)

Somewhat related - serilog/serilog-settings-configuration#386 found that the parser for the log level enum in configuration was inconsistently case-sensitive and case-insensitive, and that got resolved to be case-insensitive everywhere. That makes things just slightly more inconsistent: enum parsing is case-insensitive, but the keys are case-sensitive.

If you're using that library, you can just update to the `3.0.0-dev-*` version, call `UseSerilogRequestLogging()` on your `IApplicationBuilder`, and add properties using `IDiagnosticContext.Add()` (available via DI).

The feature is described in more detail here: https://github.com/serilog/serilog-aspnetcore/pull/94#issue-290980797

In the future, it's likely that some part of this will be implemented within `LogContext`.

If you have questions or feedback (or if this turns out to be perfect!) it would be great to hear.

 * Example of usage: https://github.com/serilog/serilog-aspnetcore/blob/dev/samples/EarlyInitializationSample/Controllers/HomeController.cs#L28

Interesting. 

I began working toward a similar solution. I already had my own middleware that was logging requests and a few custom Enrichers that pulled information from the HttpContext. 

The solution I had been working toward was to create an IRequestLoggingScope which wrapped IHttpContextAccessor and stored log properties in HttpContext.items. This seems similar to your IDiagnosticContext except it uses HttpContext.Items instead of AsyncLocal. Then, a registered enricher would pull data out of the cached HttpContext.Items collection and add it to the log event.

comments.body:
Hi @RushuiGuan - thanks for the note.

Package versions and assembly versions have no fixed relationship. We've used the immutable 2.0.0 assembly version deliberately throughout the entire Serilog 2 release series, and although there are downsides, it's also avoided many painful scenarios. (The GAC is unfortunately going to be painful whether we do this or not .. :-))

Thanks again; I'm closing this as by-design, but hopefully someday we'll all be completely free of the GAC, strong naming, etc. etc.!

Hi @nblumhardt, thanks for the reply.

Assembly versioning is used at runtime and should aways uniquely identify a binary.  When multiple versions of the same assembly are referenced, users can use binding redirect to determine exactly which version to use.  Dotnet even allows us to reference multiple versions of the same assembly at the same time.  All this is no longer possible since the serilog V2 assemblies have exactly the same version.  

Logging is such a common library, it is common for a program to reference multiple versions at the same time, often not by choice because of third party dependencies.  Versioning your assembly this way leaves the user with no way to resolve the conflict.  Depends on the runtime and how the assemblies are referenced, the program may or may not run at all.

The "painful scenarios" have been solved many years ago.  What's left is a proven working system.  Please reconsider.  Thanks!

Thanks for the thoughtful reply. I know there are pros/cons to the scheme we've chosen, and unfortunately you might be stuck with a scenario (e.g. SharePoint, _System.AddIns_, or some other GAC-heavy application model), where some limitations come through.

For modern .NET projects that use NuGet and deploy their libraries alongside executables, the current scheme works well; the version used at runtime will be determined by which DLL gets deployed, and this comes down only to which NuGet package version is installed.

At deployment time, MSI and other versioned artifact deployment technologies work with this because we ensure the file version is set to the package version, not the assembly version:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/342712/59084542-f7ce9780-893e-11e9-8684-5056d7faaeed.png)

The plus side for most use cases is the elimination of unnecessary run-time assembly loading failures and binding redirect issues. It's really cut out a massive amount of trouble - _Serilog_ is the third-most downloaded non-Microsoft package on NuGet, so we measure the success of this strategy by the amount of inbox traffic we're _not_ getting about it 🙂.

What tools are causing you trouble? Happy to help resolve your version conflict if you can send some more details.

comments.body:
It would be nice to go back in time and build levelling support into enricher configuration methods, much like we've done with sinks, but there's a lot of churn involved in that.

Alternatively, we could make it possible for a levelled enricher wrapper to be written:

```csharp
    .Enrich.AtLevel(LogEventLevel.Verbose, e => e.WithMachineName())
```

We provide `LoggerSinkConfiguration.Wrap()` so that wrapper sinks can modify the behavior of other sinks, and `Enrich.AtLevel()` could be built on a similar `LoggerEnrichmentConfiguration.Wrap()` method, were one available.

Thoughts? Are there any other use cases that could be implemented on top of this? Would a similar method for destructuring also find use?

👍 for leveled enrichment.
Leveled approach would be also helpful for destructuring, omitting certain properties on higher levels but adding them on others. It should support including or excluding configuration with list of levels and higher / lower than level approach.
In one of our projects we used forked [Destructurama.Attributed](https://github.com/destructurama/attributed) with added attribute `LogAtAttribute(LogEventLevel level)` for ignoring properties below defined level, but performance of that implementation was not optimal for widespread use and we ditched it after the project matured and verbose /debug logging was not needed as much.

Just looking at the example again, we'd need to use `LoggingLevelSwitch` with the API if we want to avoid having to re-specify the minimum level:

```csharp
    .Enrich.AtLevel(LogEventLevel.Verbose, levelSwitch, e => e.WithMachineName())
```

> In one of our projects we used forked [Destructurama.Attributed](https://github.com/destructurama/attributed) with added attribute `LogAtAttribute(LogEventLevel level)` for ignoring properties below defined level, but performance of that implementation was not optimal for widespread use and we ditched it after the project matured and verbose /debug logging was not needed as much.

Could you give some details about bad performance issues ?

Is it basically a "bad" idea to use serilog enrichers, as these impact on application performance?

@vlm `.Enrich.AtLevel(LogEventLevel.Debug, levelSwitch, e => e.WithMachineName())` would mean the enricher would only apply when the `levelSwitch` is set to `Debug` or lower (e.g. `Verbose`).

Unless the level switch is used to connect the logger configuration to the extension method, we'd need to come up with some other kind of internal mechanism for the extension to learn the "final" minimum level - which might be more investment than we'd currently want to make in this feature (although not off the table for future consideration).

#1316 introduces `Enrich.When()` as a catch-all way to implement this. I think the feature as originally envisioned in this PR is still worth considering, but the need to work with level switches and so-on makes the API potentially confusing.

Here's how it could be done:

```csharp
var levelSwitch = new LoggingLevelSwitch();

Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .MinimumLevel.ControlledBy(levelSwitch)
    .Enrich.When(_ => levelSwitch.MinimumLevel <= LogEventLevel.Information, e => e.WithMachineName())
    .WriteTo.Console()
    .CreateLogger();
```

Because `LoggerEnrichmentConfiguration.Wrap()` is public, the `.Enrich.WhenMinimumLevelIs(LogEventLevel.Debug, levelSwitch, e => e.WithMachineName())` type of extension could be written in a separate assembly, and could benefit from `<appSettings>`/`appSettings.json` support from level switches and actions.

👀 on the PR appreciated :-)
Looks awesome to me! And btw, how would be appsettings configuration for this look like?

@andre-ss6 the settings support for this would need to be similar to what we have today enabling `WriteTo.Async()`, `WriteTo.Logger()` and a few more scenarios. I haven't spent any time on the details, though.
The above is now available in the 2.9.0-dev-* packages.

Thanks for the report and investigation :+1:

It's possible C# just marks types containing extension methods this way because, in C#, extension methods are declared in `static` classes, and static classes translate to `abstract sealed`.

Serilog uses this as an optimisation; it's not a super-critical one, but would be good to maintain if we can. I wonder if we can check top-level assembly metadata to figure out whether the assembly is a C# or F# one, and filter accordingly?
I have a feeling an unlinked PR addressed this already; please let me know if not and it's still an issue. Thanks!

The fact that F# types that look static are not (i.e. are not marked abstract and sealed) is a common confusion with a workaround, see https://stackoverflow.com/a/13419343/11635 and the linked related dotnet issues - hopefully a resolution of those (e.g. if `type private () =` could imply a static class, i.e. auto production of `[<Sealed; AbstractClass>],  will make it less likely for F# authors to run into this.

@nblumhardt 
I think I figured it out. Someone configured a scale out rule on this specific service so Azure created 3 instances. All the instances share the storage where the logs are stored.
Each instances tried to access the same log file which is not possible because it is locked by the first instance therefore they create their own log file (shared access is off).

What would be your guidance in this case? Enable shared access so that all instances can log to the same log file or somehow make sure that their logging is completely separate (don't know how to ensure that though, maybe use the machine name as some kind of indicator to create separate log files)?

Hi @mruf -

Separate log files could be a reasonable option, but keep in mind that old file sets won't necessarily be rolled/cleaned up unless the machine name or other log file identifier is fairly stable.

Leaving things as-is, with `_001`, `_002` files, etc., is also possibly workable, as is opening and closing the file for each log event (though this has serious performance implications).

Using `shared: true` has led to file corruptions on Azure Files storage, possibly because it does not implement atomic append, which is used by Serilog's file sink to speed up this scenario. May be tolerable if you don't want to programmatically process the files.

IMHO log files are a poor fit for multi-process deployments - file sharing almost always comes with some kind of compromise. Personally I'd try to replace the file-backed logging with some kind of centralized or service-based log server. It's more effort to get started, but the experience can be night-and-day-better.

HTH!

Hi! Thanks for all the details 👍 

This looks like it could be a case of the default Seq (`PeriodicBatchingSink`) sink buffer size being too big given the size of the events being logged. When the Seq server is unavailable for whatever reason, events are held for up to 10 minutes to support retries.

It's unusual not to see `System.String` in a memory report like this, though - is that excluded somehow?

If there's some issue Seq-side causing the server to become unavailable, there should be evidence of this in the diagnostic report under _Settings > Diagnostics > Download a full diagnostic report_. Sending that to support@datalust.co would confirm that.

On the Serilog side, you can reduce the buffer size by passing `queueSizeLimit` to the `Seq()` configuration method:

```csharp
    .WriteTo.Seq(..., queueSizeLimit: 10000)
```

(The default is 100,000.)

Hope this suggests some possible courses of action.

Cheers,
Nick

We tried setting it to 10,000, and still ran into the same problem.  It definitely seems tied to the number of loggable events that fire off in a short timeframe.  In addition, some of these logged strings are rather large (for example a 1000ish line sql insert statement), which, since they are being held in memory for retry, is itself a memory hog.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33524074/57328182-59001280-70d6-11e9-93c0-407beb1c7581.png)


System.String does not appear on the snapshot at all.  Not sure if it is getting excluded by Visual Studio or not.

I have sent the diagnostic logs to datalust.co

Thanks for the follow-up, we received and replied to your report :+1:

Given the huge strings involved in EF query logging, turning it off completely is likely to be the best solution, here. Logging a large number of potentially 400k+ events in a short period will require some tuning/infrastructure upgrades, otherwise (reasonable if the data is valuable to you, of course).

Hope this helps!
Nick

Increasing the level of logs that gets sent to seq to Warning during data seeding removed most of the memory issues.  Logging those transactions isn't important at all, so it seems like a good fix.

I think our original issue was too many logs getting sent at once overwhelmed seq and created the backlog in memory and when we changed to larger but less frequent inserts, the size of them caused processing problems.

TY for your assistance.

Hi,

looks nice ! 

I do have a few suggestions for it to fit better within the *Serilog* ecosystem. 

1. Because the project deals mostly with `Destructure`-ing, it would feel more natural if the added extension method was on top of `LoggerDestructuringConfiguration` instead of `LoggerConfiguration`. (you can refer to the projects under [Destructurama](https://github.com/destructurama) to get an idea). This has the added benefit that it makes the configuration method usable through the different *settings* providers (`AppSettings`, `Configuration`, `KeyValueSettings`).

2. For discoverability, you would normally put your extension methods in the `Serilog` namespace, so that they automatically show up without needing any extra `using` statements (but keeping your class in their own namespace is recommended)

3. It's probably me being paranoid, but I usually create all my class as `internal` by default ... and only mark them as `public` if it is really needed :) 

4. about the name of the package, I think @nblumhardt will be the best to give recommendations ... but I think that the `Serilog.` prefix is reserved on nuget.org ... so you may need a different prefix / root namespace...

Also, maybe another suggestion / possibility would be to see if your project could be added to the `Destructurama` organization, which already includes several `Destructuring` extensions for Serilog : https://github.com/destructurama

This would probably also make your package easier to find. (there is for instance a package called `Destructurama.JsonNet` which adds destructuring for `JSON.NET` types .... and it would make a lot of sense to have `Destructurama.NodaTime` ....

Thanks @tsimbalar  for your feedback - it's very much appreciated :)

I'll create a new branch asap to look at implementing suggestions 1 and 2 and anything else which may flow from this Issue (indeed I had hoped to do it today but you know how it goes).

I'm in mixed minds about declaring the deconstruction classes as `internal`. I see your point; furthermore my project is modelled on [NodaTime.Serialization.JsonNet](https://github.com/nodatime/nodatime.serialization/tree/master/src/NodaTime.Serialization.JsonNet) where the equivalent classes are indeed `internal` and what's good enough for Jon Skeet is certainly good enough for me... On the other hand, my thinking was that by making the classes `public` it would allow users to cherry pick just the deconstructors they need without being compelled to load all of them. Perhaps a reasonable compromise would be to mark the classes `internal` and add extension methods for each NodaTime type? Or maybe I should concede? Not sure at the moment.

With regards to the organisational issues and naming:

Hi folks finding this issue!

Here's a quick checklist for figuring out why Serilog might be triggering high memory usage in your application:

1. Are you using `@` to serialize arbitrary/unknown objects into your logs? Serilog is a serializer; it has some basic safety features like graph depth limits to try keeping your process alive while you identify the issue, but you'll need to fix your usage.
2. Are you formatting arbitrarily large strings into log events, either into their messages, or into text output? Again Serilog will try to keep chugging on while you sort this out, but this is also a usage issue that needs to be fixed.
3. Are you enriching your logs with enormous objects, perhaps using a plug-in like _Serilog.Exceptions_ to attempt serialization of a type not understood by it? Try removing the plug-in or reconfiguring it to handle the type in question.
4. Are you using a sink that buffers events - either an asynchronous or batched one - and something is causing the sink's buffer to fill with too much data? Most sinks have buffer size limits with reasonable defaults, but try removing the sink, and if that sorts out the problem, try to reconfigure it.
5. Post your configuration and logging code to Stack Overflow with the `serilog` tag.
6. Use a memory profiler to dig into what's going on. If you do in fact find a memory leak in Serilog, please report it, we aggressively hunt down and fix anything of that sort.

I'll/the maintainers will add to this list if more suggestions come up. Good luck! We're watching that `serilog` tag on SO, so if you're here looking for help and found a locked thread, that's the place to go.

Hi! This will unfortunately be due to memory corruption happening either:

 * Somewhere else in the process (writing over the heap),
 * Because of some incorrect unsafe/native code somewhere in the thing being destructured, or,
 * Because of a concurrency issue (perhaps destructuring an object that includes unsafe code, that's being concurrently modified elsewhere)

Of these, it's most likely to be the first. Serilog itself doesn't contain any unsafe code (that I can recall), so it would be difficult for this to be caused by code in the Serilog library itself.

Hope you're able to track it down; https://stackoverflow.com/questions/3245185/how-to-debug-accessviolationexception-coming-from-native-code might be a starting point (or at least suggest some keywords to follow).

On the downside, these are sometimes hard to locate. On the upside, it's a truly satisfying debugging task when you're able to find one. Good luck!

`NLogFormat` compatibility, as you're effectively requesting would mean doing cascading renames, which is hard to do correctly, safely and efficiently, especially in the face of multiple writers. I did ask for https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-file/issues/40, which makes a whitelist regex in the splunk forwarder config less messy as it means not special casing - but that's just gold plating. There are 2 small things that catch my eye and that you may want to check : 

- in your JSON configuration, I would expect to see 

```json
"Using": [ "Serilog.Sinks.File" ],
```

in order to import the File Sink and make it available in the config.

>  the `$` stringification operator will convert the property value to a string before any other processing takes place, regardless of its type or implemented interfaces.

this could explain why you see `cbw.service.models.Routes.UpdatePermission` and not a destructured object. The operator you want to use is the *destructuring* operator `@` described [in the documentation](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Structured-Data#preserving-object-structure) as well.


By the way, something I don't see here but is quite important to remember is to `Dispose` the logger you inject in the `SerilogFactory` constructor when you app exits, in order to force flushing pending messages. See https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Lifecycle-of-Loggers#without-using-log for more details. (I don't know much about *ServiceStack* so this may actually be taken care of there already).

comments.body: @nblumhardt @tsimbalar: Am I out of context with my need?

Hi @mariopasquali, thanks for the well-considered issue 👍 

I think it might be reasonable to consider this a bug - padding should probably still apply even when no value is present for a property. It'll need some time and investigation at our end, though.

Cheers,
Nick

Hi @nblumhardt, thank you for considering my feedback, much appreciated. 

Resolving the padding would indeed be a great step towards having a more readable text output. 

The other side of my message was about what I could qualify as "decorative characters", so basically characters used to decorate properties to make the text output more readable. (like spaces, dots, etc).  I am not sure if this is the right place or way to discuss this so let me know if I am not reporting this the right way. 

Before taking the original case in my first message, let's consider the simple case:

`{SourceContext}: {Message}`

I believe this is a pretty this is a pretty common case.  It should also be pretty common that SourceContext is not always informed.  The need here is obviously to not have the decorative characters ": " if the SourceContext is not present.  I would like to have a way to associate decorative characters to a property so if the property is not present, the decorative characters would not be put in the formatted text.  There are a few ways to achieve this.  I thought about an approach to open discussion:

`{SourceContext;$: }{Message}`

The above template use a suggested property formatting option.  The formatting is specified after ';'.  '$' is the placeholder for the formatted property.  This example works well in this simple example.  If SourceContext is missing then only Message will be printed out, easy. 

My first email actually had a slightly trickier case:

`{ClassName}.{MethodName}: {Message}`

Where ClassName and MethodName potentially optional.  The additional difficulty is that if ClassName is missing then MethodName should not be printed even if available.  I am not sure if this is a too special case that it is not worth supporting, but for the sake of the discussion I tried expressing this with my suggested extended template format:

`{ClassName;${Method;.$}: }{Message}`

The trick is to embed a property to the formatting of another.  The extended template is still simple and readable, 

I will stop here for now, waiting feedback to understand if it is worth pushing the discussion further. 

Cheers,
Mario

Thanks for the follow-up, Mario, and sorry I missed replying to the second part of your message.

The goal of Serilog's template syntax is to be/remain as close as possible to the .NET format string syntax, so it's not likely we'd address the second item here via this ticket.

There's a lot of room to plug in new/alternative text formatters, though - the case of "conditional" formatting is very interesting. I've thought in the past about writing an alternative formatter to support this (either with a custom syntax, or something like Handlebars), but it would be a separate project to Serilog's core.

Thank you for the comment Nicholas.  I am totally fine of having this as a separate project and this is actually what I was looking for initially, but I didn't find any way to extend the Serilog templates in a way that would work with existing Serilog sinks.  I briefly explained the approaches I considered in the last paragraph of the first message.  

Did I miss something that would enable me to create the desired functionality?

Thank you,
Mario
(sorry, didn't mean to close it)

Hi Mario - regarding how to maintain compatibility with existing sinks, all of the text-based sinks accept an `ITextFormatter` that is responsible for rendering out events as text. The default [`MessageTemplateTextFormatter`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Formatting/Display/MessageTemplateTextFormatter.cs#L33) does this for the regular output templates. Your alternative plug-in would need to implement the same interface, and then be passed in via methods like `WriteTo.File()` etc. - HTH.

One note regarding the alignment issue; fixing it will create a regression for anyone currently relying on it to squeeze two properties into the space of one, e.g. `{RequestId,10}{MessageId,10}` in cases where one or the other property, but not both, will be present.

Therefore I think we should save the fix for the 3.0 milestone.

> fixing it will create a regression for anyone currently relying on it to squeeze two properties into the space of one

Maybe it would help to come up with a flag `KeepPaddingForEmptyProperties` with `false` as default as to ensure backwards compatibility (if I'm wording it correctly).

**LE:** maybe `{!RequestId,10}{!MessageId,10}` to keep padding. `!` inspired from the `!important` suffix used in CSS.

I write here because I would want a feature of console/file sink where you can prepend/post-pend tab or new line (maybe extended to any string) to properties in output and find it to be a particular case of this discussion. Also, reading this issue looks like the implications of what is desired are much more complex than what I've imagined for my narrower case.

What would be useful in my opinion to be able to do in `outputTemplate` is `{t|prop}{n|anotherProp|n}`. If `prop` is "value" and `anotherProp` is empty, rendered output is only `\tvalue`. But I see as equally relevant cases where tabs/new lines are to be kept for empty properties.

**LE:** `{!n|!anotherProp,10|!n}` for keeping both new lines _and_ the padding.

In case it makes sense, is there any chance that a feature strictly for tabs/new lines could be developed independently of the bigger picture that @mariopasquali sees ? Or as a basis for it?

_I can move this comment elsewhere if it's not suited here._

@nblumhardt & @mariopasquali : I looked through `MessageTemplateTextFormatter` and connected classes. I'd love to contribute to your work, Mario, if you'll take this for a PR?/separate project or to try myself to achieve this whole thing if specs are made clear / consensus is reached - as I would really like to see implemented a way (`!`) to enable/disable that "keeping" for each part (pre- ; main ; -post) of each placeholder. I think this 3-part model obtains more flexibility of decorating a property.

**LE:**
> The additional difficulty is that if ClassName is missing then MethodName should not be printed even if available.
> `{ClassName;${Method;.$}: }{Message}`

`{ClassName|{.|Method}: }{Message}` - The `{.|Method}: ` part will not show when `ClassName` is missing because it is not prefixed with `!`.

_Serilog.Expressions_ has some features that should now cover everything discussed in this PR. I'm still interested in improving this behavior, but since it's been stale for so long I'll close it now, and we can reopen if the Serilog.Expressions route is unfruitful. Cheers!

Hi Sacha,

 I think what you want is : 

```csharp
Logger.ForContext("LoggingEnvironment", loggingEnvironment, destructureObjects: true).Error("{Category} {Message}", LogCategory.BUS)
```

This allows to add properties that are not in the rendered message.

See https://stackoverflow.com/questions/30637416/how-can-i-add-a-named-property-that-is-not-part-of-the-message-template .


Also, if your `LoggingEnvironment` is known early enough in your app, you could probably apply it globally when setting up your logger : 

```csharp
new LoggerConfiguration()
  .WriteTo.Sink(/**/)
  .Enrich.WithProperty("LoggingEnvironment", loggingEnvironment, destructureObjects: true)
  .CreateLogger()
```

comments.body:
Thanks for getting in touch!

This is by design - the `messageTemplate` parameter to logger methods accepts a [message template](https://messagetemplates.org), expecting placeholders like `{This}`, not a literal string. In message template syntax, `{{` is an escaped `{`.

You can achieve what you're after with:

```
            Console.WriteLine(oneOut);
            Log.Debug("{Output}", oneOut);  
```

Installing https://github.com/suchiman/seriloganalyzer will help catch usage issues like these. HTH!

For more regarding all this: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/49678739/logging-a-literal-message-in-nlog-and-or-serilog (TL;DR NLog special cases the single arg writes like you're anticipating - Serilog is self-consistent but not consistent with that ;) )

comments.body:
V quick thoughts
- buffering and selectively emitting like this can be very powerful and necessary - and it can also kill perf, so providing something general is going to be a heck of a challenge.
- you still want your logging to work _and log early_ during the failure, so buffering may be problematic
- this seems to split between framework integration and more general buffering - as the split in the cited repo does - if you're not talking about actually doing something like that, what specific items do you feel are general enough to consider in this global context and/or what do you specifically feel Serilog Core might need to do ? There's a necessarily insanely high bar for putting stuff in this specific repo, I'd say....

@bartelink Thank you for your thoughtful feedback.

Perf is a good point. I see that the Serilog core repo (i.e. this one) has automated perf tests and baseline results, which will help validate that any changes don't degrade perf more than allowed. What do you think would be an acceptable overhead? Additionally, it occurs to me that some sinks will likely have locks, e.g. we only want to be writing one event to the console at a time. Maybe buffering these up into bigger writes could _improve_ throughput?

That's a good point about failures. We wouldn't want this functionality to cause logs to be lost during critical times, e.g. high memory pressure. With respect to "early", maybe there should also be configurable flush intervals 🤔 

I'm afraid I don't quite understand your third point - could you clarify? I raised the issue in this repo as I guessed it to be the most relevant place. I didn't intend to imply that changes would be necessary in Serilog Core. I'd be happy to move this conversation anywhere more appropriate.

>Additionally, it occurs to me that some sinks will likely have locks, 

Enrichers run on the app thread to capture things which get stored in the `Properties` of the `LogEvent`, then they get presented to each `Sink` in sequence without any concurrency in the mix (typically one uses the `async` Sink to offload work to a background thread; some sinks such as `seq` do such offloads internally).

In terms of both packaging, decoupling, and not burdening the system as a whole, it thus likely will make sense for anything you do to hook in as a Sink (caveat: I don't know the full extent of what you want to do)

> I raised the issue in this repo as I guessed it to be the most relevant place. 

Not suggesting it isn't; my nudge was more to consider that your best route to achieve this goal might be to write a Sink as opposed to building it into the core - i.e. before any impl takes place, 1. identify high level plan here 2. put issues proposing the extension in a relevant repo

Definitely have a look in the `serilog-sinks-async` repo where Nick took me through this ~6m ago (that sink is also an interesting read in that it accomplishes a lot without much code and the readme and tests covers very many aspects of an interesting sink).

Just running through and tidying up the tracker - thanks for raising this @aidansteele . I think there are some different implementations along these lines already in the wild, e.g. see https://www.nuget.org/packages/Serilog.Sinks.Buffered/ - it'd be great to explore the concept further but as @bartelink suggests, it would be better focused on a sink rather than the core at this stage. Please let us know if you end up making progress - would love to follow along if you create a repo with this goal!

Hey! Thanks for the feedback, @PureKrome, appreciate the input 👍 

Personally, and I may be out on a limb :-), I don't think it's a great idea having loggers in DI, registering loggers with the container, and so-on, and would vastly prefer the use of the static `Log` class, myself. The samples use it because I think it's the pit-of-success path.

I feel like ASP.NET jumped the shark with this- DI is about communicating the dependencies of a component, and cluttering up its constructors with `ILogger`s communicates nothing important ("this class does logging!"). Constructor real-estate is super-valuable when you use IoC a lot.

If you're writing in a more functional style with lots of static methods, passing `ILogger`s around also becomes a chore. If a component way down deep in a call graph needs to log, all of the callers need to get involved - transitive dependency churn.

RE unit testing, I don't think logging should be enabled during unit testing, or log events tested, personally - though there are some tools for out there for capturing async-local events logged through the static logger. Log events should be cheap to add and trivial to change without test impact, otherwise the logging gets stale since no one wants to have to modify tests in order to improve the content or punctuation in a log event/message.

Of course, opinions vary widely, and apologies if in my haste to get a quick reply to you on a Friday afternoon if I come across a bit dogmatic and opinionated :-) The choice of static `Log` in all the samples is conscious, though, and the product of a lot of soul-searching already, so not keen to change this. I've also used this idea of an event DU in the properties to death in another set of libs - it works well in that I get to test behaviors and logging while not having to introduce a logging abstraction. The value for me is in the fact that I get two critical things for free that are hard to get right:- 1. good perf 2. clean and clear logging statements that I don't need to explain or document the mechanism behind.)

One idea I've been mulling over is to have a formal `Metric` or `Event` in `LogEvent` that formalizes (in the same way that `Exception` does) the notion of some intentional payload to which one would actually be safe to attach a dependency to. comments.body:
Thank you for your suggestion! I once wanted to do this too.

What I came to realise is that it would further discourage the use of better variable names, and decrease the motivation to use better message templates, and decrease the opportunity to learn about them.
Also, it looks a bit like an abuse of the `Format` property, can you comment on that please?

> What I came to realise is that it would further discourage the use of better variable names, and decrease the motivation to use better message templates, and decrease the opportunity to learn about them.

That probably needs clarification since it's not clear why it will decrease motivation and how current implementation enforces it, because what I did several times is remove string interpolation from logging and replace it with templates. People are accustomed to string interpolation and they write code like this:

```csharp
Log.Logger.Info($"Whatever I {need} to log"); // let's not discuss usage of global logger, it's out of scope
```

And you need to change it everywhere to:
```csharp
Log.Logger.Info("Whatever I {need} to log", need);
```

if you want to use the power of serilog and structured logging. Because if you don't, people will just log strings and will parse them afterwards.

I don't think that effort to write good template is different in those two cases:
```csharp
Log.Logger.Info($"Whatever I {need:Reason} to log");
Log.Logger.Info($"Whatever I {Reason} to log", need);
```

About the learning point. Unless you'll have some analyzer that fails compilation by default on bad templates, only small amount of people will learn about templating. And you can do that for string interpolation:
```csharp
Log.Logger.Info($"Whatever I {need:Reason} to log"); // OK
Log.Logger.Info($"Whatever I {need} to log"); // Compile fails
```

People will be able to disable it or lower severity of compile errors in their projects.

Also, those methods can be provided as an extensions methods, probably and via separate package, if you don't want include it to core from the start. We can measure adoption of feature this way.

> Also, it looks a bit like an abuse of the Format property, can you comment on that please?

It's used in EF core that way. [Docs](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/ef/core/querying/raw-sql#passing-parameters), [source](https://github.com/aspnet/EntityFrameworkCore/blob/b969be3431415dfe224dfb3c7804592bb4b6c661/src/EFCore.Relational/RelationalQueryableExtensions.cs#L62)

> Also, those methods can be provided as an extensions methods, probably and via separate package, if you don't want include it to core from the start. We can measure adoption of feature this way.

Seems like a reasonable thing to try in this case :+1:

> Unless you'll have some analyzer that fails compilation by default on bad templates,

See: https://github.com/Suchiman/SerilogAnalyzer - there's a NuGet-installable package that will do this.

Definitely let us know if you are able to publish the extension package, interested to hear how it turns out; we can list it on the community packages section of the wiki 👍

There's also the problem with [`string` overloads being picked over `FormattableString` overloads](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/issues/46):

> We generally believe that libraries will mostly be written with different API names for methods which do different things. Therefore overload resolution differences between FormattableString and String don't matter, so string might as well win. Therefore we should stick with the simple principle that an interpolated string is a string. End of story.

If these methods were introduced, they'd need different names in order to pick the correct overload. Also

> Some library APIs really want consumers to use FormattableString because it is safer or faster. The API that takes string and the API that takes FormattableString actually do different things and hence shouldn't be overloaded on the same name. Library authors will want to lead people to use interpolated strings, hence it should have a shorter name.

That ship has already sailed, so the "preferred" way would unfortunately have more verbose names.
Closing as we're not likely to act on this in the core project right now, but keep us posted if you explore it further, @aensidhe!
Another downside is that Rider/Resharper validates that the variable being formatted implements `IFormattable` through the `InterpolatedStringExpressionIsNotIFormattable` inspection.

Here's my solution
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/61816775/c-sharp-serilog-how-to-log-with-string-interpolation-and-keep-argument-names-in/61816776#61816776

I've just published a library (with extensions to Serilog, NLog, and Microsoft ILogger) which allows writing log messages using interpolated strings and yet defining the property names through different syntaxes. 
Would love to hear some feedback.
https://github.com/Drizin/InterpolatedLogging

Thanks! Not sure which extension point is going to work best, there are a few options.

There's already the `ITextFormatter` interface that can be plugged into most sinks including `File` - I'd investigate that first.

An `ILogEventEnricher` can modify event properties as they pass through the pipeline, but can't do much with message templates.

`LoggerSinkConfiguration.Wrap()` can completely wrap a sink, and can thus mutate events in any way you desire before passing them on. _Serilog.Sinks.Async_ consumes this if you're curious to see how it works; I think there are other examples out there (https://github.com/nblumhardt/serilog-sinks-timewarp is another).

Finally, adding a hook point on the file sink to wrap the `File` used behind the scenes - e.g. - `onOpenFile: ...` - would be the way to go for binary encodings.

HTH!
Closing this for now as it's been idle for a while, but please let us know how you went, if you were able to make any progress, @AlexaCodex ! 👍

Hi! `AccessViolationException` doesn't usually indicate a memory leak - rather, the program is trying to read or write from a memory address that's not valid in its address space.

The call stack here indicates that this is happening during `ExceptionEnricher.Enrich()` - chances are that the root cause is elsewhere, but the failure is happening while reading through properties of the `Exception` object passed to a logging statement.

Removing exception enrichment from your logger configuration might mitigate the problem; collecting a crash dump and inspecting the memory contents around the location of the invalid pointer will be necessary, otherwise. You might save some time and pain by determining what changes (particularly libraries, runtime, etc.) were made at around the date the problem started occurring, and selectively roll those back until things resolve.

Hi Sean,

actually, the `ForContext()` methods return a new logger, with "extra enriching", but do not affect the `logger` they are called on.

Basically when you do `this.logger.ForContext("TestProperty", "TestValue");` , `this.logger` is not changed at all.

You can either : 

1. chain method calls if you only want to enrich once : 

```csharp
this.logger.ForContext("TestProperty", "TestValue")
           .Debug("Starting the process of adding a beneficiary.");
```

2. store the `ForContext()`ed logger in a separate variable : 
```csharp
var contextLogger = this.logger.ForContext("TestProperty", "TestValue");
contextLogger.Debug("Starting the process of adding a beneficiary.");
```

3. use the `LogContext` if you want all the log events generated in a given scope to be enriched ... See wiki page : https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Enrichment#the-logcontext

I hope this helps !

comments.body:
It turns out the sinks decide whether and how to output `$type` which makes sense when I think about it, and Console, at least, always does this if a type is known and it decides the data value is a "structure" type.

My _Delegate_ example above returns a `dynamic`. That and the `Expando` examples take slightly different paths through Serilog. The `dynamic` does represent an anonymous type by the time Serilog considers it, and it is [visited](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-console/blob/dev/src/Serilog.Sinks.Console/Sinks/SystemConsole/Formatting/ThemedJsonValueFormatter.cs#L107) in the sinks as a "structure" log value type which is appropriate for anonymous types.

On the other hand, `Expando` is recognized as `IEnumerable` but it fails the attempt to represent it as `IDictionary`. For some reason the `IsConstructedGenericType` fails in `Serilog.PropertyValueConverter` [`TryGetDictionary`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Capturing/PropertyValueConverter.cs#L312). I also suspect it would fail the `typeof(Dictionary<,>)` check because it implements `IDictionary`, I don't think it derives from the concrete dictionary type. As a result, `Expando` also falls through and gets visited in the sinks as a "structure" log value type.

I only mention this because if I or anyone else wants to address this issue, `Expando` should probably be fixed completely within Serilog's `PropertyValueConverter`, whereas `dynamic` / anonymous type representation is looking like a sink-configuration issue (a switch indicating whether to output the `StructureValue.TypeTag` in the various value formatters). 

But I use anonymous types a lot in my libraries -- maybe I'm the only person bothered by it!

(As an aside, debugging into Console was quite the hassle... my delegates package is .NET Standard 2.0 whereas most of Serilog is still 1.x, and the SDK mismatch meant I had to clone everything, unwire it all from NuGet, rebuild local debug versions and point everything at everything else...)

So those are my proposals:

- Fix `ExpandoObject`-handling in `PropertyValueConverter`
- Consider a switch for sinks about whether to ignore `LogEventPropertyValue.TypeTag`


Edit: 
In terms of recognizing an `ExpandoObject`, for `Type t = typeof(ExpandoObject)`:
- clearly this is false: `t == typeof(Dictionary<,>)`
- but _this_ is true: `t.GetInterface(typeof(Dictionary<,>).FullName)`)
- and the above is true for a real `Dictionary<,>` as well.

To me it looks like the `IsConstructedGenericType` test is unnecesary -- just look for the generic dictionary interface, cast it, then use the cast to validate the key is valid.

Bah... `Type.GetInterface` isn't available in .NET Standard 1.3. Boo!

Personally, although I wish you all the best and I'm glad to hear others are becoming more interested in structured logging, I don't think there's any chance whatsoever of settling on a single standard for this.

Would a more valuable project here be a set of adapters that could transform any arbitrary format (Elastic's, CLEF, GELF, NLog's etc.; newline-delimited vs streamed vs array-format) into any other? comments.body:
Hi,

thanks for filing an issue. The behavior you observe is *by design* and is the expected behavior.

If you want to attach extra properties that are not part of the *message template*, you should use one of the `.ForContext(...)` overloads (see https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Writing-Log-Events#correlation ). 

In your case, that would mean : 
```csharp
Log.ForContext("First", new { Param1 = "Test1" })
   .ForContext("Second", new { Param2 = "Test2" })
   .Debug("Hello World");
```

It turns out I asked a [similar question on Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/30637416/how-can-i-add-a-named-property-that-is-not-part-of-the-message-template) back in the days :-D  

There is also a [great series of articles](https://nblumhardt.com/2016/06/structured-logging-concepts-in-net-series-1/) by @nblumhardt that I would recommend, and in particular, this post covers *context enrichment* : https://nblumhardt.com/2016/08/context-and-correlation-structured-logging-concepts-in-net-5/ 

I hope this helps !
Thank you!

comments.body:
I am wondering if adding a *suffix* after a key should just be globally accepted everywhere to allow adding *duplicate-ish* settings, and not only for the `:with:` method calls .... 

For instance, in order to add `Destructure.AsScalar(typeof(Foo))` and `Destructure.AsScalar(typeof(Bar))`, we would end up with : 

```xml
<add key="serilog:destructure:AsScalar.scalarType" value="My.Namespace.Foo"/>
<add key="serilog:destructure:AsScalar.scalarType" value="My.Other.Namespace.Bar"/>
```

which won't work as expected because the same `key` appears twice...

One option would be to allow a *suffix* after the actual parameter directive, no matter what, and allow : 

```xml
<add key="serilog:destructure:AsScalar.scalarType:foo" value="My.Namespace.Foo"/>
<add key="serilog:destructure:AsScalar.scalarType:bar" value="My.Other.Namespace.Bar"/>
```

but I'm not super happy about reusing the character `:` with a different meaning here ... 

The other question is also, when a method accepts multiple parameter, we need to be able to see that several lines go together and group them to resolve to an actual method call ... So that would mean understanding that some groups of settings belong together : 

```xml
<!-- We actually configured our pipeline with 2 instances of the same Sink class ...-->
<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param1:first" value="value of param1 for first"/>
<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param2:first" value="value of param2 for first"/>

<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param1:second" value="value of param1 for second"/>
<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param2:second" value="value of param2 for second"/>
```

again, the choice of character `:` is a bit misleading ... 


I'm thinking something along the lines of 

```xml
<!-- We actually configured our pipeline with 2 instances of the same Sink class ...-->
<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param1#first" value="value of param1 for first"/>
<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param2#first" value="value of param2 for first"/>

<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param1#second" value="value of param1 for second"/>
<add key="serilog:write-to:MySink.param2#second" value="value of param2 for second"/>
```

i.e. using the `#` that is kind of a well-known symbol for *identifier* (and useful for grouping), but also has a meaning of *comments* that are ignored by the compiler in other languages ...

In the case of the `With()` family of configuration methods that would give us : 

```xml
<add key="serilog:enrich:with#myEnricher" value="My.Namespace.MyEnricher"/>
<add key="serilog:enrich:with#anotherEnricher" value="Your.Namespace.AnotherEnricher"/>
```

The `using` directives would then be a bit misaligned, though, but accepting both `:` and `#` seems feasible ...

Whatcha think ? :)

I really like the use of `#` as a comment-like marker that also provides uniqueness. I feel that `#` instead of `:` emphasizes it isn't part of the key-as-call-stack (so to speak). Originally I was worried about the disparity of first saying it provides uniqueness, but then also saying it links argument list keys, but the reality is that this usage still feels right to me.

There are actually requests for this (meaningful keys), for example, twice in https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-configuration/issues/70, but they're rooted in the common frustration with `WriteTo` exposing implementation details (the need for a unique indexer) to the user -- a leaky abstraction I think we should design away for config sources that allow nesting -- not the case with KVP, of course. But it's great that your `#` syntax could solve other problems.

In fact, last year Nick started https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-configuration/issues/49 to discuss streamlined `WriteTo` syntaxes. I voiced an opinion that the user shouldn't be burdened with the need to manage unique keys. There I imagined generating completely internal unique keys, but the `#` approach means the key would remain human-readable (with or without a machine-generated uniqueness suffix, as needed), which would be a big plus when debugging. As you know, the reflection plumbing in config packages gets pretty complicated.

Minor, but I think the issue title is a little misleading, it isn't really limited to the Enrich, Destructure, and Filter features (as your second post illustrates with WriteTo examples).

I'm working through open issues and closing most of those that have no activity in the past 12 months as `stale`. This helps us track and prioritize the issues that have the most impact.

If you believe that this issue still needs attention, please feel free to comment here. Thanks!

comments.body:
Hi,

You are using the default *output format*  for the *File sink*, which is 
`{Timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff zzz} [{Level:u3}] {Message:lj}{NewLine}{Exception}`. 

This means that by default, you will see the *rendered message + properties* (`{Message}`) but not attached properties (like *contextual information*) that are not part of the log message template.

You can use the `{Properties}` element in the output format to show *remaining* properties that are not used in the log message template. This is documented here : https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Formatting-Output#formatting-plain-text 

If you try : 
```
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
                .Enrich.FromLogContext()
                .WriteTo.File(logsFile, 
                    outputTemplate: "{Timestamp:yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff zzz} [{Level:u3}] {Message:lj}{NewLine}{Exception}{NewLine}{Properties}"
                    rollingInterval: RollingInterval.Day)
                .CreateLogger();
```

You should see the extra properties (like `SourceContext` or values from `LogContext`). 
You can also change formatting of the `{Properties}` to `{Properties:j}` for JSON-formatting of the properties.

I hope this helps !
