comments.body:
So I think there are two parallel tasks here:

1. where to organize the "reference" documentation.
1. How much to put in each projects readme file.

Regarding the second here is what I see:

* All the readmes should have the current examples expanded to three forms 
 * configured that part of the project in code
 * configured in app.config
 * configured in appsettings.json.
* All the readmes for sinks should list the overload methods that the config file plugins will invoke via `WriteTo`.

I think that's an easy thing to work towards. Its a lot of redundancy, but it lets you a person coming into Serilog understand where to look to dive deeper.
Please take a look at the issue @merbla linked above... I made detailed notes on my on-boarding experience.

I agree with @zippy1981 that there are two facets to consider: the reference docs and standarization of what goes into each repo's README. However, I feel the README content should be minimized and generally static: a brief description of the purpose of the repo, useful bits of automated information (such as build status and version badges), and only three links back to the reference docs:

- a general "Getting Started with Serilog" page to guide completely-new users to introductory material (and simultaneously expose them to our handy new consolidated reference documentation),
- a package-specific "How to Use Serilog.Foo.Bar" page, which is a top-level introduction to using the package and links to more detailed package-specific topics (such as the different types of configuration options mentioned earlier) -- effectively much of what you get in the READMEs out there today,
- and finally, a package-specific "Contribution Guidelines" page, which tells new devs who want to contribute fixes and changes about the internals of the package (and explains the requirement to keep the docs up to date).

I think README should be minimal and static because we need PR contributors to also maintain any related documentation changes. I believe updating the docs should be _mandatory_ (enforced by anyone with merge rights) when a PR introduces changes that impact the docs. If you confuse the matter by saying, "some things go into the README but other stuff belongs in a separate documentation repository," virtually every dev in the world will take the path of least resistance and update the README, and we'll end up right back where we are now.

This leads to two big questions about the reference docs: where do they live, and what is in them?

Since github wikis don't support PRs, I propose using the free, webhook-driven [ReadTheDocs](https://readthedocs.org/) service to convert markdown in a git repo to their easy-to-use format. If you're not familiar with this service, a great example is the IdentityServer4 docs: [here](https://identityserver4.readthedocs.io/en/release/quickstarts/3_interactive_login.html) is a random link into the middle of their current docs, and that page is stored on github [here](https://github.com/IdentityServer/IdentityServer4/edit/release/docs/quickstarts/3_interactive_login.rst) (although they use RST format instead of markdown).

We could hook that to the existing but unused [serilog-docs](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-docs) repository. ReadTheDocs works like other webhook tools like travis and appveyor: a merge to master triggers a new build and the public-facing docs are updated automatically. They also provide links to download the docs in other formats like PDF, tag-based versioning (we could have dev and release docs...), and a ton of other features. (Exporting as eBook is cool, when I was new to IdentityServer I pulled down their docs into Kindle on my phone and started learning how it works during a cross-country flight.)

I think we keep this manageable by standardizing how we migrate each package. The Serilog wiki covers a lot of the introductory material that could be migrated as the general intro content. As described earlier, each Serilog package would get its own dedicated section (folders in the git repo) with subsections (files in the git folders) for the package intro page, configuration examples, PR contribution/orientation info, and longer term, whatever else might be appropriate to the individual package.

I think this is enough to allow us to actually migrate everything we have out there today, yet offers enough flexibility that individual packages with more complex needs can still expand on the minimally-required template. Naturally we'd use the template ourselves and the initial migration should mostly become a lot of cut-and-paste work.

comments.body:
Hi,

What you want in that case it to use the [File ](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-file)Sink twice when specifying your configuration, but use different _formatters_ in each.

For machine processing, I would recommend that you use `CompactJsonFormatter` from [Serilog.Formatting.Compact](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-formatting-compact) (needs installing from Nuget) , but you can also use `JsonFormatter` that is included with Serilog (see https://github.com/serilog/serilog-formatting-compact#comparison for a comparison of the two).

This would look more or less like : 

```csharp
var log = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .WriteTo.File("humans.txt")
    .WriteTo.File(new CompactJsonFormatter(), "machine.txt")
    .CreateLogger();
```

a) can you indicate what your preference is in terms of splitting the json from the text into separate files (most people want all text or all json at top level)
b) I assume you know about `RenderedCompactFormatter` - can you comment whether that helps (I use it for json - means I can send json to splunk and still port ugly regexy alerts and dashboards from what used to be text only logs)

Serilog's view of the world is broken into _capturing_, where we decide on the representation of a nugget of data, and _rendering_, where the nugget is formatted out for machine or human. There are advantages of doing this for the in-between event processing stages, where data can be transformed/modified uniformly.

It's reasonable to want to capture an object in two different ways for the different purposes, but it's not a scenario Serilog is likely to incorporate.

HTH!

Just to summarize where I think this landed..

 * Serilog's `LogEvent` is not thread-safe for readers concurrent with writers; concurrent reads are fine, but only in the absence of writes
 * Serilog makes this work by following two rules:
   - In the Serilog pipeline, modifications are only permitted during enrichment, which happens synchronously before the event is passed to any (potentially-asynchronous) sinks
   - If an event needs to be "modified" other than during enrichment, a copy is made and the copy is passed on to be modified instead (you can see this in action in `SecondaryLoggerSink`); this avoids modifying the original event, which may already be being processed asynchronously by other components
 * Loggers can mutate the events passed into them via `Write(event)`, and so events emitted by one logger must be copied before calling this method (i.e. as per `SecondaryLoggerSink`)
 * The code in question passes events into a secondary logger without doing this

(Really all of this boils down to a simple rule: modify events in enrichers, don't modify events in sinks.)

Because the app and pipeline are quite complex, it's difficult to offer a more precise analysis here, but, breaking the rule will result in the kind of exception that's being reported, and removing the offending code (or working around it by relying on `WriteTo.Logger()`'s implicit copy) does cause the issue to disappear, so I'd say we're as close to conclusive as possible at this point.

There are heaps of opportunities to design more bullet-proof pipelines based on immutable events (I've been working on one for a year or so on the sidelines..) but getting performance and allocation overhead competitive with the current design is a decent challenge. I think we should close this issue now, but keep an eye on future opportunities.

It will solve the threading issue but inner sinks could observe enriched events of each other as side effects because of `LogEvent`'s mutability + increased allocations so I'm not sure if this needed (since there were no complaints for the 1.0-1.1)

Thoughts?

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Configuration/LoggerSinkConfiguration.cs#L222

@nblumhardt I think it's a bit different. The problem with the `Wrap` is that `1.2.0` can create different pipelines depending on how you configure:

```
                   ̶  BackgroundWorkerSink -> WrappedSink1
                  /
SafeAggregateSink  ̶̶  BackgroundWorkerSink -> WrappedSink2
                  \
                   ̶  BackgroundWorkerSink -> WrappedSink3
```
or 
```
                   ̶  BackgroundWorkerSink -> WrappedSink1
                  /
SafeAggregateSink  ̶̶  WrappedSink2
                  \
                   ̶  WrappedSink2
```
etc.
To make it usable with `Async` it should create this:
```
                                                                ̶  WrappedSink1
                                                               /
SafeAggregateSink -> BackgroundWorkerSink -> SafeAggregateSink ̶ ̶  WrappedSink2
                                                               \
                                                                ̶  WrappedSink3
```

The `1.0-1.1` create this pipeline:
```

                                                                         /
SafeAggregateSink -> BackgroundWorkerSink -> Logger -> SafeAggregateSink ̶ ̶  WrappedSink2
                                                                         \
                                                                          ̶  WrappedSink3
```
There is no `SecondaryLoggerSink` and no `LogEvent` copying because it doesn't rely on `.Logger(..)`. So the _lightweightness_ of using `Wrap` is pretty symbolic in this case.

```
   .WriteTo.Async(c => c.Sink(new LoggerConfiguration().Enrich.WithProperty(...).WriteTo.Sink(...).CreateLogger()))
         .CreateLogger();
```

Hope you all had a good weekend. I've taken another look and put together #1165, which ensures we reliably get either:

```
                                                                ̶  WrappedSink1
                                                               /
SafeAggregateSink -> BackgroundWorkerSink -> SafeAggregateSink ̶ ̶  WrappedSink2
                                                               \
                                                                ̶  WrappedSink3
```

Or:

depending on the number of sinks inside the wrapper.

The PR also disables `Enrich` etc. within the wrapped configuration block, so `wt.X().Enrich(...)` becomes benign.

That one has always been present - guiding people towards chaining in `WriteTo.Logger()`  - rather than writing a sink that forwards events on to a logger - seems like reasonable defense.

comments.body:
Hi Mike,

Unfortunately it's a bit of a complex area to sum up in a quick reply - things have evolved to where they are right now via a fairly long process, with perf also playing a significant part. Probably best to tackle it scenario-at-a-time :-)

Given your `AppDomain` example, the issue here is that _capturing_ happens once, to create a `LogEvent` with properties that are either scalar or structure values. The sinks don't get to choose how this is done, and there's no conversion between scalar and structure representations of the same piece of data because by the time you have one or the other, the original, source `AppDomain` object may be long gone.

Hope this helps; if there's another particular scenario that would be a better focal point let me know. Cheers!

OK @nblumhardt thank you for the explanation there.  Please note that I am indeed discussing the capturing of data, or rather, the _configuration_ of capturing of data.  That is, if I have configured a destructuring policy for a particular type, but that policy isn't being recognized and adhered, then why am I bothering to define it? 😄  To quote the documentation that is adding to my confusion here (emphasis mine):

"When Serilog _doesn't recognise the type_, and no operator is specified (see below) then the object will be rendered using `ToString()`."

In the case I am describing, I have provided serilog the definition of a type and what I would like to do with it by way of the destructuring policy, but in my view it is not being recognized.

One of the concerns here is that by forcing the use an operator `@` or `$`, you are forcing the consumer to change their template, which would mean a different hash which complicates the subsequent analytics as a result.

I hate to suggest it, but it is almost as if we require a `ISerializationPolicy` that captures the behaviors around how destructuring and scalar behaviors are defined. 😆 The policy is what then returns the `LogEventPropertyValue` which is then used by Serilog.

Along such lines, the other issue I am seeing is the use of `ToString` to determine the scalar value of an object.  It would be incredibly valuable to configure control over this as well.

FWIW, I am more than happy to send a PR to address these points. 🤓

Hi Mike, thanks for the reply. Opting into `@` is pretty central to Serilog's design - there are other ways to look at the problem. `"{@Foo}"` says, _I'm recording the details of this here `Foo`, and I'm okay with the cost of that_, while a few lines of code away, a `"{Foo}"` says _I just want to record what this is_ ... i.e. usually it's `ToString()`.

There's also a very strong performance motive for keeping destructuring policies out of most logging statements; although it might be possible to query policies without a big perf hit, there are a lot of trade-offs involved. This is why extending the set of `IScalarConversionPolicy`s hasn't been a desirable scenario so far - they're individually queried for each logged value, every time.

I would love to dig in further, but this could end up being a very long reply, so I should leave it here - but I should add: I am sure there are opportunities to improve ergonomics, here. Changing the opt-in requirement of `@` probably isn't on the table, but some better control of scalar conversion seems reasonable. It's just that for the possible gains, the implementation effort and mountain of tedious benchmarking work that would come with it keeps me away :-)

This is where that perf challenge rears its head :-) .. after the change, we'd go from a very quick capturing of scalar values under destructuring, to a slow check through every policy. The ordering there is deliberate, unfortunately.

I'm afraid there's not a great workaround; you could define a `ScalarWrapper` type and do:

```csharp
Log.Information("Hello {AppDomain}", new ScalarWrapper(appDomain));
```

and then use `Destructure.AsScalar<ScalarWrapper>()` to get the behavior you want. Ugly, I admit :-) Flipping this around to use a wrapper type on the destructuring side might be a fraction nicer.

But on the whole, scalars aren't really designed to be used this way - the requirement that scalar values be thread-safe (and practically immutable) makes them a poor fit for a formatting aid. Your initial identification of `IScalarConversionPolicy` as the extension point seems close to the mark - it's just that for an edge case, the work involved in designing/adapting/benchmarking the mechanism seems on the high side :-)

> after the change, we'd go from a very quick capturing of scalar values under destructuring, to a slow check through every policy

Ah, OK.  I didn't realize that you could destructure scalars, but sure enough in the block above the code that I outlined there is a check for destructuring a `string`.  Seems like that should be defined in a `IDestructuringPolicy`, however. 😉 Are there any other scalars that are typically destructured?  The reason I even ask is that changing the order of the statements did not break any tests, which of course raises my suspicions here. :)

In the meantime I will continue to mull this and give some thought to your `ScalarWrapper` suggestion.  Thank you for your time and insight @nblumhardt !

Alright, I figured this one out.  Both Console and Trace sinks accept a `ITextFormatter`.  I'll simply decorate them, intercept the values and pass the new ones to the decorated component.  Piece of cake. 🍰  Closing now and chalking this one up to newb/user error.
Nice! Glad you found a workable alternative :+1:

Hi, and thanks for getting in touch!

This doesn't sound so much like a problem with file sharing, as with your FTP client; Serilog's file logger allows other processes to read and write to the file, but any that try to take an *exclusive* lock will fail.

This is the situation that `keepFileOpen=true` is working around; we don't currently have an alternative in Serilog - it's not an undesirable feature, but AFAIK it has a pretty heavy performance overhead so no one has looked at it in earnest so far.

I believe you can configure *AzureTableStorage* also via the appsettings, passing the arguments to call the method: 

You could probably load everything from the `<appSettings>` if it looks like this : 

```xml
<!-- global minimum level of serilog-->
<add key="serilog:minimum-level" value="Information" />
<!-- writing to file -->
<add key="serilog:using:File" value="Serilog.Sinks.File" />
<add key="serilog:write-to:File.path" value="log.txt" />
<!-- writing to Azure Table Storage -->
<add key="serilog:using:AzureTableStorage" value="Serilog.Sinks.AzureTableStorage" />
<add key="serilog:write-to:AzureTableStorage.connectionString" value="TheConnectionString" />
<add key="serilog:write-to:AzureTableStorage.restrictedToMinimumLevel" value="Fatal" />
```

And in your code, calling `.ReadFrom.AppSettings()` as usual ... 

Configuring the *AzureTableStorage* sink with `serilog:write-to:AzureTableStorage.restrictedToMinimumLevel` `Fatal` mostly remove all the noise from *AzureTableStorage*. While not technically disabled, in most scenarios, it's close enough ! And you can change the value later on when you actually need all the noise ...


Anoter option is to use `.ReadFrom.AppSettings(string settingPrefix)` to load the config in 2 shots and do something like : 

```csharp
var logConfig = new LoggerConfiguration
                .ReadFrom.AppSettings(); // load the serilog:* settings

bool azureTableStorageIsEnabled = ReadValueFromConfigSomewhere();
if( azureTableStorageIsEnabled ){
    logConfig = logConfig.ReadFrom.AppSettings("azureTableStorage"); // load the azureTableStorage:serilog:* settings
}

Log.Logger = logConfig.CreateLogger();
```

and have a config file like this one : 

```xml
<add key="enableAzureTableStorageLogs" value="true" />
<!-- global minimum level of serilog-->
<add key="serilog:minimum-level" value="Information" />
<!-- writing to file -->
<add key="serilog:using:File" value="Serilog.Sinks.File" />
<add key="serilog:write-to:File.path" value="log.txt" />
<!-- writing to Azure Table Storage -->
<add key="azureTableStorage:serilog:using:AzureTableStorage" value="Serilog.Sinks.AzureTableStorage" />
<add key="azureTableStorage:serilog:write-to:AzureTableStorage.connectionString" value="TheConnectionString" />
```

I hope this helps :)

You can find more details about the syntax for the configuration formats in here : 
- [*Serilog.Settings.AppSettings*'s repo](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-appsettings)

comments.body:
Hey folks!

`LogContext` is a stack - so it needs to be pushed/popped in order. If you skip the top-level element and instead pop something half-way down the stack, this will pop everything above it, by design.

If you have  slightly different use case, implementing an `ILogEventEnricher` that uses its own `AsyncLocal<T>` storage should cover it.

Let me know if I'm off track :-)

Cheers,
Nick

Hi Nick,

I believe they are pushed/popped in order in the repro, actually :p 

I see that the order is : 
1. Push A 
2. (Async) WAIT
3. (Async) Push B
4. disposable2.Dispose() (= Pop B)
5. disposabe1.Dispose() (= Pop A)

Or am I missing some asumption here ?

Ah, sorry, I misread the code 👍 

I think this probably stems from the tree-like nature of `AsyncLocal` - child tasks inherit the async local state, but it's copy-on-write so changes don't flow back up to the parent task.

It's been a while since I dug around in here so I could again be missing something entirely, but my current guess is that this is "expected behavior" for `AsyncLocal` and not something we necessarily want to try working around in Serilog. Happy to help dig into it further if anyone has an alternative interpretation :-)

yes, as far as i know you are right on AsyncLocal<> behaviour. But since the Logcontext enricher uses the dispose pattern, i expected it to work like described in this issue.
After a little more thought, if it would work like that, flowing properties back to the parent, you would have an interesting case when a task spawns multiple children and they also push properties to the context. Which properties to keep in the parent? All of them? Should the child tasks share the properties? I'm not sure if you want to change these behaviors for Serilog.Logcontext. Maybe a separate SynchronzedLogcontext is needed, with different semantics.

I would add that this behavior is the result of `AsyncLocal` usage and immutable stack as its storage. So when `AsyncLocal` restores its state when leaving the method it restores snapshot of the stack it have. 
If the stack was mutable it would produce \*desired\* behavior but also could mess things up such as one async context could observe changes in another since copies of the async local state are shallow.

I am kind of wondering then, if the behavior is the same between .NET 4.5.* and .NET 4.6+/.NET Core ... since 
- .NET 4.5.* relies on Remoting/`CallContext`
- .NET 4.6+ / .NET Core relies on `AsyncLocal<>`

I read here https://stackoverflow.com/a/31708169/474763 that they have a different behavior : 

> Technically, there's a big difference in the implementation as the CallContext is cloned each time it is copied (using CallContext.Clone) while the AsyncLocal's data is kept in the ExecutionContext._localValues dictionary and just that reference is copied over without any extra work.

I'm kind of confused around all that, so sorry or the dumb/irrelevant comment :)

:+1: thanks for all of the extra info @ivankoster.

I think the way to look at this is that `LogContext` isn't so much a "disposable-based API" as a scope-based one. You can't, for example, take that `IDisposable` and pass it over to another thread and assume anything sensible will result. `using` is the primary scenario we're targeting, and beyond that some knowledge of the `async` machinery is going to be required. "Fixing" this would mean somehow reinventing TPL, I think.

Voting "close"/"by design" :-)

@tsimbalar I believe behavior is the same for `4.5` and `4.6 / .net core` in this context, because CallContext works across await points since 4.5 like `AsyncLocal`, so the main difference in implementation details / api / usage as pointed in SO answer.
But for .net 4.0, for example, with `Microsoft.BCL.Async` the behavior would be defferent since  `CallContext` would not work across await points on that runtime

@nblumhardt I'm fine with letting it "as is" ... I'm glad this issue  showed up, I learnt a few things here :) :+1: 

@skomis-mm  thanks for clarifying :+1:

Hi @YINZHU2016 , 

I think the issue here is because you are using variables (`outputTemplateStr`, `fileSizeLimitBytes` etc ) in your configuration instead of directly using literals like `"a string"` or `15` ... and the analyzer cannot guess the value of those variables (it only has access to the code source, not the values) ... 

I'll close this issue for now to avoid side-tracking. If you find issues while using *SerilogAnalyzer*, feel free to open an issue in the corresponding repo : https://github.com/Suchiman/SerilogAnalyzer

Imo the practice of putting the entire build up of the logging system into configuration is misguided. It results in a fragile implementation that requires deep understanding of the system's internals on the part of deployment teams to manage safely.

Far better to build up your logging system in code and just expose minimum configuration necessary that represents those aspects of your logging setup that it is actually useful and necessary to adjust.

The first implementation of our N-tier microservices architechture system using Serilog with an ELK stack had 20 config files per customer installation (each installation consists of a main and backup server). This created workload, risk and cognitive overload for our ProdOps team. We've just refactored the whole thing to build up the logging system in code and just expose in the application's own appsettings.json file the half dozen values that it will be necessary for ProdOps to manage.

Just because you _can_ build your entire system in configuration doesn't mean you _should_.
_Misguided_ might be a bit of a strong word 😄, but, configuration-in-code with a sprinkling of simple config file values is also the approach I default to as well 👍

comments.body:
Thanks for the suggestion!

In your particular scenario, would a successful flush imply success, or just best-effort? (I.e. if events had to be dropped because of a network failure, would `Flush()` throw exceptions?

I would think the contract needs to be stronger than "best effort" as there really should be an unrecoverable issue (e.g. network failure, buffer exhaustion) before a proper implementation would choose to drop events.  Obviously different sinks would have to address what this means within the confines of their unique constraints.  As an example, for disk based logging, I wouldn't expect Flush to fail because events were dropped due to insufficiently available disk space.  But at the same time, I would consider a disk sink to be an improper implementation if it just dropped events in response to a Flush for no reason other than it was an easier way to implement Flush.  :)  

Perhaps Flush's result should indicate only progress but return an eventual boolean that indicates whether events might have been dropped.  E.g.:

````csharp
    Task<bool> Flush();
````

Where the result would never fail just because events were lost, but would return false.  (It might fail for some other reason if Flush actually encounters a failure condition.)

Out of curiosity, what is the semantic for CloseAndFlush/Dispose today?  Do network sinks drop events when they are called?

Network sinks tend to buffer events for a set amount of time (say, 10 mins) during which they'll keep re-trying, before dropping events to prevent memory issues.

Is `AuditTo` a potential fit for what you're aiming to achieve?

```AuditTo```, if I understand it correctly, doesn't seem like quite the right fit.  It has an implication on every event that is written to a sink.  Flush doesn't imply anything about normal log action and has zero cost unless Flush is actually called.  Flush is just a signal to the sinks that *now* is a good time to write any buffered writes (as opposed to whatever aggregation policy they normally apply).

Network sinks buffer, but when you are about to CloseAndFlush they know that the pipeline is going to end.  Don't they have to force their pending writes then?  What do they do if the network isn't available at that moment?  Does CloseAndFlush block until the network comes back up?

Thanks for the reply!

> has zero cost unless Flush is actually called.

Not necessarily true for all sinks - there's a bit of synchronization that would be required for this I think (fair to assume that it's minor but nonzero)

> What do they do if the network isn't available at that moment?

Fail and drop events, at the moment; blocking shutdown was considered, but could be a cause of production outages in some cases (we're upgrading an app, start shut-down, block at the last minute, and can't then get the new version of the app running.)

Auditing does have some more cost; it'd be interesting to know though whether your actual application scenario can be re-cast in a way where the critical events are audited instead of going through the regular pipeline. It's not a complete replacement for flushing, but when digging into specific situations (audit an event before calling an external credit card payment API, for example), then auditing often turns out to be the better solution.

Definitely can't rule out adding flush at some future point, but it (like auditing) would require ecosystem buy-in, so it's a long way off at best.

Just for interest's sake, if you can share any details of where you would need to insert the flush calls in your app, it would be great to have the data point.

Thanks again!

Nicholas, 

Sorry for the late response on this (got busy with something else).  So far I have run across two scenarios where Flush would have been useful:

1.)  Assert failure implementation:  Here we are following a fail-fast strategy such that Asserts lead basically to an Environment.Exit.  Before exiting the process an attempt is made to flush the log buffers, snapshot the stack of the failing thread, etc.  It would be great if this could Flush.  The main thread typically is sitting on a using to Dispose, but it may be the thread asserting and we won't return up the stack from the Assert call.  The asserting thread will be blocked so Flush would either have to be sync or async but not require the caller to run.  If ILogger doesn't implement Flush or IDisposable the only access to Dispose is through a global static of the root of the pipeline (which we try to avoid - i.e. capability based model).

2.)  Test framework:  Here we create a logger in the suite and reuse it for each test method in the suite.  It would be great to force a Flush in the test clean up method.  This has two benefits:  a.)  it ensures that a crash from a subsequent test won't drop the log of a previous test thus confusing the investigation, and b.) for log output redirectors (like VSO's build/test automation) it ensures that when they capture and then tear the output per test method that they associate the right log entries with the right test method.

It the first case "best effort" in terms of losing events is the best we can ask for, but in the latter case I'd expect no events to be lost unless an unrecoverable failure occurs that should result in the test failing.

Hope that's useful.

Jason.

Hey, thanks for the reply! Great data :+1: 

1. `Dispose()` on `Logger` is a synchronous method and doesn't require the caller to run :+1: ... `ILogger` is not disposable, but if you check the return value of `CreateLogger()`, it's the concrete `Logger` type - you can e.g. register a delegate linked to its `Dispose()` method for close/flush purposes if you're using IoC and not setting up the global `Log` class.

2. In tests, logger mocks usually run synchronously, so there's no need to flush; i.e. I usually (when I can't avoid it, or if I'm testing logging infrastructure), have an `ILogger` or `ILogEventSink` set up that adds `LogEvent`s to a synchronized collection somewhere. If you have to use a non-local logger for tests, you can also try `AuditTo`, which logs synchronously and requires no flushing - `File()` and `Seq()` are the two sinks that have been updated to support it currently, but more can be added.

Hope this helps,

title: Lack of guidance on this pattern

comments.body:
Hi @invino4 - this should do the job:

```
var silent = new LoggerConfiguration().CreateLogger();
```

A little expensive for library code since it requires several allocations.  Something like:

````csharp
    m_logger = (logger ?? Log.NullLogger).ForContext<SomeClass>();
````

where ```Log.NullLogger``` was a static thread-safe singleton would be cheaper.  What do you think?
Still a little awkward, perhaps we should zoom out and look at the scenario in more detail, to see whether there's a better pattern for this?

Makes sense.  The scenario is that I have a number of libraries that are fairly general purpose.  In all of these libraries (and most of my software) mutable global variables are strictly avoided to promote composability, race-free operation, etc.  Strictly speaking, all capabilities are passed down when needed including logging.

Some of the consumers of these libraries are using logging.  If logging is in use, then there is some value in passing a logger to the libraries so they can log their actions (or even do Debug or Verbose/Trace logging).  However, if logging is not in use by the consumer it is onerous to have to pass a logger to the class.  Now the class can easily specify the capability as optional, however, in implementing the class I don't want this flexibility to either complicate the code or negatively impact performance.  The easiest way to prevent this is to ensure that the m_logger field is never-null (and usually readonly).  Now the reasoning about the existence of a logger is confined to the constructor.

Assigning the m_logger to an immutable static implementation (effectively a compile-time constant) is nearly free in most runtime environments (and can be truly zero-cost in the presence of tracing JIT or Whole Program Optimization).  This makes the pattern suitable for both class and struct implementations without having any impact on the allocation profile.  E.g.

````csharp
   for (int i = 0; i < 10000; i++) {
      MyStruct s = new MyStruct(logger: null)
      ...
   }
````

This loop silently, implicitly makes 10000 allocations.  If it is easy, I'd like to avoid this.

> Assigning the m_logger to an immutable static implementation (effectively a compile-time constant) is nearly free in most runtime environments

It should be easy just to create your own `static readonly ILogger NoLogger = new SilentLogger()` to get going, but having a `Logger.None` on the Serilog side does also sound nice. Open to a PR, if anyone is interested in pursuing this further 👍

Hi,

Someone correct me if I am wrong, but the *File* Sink is not synchronous. Log events are generated when the log statements are called (and may have very very close timestamps in a tight loop), but the actual writing to the file is deferred and batched. 

I believe this is similar to the behavior you would have in log4net when configuring it to be asynchronous with batches like in this article : http://www.nimaara.com/2016/01/01/high-performance-logging-log4net/ .

What is happening in your case is that the logging statements are probably slowing down your code (just a bit, we are talking about miliseconds here !).

You would probably have the same kind of performance if you used `AuditTo` instead of `WriteTo` in your Serilog configuration code : 

```csharp
string customTemplate = "{Timestamp:dd/MM/yy HH:mm:ss.fff}\t[{Level:u3}]\t{Message}{NewLine}{Exception}";
_fileLogger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .MinimumLevel.ControlledBy(LevelSwitch)
    .AuditTo.File(_logFile, 
              shared: true, 
              outputTemplate: customTemplate,
              fileSizeLimitBytes: rollOver, 
              rollOnFileSizeLimit: true)
    .CreateLogger();
```

(using `AuditTo` ensures the event is written to the sink before returning)

Given that Serilog will turn out to be one of the smallest possible dependencies of your services, I think the strategy of building facades is going to fall short: it seems infeasible (or unproductive) to try writing a dynamic facade for every dependency that's common to all of the services. I can see why you're looking for the functionality you describe, but if it was to match properties in that way things could get rather brittle in your codebase.  Picture you have an ASP.NET site and, somewhere in your pipeline, you decide to add a LogContext.Push() call so that every log event for the call now has `userId` being logged.

However, 6 months ago you, or some teammate, already added some log messages for some process on the admin screen governing the creation of new user accounts.  Part of the log message includes a placeholder for something you're going to log as `userId`.  Suddenly you've broken your logging code in a subtle way

Thanks for getting back at me :ok_hand:

Without any deeper knowledge of Serilog's inner workings, it would make sense to me if:

1. the "holes" and number of arguments are the same, use the explicit arguments to fill the holes.
2. the number of holes does not match the number of provided arguments, use enrichers to set any property match any hole in the provided template, then try to match the provided arguments.

I've only just started monitoring GitHub issues again, but I recall there were changes made a release or two back in this area, specifically to do with the holes and number of arguments.

Searching...

Found it :)
According to the release notes, v2.5 included https://github.com/serilog/serilog/pull/944
That links to https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/825 as well for a bit more context

I appreciate it's almost the opposite of what you're after but the changes suggested would need to keep that long discussion in mind.

I wonder if there could be a new logger.[Level]Bag() call   (where Level is debug, information, etc) and, instead of taking in multiple arguments, it just accepts a string and an object that has its properties enumerated and matched to the message template.  For your case you could then be sure that holes were aligned with values based on name, not position, which would be much less brittle.  The object passed in could be a C# anonymous class instance.
Exceptions can be logged as usual by having an overload taking the exception as the first parameter.

So something like
```
logger.InformationLevelBag(
    "widget {widgetId}, priced {widgetPrice} created for tenant {tenantId}", 
    new {
        widgetId = 1234,
        widgetPrice = 56
});
```

with tenantId coming from ambient context.

For sanity reasons it could do case-insensitive string matching of the properties.  Extra properties of the object would be logged out if the {properties} string was present in the message template.

Yes it's an object allocation, but it'd at least be a definite easy collect for the GC.

Note: this may well have already been suggested somewhere else in the massive list of Serilog issues :)

Thanks for all the input, folks! Closing this one for now, would be good to reopen if there's new perspective on top of the earlier lengthy discussions.

In a nutshell, though, `LogContext` is _nonlocal_. It shouldn't be possible to break/change the handling of log statements deep inside a call chain just by pushing properties onto the stack higher up. Trade-offs both ways, but switching tactics now would be a big undertaking and only viable with some really strong motivating cases.

Serilog Analyzer (VS add-in) will detect and reject these cases as invalid use of the API, highly recommended if you're able to install it 👍

There is already `MinimumLevel.Is(LogEventLevel level)` : 

```csharp
new LoggerConfiguration()
                .MinimumLevel.Is(LogEventLevel.Debug)
                .WriteTo.TraceWriter(context.Trace)
                .CreateLogger();
```

So you could just *parse the enum* :

```csharp
var level = (LogEventLevel) Enum.Parse(typeof(LogEventLevel), "Debug");
new LoggerConfiguration()
                .MinimumLevel.Is(level)
                .WriteTo.TraceWriter(context.Trace)
                .CreateLogger();
```



You may also want to use the `Serilog.Settings.*` Nuget packages that allow to read logger configuration from [AppSettings in a `.config` file](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-appsettings) or from a [`appsettings.json` file](https://github.com/serilog/serilog-settings-configuration).

Thanks for the follow-up. No, it sounds like you're trying to serialize a `HttpResponseStream` object somehow, perhaps indirectly, through Serilog. The serialization process calls property accessors, which can do odd things when objects aren't designed with serialization in mind. Any luck tracking down the log line that is causing it? Cheers!

Thanks for the follow-up!

Serilog does already limit serialization depth, but with custom code in the logging pipeline there are many possible paths to insert recursive calls that can't be detected.

It's possible, though, that the loop is not infinite but rather **very** slow because the debugger does a lot of work upon each exception being raised. Attempting to serialized the response stream a few dozen times by traversing the object graph along different edges could add up to quite a long delay.

I think the best route would be examining the stack frame around:

```
Serilog.dll!Serilog.Core.Logger.Verbose<string, string, System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, object>>(string messageTemplate, string propertyValue0, string propertyValue1, System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary<string, object> propertyValue2)
```

:+1: worthwhile discussion to have.

I think this would be called `LogEventLevel.Off` to match conventions in other frameworks. It would have to be a member of `LogEventLevel` in order to work in all the places levels can currently be specified - we could go through and add `disabled` flags, but then the convenience of just flipping some existing level configuration is lost.

The key issues are to:

 * ensure it's impossible or very difficult to create a `LogEvent` with the level `Off`; unless we start adding `if` checks everywhere, one could still create an `Off` event and have it traverse the pipeline
 * make sure there are no scenarios where `switch` statements in Serilog or client code would fall through to a previously unreachable case

Neither is a _huge_ issue, but the first one doesn't quite sit comfortably with me (it's the original reason for no `Off` member). On the other hand - turning logging off by not adding sinks or configuring the pipeline _is_ semantically correct :-)

Just trying to think through other ways to address the scenario, I think it's fair to assert that when this issue is raised, it's almost always in relation to runtime configuration.

Perhaps, if that's the case, more ubiquitous support for filters and https://github.com/serilog/serilog-filters-expressions might be the answer?

I.e. to turn Serilog off at runtime via configuration, one could use:

```xml
<add key="serilog:filter:ByIncludingOnly.expression" value="false" />
```

There's also `LoggingFilterSwitch` in the same package, for the equivalent to `LoggingLevelSwitch`.

I don't know exactly what it would mean to push this as the alternative - it already exists, but it's not super-discoverable and needs an additional package. Thoughts?

@nblumhardt I hadn't thought about the `filter` alternative. That sounds like a good way ... although, for an app that is already deployed in production but dot deployed with the proper dlls/packages, I believe specifying it in the config file would not work, or maybe even crash the app 😞 

I do agree that it doesn't really make any sense in scenarios other than via the *configuration* APIs and also the best way to *disable* something is to *not add it* in the first place 😃 , so maybe that's something to think about in the *configuration*/*appsettings* packages but that should not impact the *Core* repo. In the *xml* side, Config Transforms can handle the removal quite well, but I believe the `Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration` is *add-only* ...

I can't help myself from thinking that this could also be considered as part of the *Combined* settings thing ... , but well *when all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail*  ... 

But maybe allowing to **remove** defined *key-value* settings when combining several configs like : 

```csharp
new LoggerConfiguration()
  .ReadFrom.Combined(b => 
    b.AddExpression(....)
    b.AddKeyValuePairs(....)
    b.RemoveKeys("write-to:File:*")
    );
```

so that the sink is not actually added in the end ... 

... or directly in the *key-value* settings format, allow to indicate **removal** instead of **addition**
```xml
<add key="serilog:remove" key="write-to:File:*,minimum-level:override:*" />
```
... not a fan of having the word `remove` in the middle of a xml element named `<add>` but 😔  ...

Another issue with introducing `Off` level is that sinks should be adjusted to lazy initialize so they won't introduce unwanted side effects. Some sinks have this (`RollingFile`), but I believe most of them are not (`File`, `Async` etc).

For the `json` there is also a way using [jdt](https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/visualstudio/2017/05/25/whats-new-and-improved-with-the-slowcheetah-extension/) [transforms](https://github.com/Microsoft/json-document-transforms/wiki) to handle scenarios where different environments should have different configurations. 

For scenarios when suppressing is temporary thing I believe having `Fatal` should be enough. Who wants to suppress `Fatal` events anyway? :)

The more I think about this one, the more I think this feature is not worth the added complexity and risk :) 

Closing it, and we'll reopen if we need to :p

What a dreadful resolution to this issue.  "Too risky, can't be bothered".

ASP.NET Core has "None" as an option by default.  This attitude makes me reconsider whether using Serilog is worth it.

@jez9999: Our community has been able to achieve big things through constructive engagement; unfortunately, the tone of your comment makes it unlikely any of the volunteers here will take time out to help you.

If this issue is important to you, working through the analysis above and providing some insight into:

 - why the workaround is unsuitable,
 - how the challenges can be overcome, and
 - how risks to downstream consumers can be mitigated,

would be the way to move this forward.

> Who wants to suppress `Fatal` events anyway? :)

I don't think it's that uncommon. An example - a framework/library logs exceptions as fatal using a dedicated logger name and then rethrows. Since they are rethrown, they end up being application unhandled exceptions so they get logged again by the host application.

Having an option to complete mute logs coming from the library by this specific logger name name with e.g. `LogEventLevel.Off` (especially as Microsoft.Extensions.Logging has `None`) would make it very simple and symmetrical to MEL. Yes there are other ways of achieving this, but it would be nice to just have 1-to-1 parity in log levels between MEL and Serilog.
I do not get why Serilog does not use MEL's LogLevel enum which would make it less code for them to maintain.

@AraHaan MEL was 'invented' after, and adding a dependency on something like MEL is not a trivial matter. Any such change should also consider the broader picture of interop/overlap with other abstractions in MEL.

Just to add 2 cents to this issue. 

We are also wanting to simply configure loggers with a `None` or `Off` level to prevent logs from being produced.

The reasoning is that we are using a logging SAAS and we have to pay for the logs that are produced. In some lower environment where logs are seldomly if ever reviewed such as a `Develop` environment we want to disable all logging via configuration to save costs and at the same time simply configure a `Production` environment to an appropriate level. If logging is ever needed in the lower environment like `Develop` it can be arbitrarily enable via configuration on demand and then disabled when no longer needed.

While this maybe possible via a filter or other hoop it makes much more sense to do it via the logging level configuration that is built in and ready to go.

It is sad that Serilog has no plans to support this feature.

@DVS-Steady

> The reasoning is that we are using a logging SAAS and we have to pay for the logs

> While this maybe possible via a filter or other hoop

It's absolutely possible with a filter, which TBH I don't consider a "hoop" at all, especially since it's ijust one additional line of code - I do this is production for a more complex use case and, it works just fine.

In your specific case though, there are simpler and more obvious options:

1. Simply don't configure the SaaS logging sink in your `Develop` environment - this is certainly the simplest and most obvious way to do it, and indeed is the way I've done it on every single project I've ever worked on that uses such sinks

2. In your `Develop` environment, set the minimum log level for the SaaS sink to `Fatal` - I imagine logs at that level are extremely rare

Thankfully I'm no longer working in my job where we were using Serilog.  My attitude in future toward which logging framework we use given Serilog's nonstandard log levels and stubborn refusal to introduce useful new ones will be simple: don't use Serilog.

I agree, we should start looking into implementing our own system similar to serilog but have it integrate directly into MEL and provide built in support for what all of serilog's sinks and enricher's support.

@jez9999 honestly, that's absolutely fine. It'd be weird if Serilog had some kind of mandate for everyone to like it and agree with its "one true way" of doing things. There are other good options out there, hopefully one fits your requirements.

@AraHaan that's also great! Please do.

Others on this thread, I'm going to lock it because unfortunately it seems to be generating noise without moving anything forward.

The original resolution to this issue was that there's some risk involved, and that we'd reopen if necessary. If anyone is prepared to work through the implications of adding `Off` **rigorously**, working through a variety of libraries and ecosystem components, and writing up how they might be affected, this would be welcome in a new issue/proposal.

The kinds of things I mean are:

 * Points in https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/1049#issuecomment-338051356
 * Components that format levels - like sinks, expression templates, etc.; which sinks will crash or behave badly if they receive an event with the `Off` level?
 * Components that parse levels - what if anything would we need to do in Serilog.Settings.Configuration and elsewhere?
 * What would be the performance impact of enforcing that no `LogEvent` could be written through the pipeline with a level of `Off`? (Could we elide the check on code paths where we know the incoming level has already been determined to be enabled)?
 * Would any changes be needed in any other APIs that accept levels (not just `ILogger`)?

If the work and risk can be properly quantified then we might have a better basis to justify making changes, here.

comments.body:
Is another option (maybe a bit more opinionated) to integrate the code from @benaadams 's https://github.com/benaadams/Ben.Demystifier and use `ex.Demystify()` (extension) to preserve the stack trace as a "demystified" (unmangled) one?

Would also cover #521.
(Meant to imply that we'd do it for all exceptions in Serilog, rather than just capture information passing over the async/periodic batching sinks.)
Kicking off an experiment in https://github.com/nblumhardt/serilog-enrichers-demystify

The _Serilog.Enrichers.Demystify_ package mutates the original exception, so it won't avoid this issue (the stack trace etc. will still just be reset by the re-throw).

It seems like the best bet, long term, is to move away from carrying the exception itself, and instead perform some capturing of some sort at the point the event is created.

Here's one half-thought-out proposal that maintains backwards-compatibility: we create an `ExceptionInfo` type, which is a subclass of `Exception`. When a `LogEvent` is created, we collect the original exception. When the log event is received by `PeriodicBatchingSink` or the async wrapper that includes an `Exception`, we instead duplicate the event and substitute the original exception for the `ExceptionInfo`.

`ExceptionInfo` would carry the original message, stack trace (via the `ExceptionDispatchInfo`?), and have additional properties for things like the original exception's type. Calling `ToString()` on the info object would yield the same result as `ToString` on the original.

Things in this plan's favor:

 * Events that don't carry exceptions don't incur any cost; this is the majority of events passing through most pipelines (and exceptions themselves come with so much overhead it's unlikely our extra allocation will make any impact)
 * Exception-based enrichment almost always appears in the root logger pipeline, so packages like _Serilog.Exceptions_ and the demystifying enricher would be unaffected
 * No API-breaking changes :-) - only the two affected packages need to be updated

Unanswered questions:

 * Are there more packages that would need to opt into this scheme?
 * Can we get "close enough" to the behavior/appearance of the original exception in cases like `AggregateException`?

Thoughts?

Mimicking original exception with the subclassed one (`ExceptionInfo`) still could create behavior change in downstream sinks when `is` operator won't work as before along with the `GetType()` and other non-virtual members (though it is seems to be unlikely that there are many sinks that use more than just `.ToString()` of `Exception`).  

> Exception-based enrichment almost always appears in the root logger pipeline, so packages like Serilog.Exceptions and the demystifying enricher would be unaffected

The other side is also true - the modified `Exception` after re-throwing will be unaffected by the exception-based enricher friends (except `Serilog.Exception` since it will create new property), so async sinks still won't get pretty stack traces for such exceptions unless you capture `StackTrace` _string_ which is the most expensive one in EH.

> Mimicking original exception with the subclassed one (ExceptionInfo) still could create behavior change in downstream sinks when is operator won't work as before along with the GetType() and other non-virtual members (though it is seems to be unlikely that there are many sinks that use more than just .ToString() of Exception).

I think this a trade-off we could probably live with, but it's not ideal.

> The other side is also true - the modified Exception after re-throwing will be unaffected by the exception-based enricher friends (except Serilog.Exception since it will create new property), so async sinks still won't get pretty stack traces for such exceptions unless you capture StackTrace string which is the most expensive one in EH.

Good point - I guess we'd need more APIs in _Demystifier_ to do this efficiently on the other side of the async operation (given the raw frames somehow pulled out of the original exception). Needs more experimentation, I guess :-)

(Just adding another thought: to really completely solve this issue, we should probably also consider a scheme to either capture or ignore `Exception.Data`.)

The runtime support is coming to `.net core 2.1` (https://github.com/dotnet/coreclr/pull/16464) (and eventually to the full framework I believe). No need to use `ExceptionDispatchInfo`. 

For the [#521](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/521) there is also [improvement](https://www.ageofascent.com/2018/01/26/stack-trace-for-exceptions-in-dotnet-core-2.1/) .

I'm working through open issues and closing most of those that have no activity in the past 12 months as `stale`. This helps us track and prioritize the issues that have the most impact.

If you believe that this issue still needs attention, please feel free to comment here. Thanks!

Hi Chris,

In ASP.NET Core, there's no ambient context (like the traditional `HttpContext`) that a simple enricher can retrieve things like the IP address from. Plugging in some middleware is the way to go; the runtime cost is little more than a handful of function calls and context allocation per request, so it doesn't get a whole lot cheaper - it would be very surprising to be able to measure any performance impact from the middleware.

Others might have some alternative ideas to add, though - thanks for raising the ticket!

Best regards,
Nick

**Sounds great, anyone have any examples of just simple adding of HttpContext information via custom middleware?**

Also, I got lucky finding {Properties} {ActionName} {RequestPath}, is there documentation for what is available stock and per enrich for people that make custom output strings?

Hi @cgountanis -

The various output properties from Serilog are described here: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Formatting-Output#formatting-plain-text

Ones like `ActionName` and `RequestPath` are being added by the ASP.NET Core framework itself - the only way to determine what's there is to explore a log stream as far as I know.

For the middleware, the second example in this comment is essentially what you need to do: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/875#issuecomment-252169224

HTH,
Nick

I had similar issue and had to write a middleware utilizing "LogContext.Push" as described here. It is generic enough to be a NuGet package and allows to customize which properties from HttpContext should be pushed to LogContext. Hope it will be useful to someone: https://www.nuget.org/packages/Serilog.Enrichers.AspNetCore.HttpContext

> https://www.nuget.org/packages/Serilog.Enrichers.AspNetCore.HttpContext

Mentioned nuget wotking for me without problems.

Using a middleware for cases like this is unsatisfactory as that loads of ASP library code executes before your middleware is hit, and in Debug or Verbose mode that ASP library code will be writing loads of log entries none of which will benefit from anything you do in your middleware.

For example. Outputting a correlation ID in your messages to correlate requests through various services. On entry to a service this ID either needs to be a new ID (if it's the first service in your achitecture to handle the request), or it needs to be populated (usually from a header passed by the upstream service). If you set this in a middleware none of the ASP library logging that executes prior to your middleware (which incidentally includes all authentiation handling)  will have the correct ID and so you won't be able to mine your ELK stack (or wherever you keep your logs) and get the full log for a request.

This is one case where an enricher is required, for the same reason that ThreadId is implemented as an enricher. However as there is no way to inject any dependencies into the enricher context one is left having to bypass the DI system and doing things like initialising a static ServiceProvider somewhere.

It would be very useful if Serilog enrichers supported integration into the ASP DI system somehow.

comments.body:
.... and I'll start first :)

## Use cases
Based on my usage of *Serilog.Settings.AppSettings*, I often end up doing things like : 

**1. Reuse enrichment values in file paths**
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<configuration>
  <appSettings>
     <!-- snip... -->
    <add key="serilog:enrich:with-property:AppName" value="MyGreatApp" />
    <add key="serilog:enrich:with-property:AppComponent" value="FrontWebSite" />
    <add key="serilog:enrich:with-property:Environment" value="Dev" />
     <!-- snip... -->
    <add key="serilog:write-to:RollingFile.pathFormat" value="C:\Logs\Dev\MyGreatApp-FrontWebSite-{Date}.log" />
```
that is writing to files whose name reference the same value I used for enrichment ... and it would be nice not to have to repeat `MyGreatApp` and `FrontWebSite` each time, and declare the value only once.
In this case I really just want some kind of "string substitution" mechanism, I guess...

**2. Disable a sink based on a condition**
That's not something that can be done right now, but typically we do not want any kind of "write-to-file" logging making it to production, so when publishing our releases we have to go through some config transforms to remove configuration of RollingFileSink or FileSink. 

It would be nice to be able to disable writing to a sink completely based on the value of a variable ... 

something like : 
```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8" ?>
<configuration>
  <appSettings>
     <!-- snip... -->
    <add key="serilog:variable:environment" value="Dev" />
     <!-- snip... -->
     <add key="serilog:write-to:RollingFile.enabled" value="environment==Dev" />
```

**3. Pass variable *by reference***
I can't think of a single use case other that the `level-switch` where it would be useful to actually pass a real "object" as an argument of a configuration method. 


_(those are examples with the xml syntax as I have no experience using the JSON configuration format)_

## Possible caveats
Some things to watch for when defining the syntax : 
- avoid symbols that needs to be xml-escaped or json-escaped
- avoid clashing with Environment variable interpolation `%VARIABLE%`
- avoid looking too much like message templates or the string-formatting used in `outputTemplate`s

## For inspiration
- maybe look at [the way NLog does variables](https://github.com/nlog/NLog/wiki/Configuration-file#variables)
Closing this one for now ... can be re-opened if necessary, but it just bothers me to see "non actionable" open issues :)

comments.body:
Thanks for the note. Yes, this looks like a worthwhile improvement to explore.

I guess there are these implementation alternatives:

 1. Only support it for target frameworks that include `ValueTuple` natively (not sure yet which these are)
 2. Support it everywhere, by depending on the NuGet package carrying the `ValueTuple` type
 3. Support it everywhere, with an add-on package
 4. Support it everywhere, using reflection only (no direct dependency on `ValueTuple` itself)

It seems like a combination of 1 & 3 could work, i.e. use `#if VALUETUPLE` to conditionally support it in Serilog itself, and distribute a NuGet package version that would need to be activated via `Destructure.ValueTuples()` for use on other TFMs.

Anyone keen to investigate?

I've been looking into this some more; I think the best representation in Serilog for tuples is, in fact, arrays...

The issue with `ValueTuple<>` is that the member names are only available through methods that consume or return tuples, not the raw tuple objects themselves (there are some discussions online around this already).

Given that we're back to then using `Item0`, `Item1` and so-on, we might as well use `[1, 2]` as the representation.

Since tuples are primitive value types, one shouldn't need to opt in with `@` to serialize them. We already have special handling of arrays under regular capturing, so producing arrays from tuples doesn't seem too far from what we have now.... Any thoughts?

Planning a first cut that targets .NET 4.7 only, deferring the decision about whether or not to take a dependency on the System.ValueTuple (package) on other platforms.
This shipped in Serilog 2.5.

title: Support for c# 7 value tuple destructuring

comments.body: Then why is a Logger disposable?

@ffMathy `Logger` is disposable so that, as the root logger, log event sinks that implement IDisposable can be disposed. If you look at the implementation of [`Logger.ForContext`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Logger.cs#L96), the logger instance being created does not get passed the `_dispose` action (unlike in [LoggerConfiguration](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/LoggerConfiguration.cs#L138-L142)), making a call to Dispose essentially a no-op.

In short, don't bother disposing `Logger` unless it's the root instance.

It's also worth pointing out - the result returned from `ForContext()` just happens, under the covers, to be castable to `Logger` today; this isn't a documented part of the API however - it's possible a future version could return something else that may not have a `Dispose()` method on it. Hope this helps!

'In' means pushing a property onto the log context. 'Out' refers to popping a value off the log context.

> allow injectiong in custom properties at log time

If a destructuring policy doesn't permit doing it elegantly, check out `ILogEventEnricher`. It's purpose is to add properties to events, or to objects attached to events, dynamically.

(If the code doing the logging has the information, `ForContext("Property", value)` is a quicker and easier way to do it.)

> strange that we need to have a special json formatter to undo the serilogization of the original objects

Capturing values through the internal object model lets pipeline components add, change or remove properties from objects, or modify the structure of the logged data. It's also the means by which log data is "frozen" so that it's both thread-safe and accurate to work with events on background threads. Great, thanks for the follow-up.

Properties in Serilog are captured using an object model that's analogous to JSON.NET's `JArray`, `JObject`, `JValue` and so-on. There are some trade-offs, but the purpose of this design is to:
- Allow transformations on the structure of the data being logged (custom capturing rules, removal/addition/truncation of property values)
- Allow structured values to be passed between threads and used concurrently, even if the raw object they were captured from isn't thread-safe (only scalars like `string` are captured as-is)

Can sometimes be a bit surprising, but has the advantages of keeping sinks and pipeline components free of concern for thread safety of the logged data, or transformations into whatever the target serialization format is.

Cheers!

Then, there would be a function to test for each signature in the convention listed below. Each method would be evaluated to see if it matches one of the signatures listed below. If the method does not match one of the signatures the test would fail. Upon matching a signature, the method would be invoked with some arbitrary arguments.

Each method should also be evaluated that it’s public, returns void, and has the `MessageTemplateFormatMethod` Attribute.

To clarify the convention that needs to be validated is (for each log level):

```
Method0 (string messageTemplate) : void
Method1<T> (string messageTemplate, T propertyValue) : void
Method2<T0, T1> (string messageTemplate, T0 propertyValue0, T1 propertyValue1) : void
Method3<T0, T1, T2> (string messageTemplate, T0 propertyValue0, T1 propertyValue1, T2 propertyValue2) : void
Method4 (string messageTemplate, params object[] propertyValues) : void
Method5 (Exception exception, string messageTemplate) : void
Method6<T> (Exception exception, string messageTemplate, T propertyValue) : void
Method7<T0, T1> (Exception exception, string messageTemplate, T0 propertyValue0, T1 propertyValue1) : void
Method8<T0, T1, T2> (Exception exception, string messageTemplate, T0 propertyValue0, T1 propertyValue1, T2 propertyValue2) : void
Method9 (Exception exception, string messageTemplate, params object[] propertyValues) : void
```
Looks good. Whoah, what an overload list! :-)

From #896, the same or similar convention based tests could also be applied to the static class Serilog.Log.
https://codecov.io/gh/serilog/serilog/src/dev/src/Serilog/Log.cs

It also looks like that support for Serilog.Core.Pipeline.SilentLogger can be added to method overload convention tests.
See: https://codecov.io/gh/serilog/serilog/src/f3c0925a614d25b3850cd4bcf2b75e33fc3b1f14/src/Serilog/Core/Pipeline/SilentLogger.cs
Closing this umbrella issue; still plenty of opportunities in there I think, but we might do better by raising specific issues for any weaker areas.

comments.body:
Hi Alexey, thanks for the report. `LogicalCallContext` and remoting has been an absolute nightmare for this feature, we thought we finally had a bulletproof implementation in 2.0 but it seems we're not so lucky :( // cc @colin-young @DmitryNaumov @gertjvr 

`LogContext` uses `ObjectWrapper` so that when an app using it calls into a secondary `AppDomain`, any enrichers pushed onto the context stack (which may be arbitrary, non-serializable, user-provided objects) remain in the source `AppDomain` and aren't serialized across with the call.

Am I correct in guessing that the application you're working on has made a call into another `AppDomain` at this point, either through remoting directly, or via SQL Server Management Objects?

Using a subclass of `ObjectHandle` that returns a custom `ILease` from `InitializeLifetimeService()` should fix this, as you suggest, but figuring out how to keep the lease alive long enough without leaking the object entirely will need some thought. Anyone have any ideas?

.NET 4.6 introduced `AsyncLocal`, which does not suffer from this problem (it uses `ExecutionContext` rather than `LogicalCallContext` for the state). We already support `AsyncLocal<>` with a build flag; I'm going to create a PR now that adds .NET 4.6 as an explicit target so that it's used instead of this horrendous API.

Which .NET Framework version are you running, Alexy?

Thanks for the great reply, appreciate the feedback.

> Yes, we use remoting. Are you sure that the problem pops up only in remoting scenarios?

I believe the problematic `ObjectHandle` lease only starts after a cross-appdomain call. All 2.0+ builds include this code, so the situations in which it becomes an issue must be fairly limited or we'd be flooded with reports by now (see more info further below).

> Ah, one more thing: a custom wrapper class or ObjectHandle descendant will need Serilog assembly in the target AppDomain to be deserialized. What if Serilog is not deployed there?

Only if the target appdomain uses Serilog's `LogContex`, otherwise the `ObjectHandle` is never `Unwrap()`ped.

> If you're OK with custom wrapper class, then I'd suggest infinite lease time + explicit disconnection via RemotingServices.Disconnect, something like this:

The copying behaviour of `LogicalCallContext` will make it hard for one single thread, that might be emptying the `LogContext`, to be sure that the `ObjectHandle` isn't still active on another logical thread. Or at least, I'd be cautious asserting anything about when the `ObjectHandle` can be disposed, because there are so many potential (mis-)usage patterns, and this API is a pain to work with.

> I'm running .NET 4.6 so using AsyncLocal is not a problem. But I'm a bit confused about ExecutionContext... I believe it includes logical call context as a part of it, doesn't it?

`ExecutionContext` is there in 4.5 but the members supporting `AsyncLocal` aren't (AFAICT).

I'll merge the 4.6 fix now and leave this issue open for discussion.

@yallie build `2.2.1-dev-00697` including the 4.6 fix is now on NuGet; it's otherwise close to identical to what is on `master`, so if you can confirm it addresses the issue for you we can push it through to a release build posthaste.

> The exception looks like someone from secondary domain attempted to use LogContext.

I think you're right, the call goes through proxies.

I believe random slot name should be ok: an ObjectHandle will leak into other domains, but no one will try to access it.

I've found it, it was not that random, but good enough to prevent the problem. Even the text was extremely precise, it my mistake it was reverted afterwards.

 Use per AppDomain slot name, so other domain won't accidentally unwrap object reference.
https://github.com/serilog/serilog/pull/733/commits/3b55d2dbcefefc97fe0db37258195190bb4a9d5b
@nblumhardt if you don't need display friendly name (I think you don't), then that's fine. I still hope we did bullet-proof remoting version and this is just a small mistake.
Righto, had a shot at fixing it in #840 - though the `AppDomain.CurrentDomain.Id` was being appended, it's not sufficient to create a unique identifier when inter-process remoting takes place.

comments.body:
Hey @DmitryNaumov, thanks for writing this up. I've been thinking about this contention point as well and would definitely appreciate a PR that improves performance.

`ConcurrentDictionary` sounds like one reasonable option, though it incurs quite a bit more latency than `Dictionary` IIRC. If you are keen to PR it up, would you be able to add to `Serilog.PerformanceTests` so that we can measure the difference between the implementations in both a single-threaded as well as a high-contention scenario?

Regarding `DateTimeOffset.Now` - it's used because it makes the naiive `logEvent.Timestamp.ToString()` call show in the current time zone by default. Sinks like Seq that use timestamps either use ISO 8601 format, which includes the offset and so gets converted correctly to UTC for storage (Seq is all UTC internally) or in a few there's a UTC conversion done before sending the event out on the wire. If I could go back in time I'd probably give `DateTime.UtcNow` preference, but the current scheme's doing the job :-)

Just adding a couple more thoughts:
- Could we switch to a much smaller per-thread cache (e.g. `[ThreadStatic]`) to achieve zero contention?
- If the cache was per-thread, a circular buffer of up to 10 items would have similar performance to a dictionary lookup
- If the cache was per-thread it'd tend to perform better when different threads are doing different things in tight loops
- Could we win some performance back by optimising the parser? E.g. get rid of more allocations, switch to using a single discriminated-union `struct` instead of `TextToken` and `PropertyToken` that could be converted to the existing `class`es lazily to maintain compatibility?

I'd guess there's quite a bit to win by reexamining the overall approach, what do you think?

@nblumhardt it's just my gut feeling but I don't think many applications using serilog would benefit from per-thread caching, just because usually 99.9% (imo) apps don't care about thread affinity. So I would start with ConcurrentDictionary just to remove readers contention.

Now about parser. Of course we need to optimize it, but I assume in most cases it parses every template once and then it is in the cache. Unfortunately the real life behavior can be different. Have you thought about performance counters or anything else to be able to collect stats on, for example, template cache hit/miss ratio?

:+1: 

The one stumbling block for a "simple" `ConcurrentDictionary` port should be: https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Pipeline/MessageTemplateCache.cs#L60

`Count` is hugely inefficient in `ConcurrentDictionary`. Guessing we can work around this however.

Performance counters are interesting but a lot of fiddly work that I'm not excited about at this point :-) Perhaps extending `SelfLog` in such a way that various metrics collectors (or perf counters) could be plugged in would have less initial overhead? E.g. `SelfLog.Count("MessageTemplateCache.Hit")` and a matching plug-in provider interface.

As a way of getting this kicked off, perhaps the first step here is to get some benchmarks added for message template parsing in a variety of straight-line scenarios, and some concurrent/contended ones?

@nblumhardt You're right, there are many surprises in CD after generic Dictionary, like cost of accessing Count, Keys/Values etc, I will be careful. But let me start with performance tests to practically demonstrate the problem of contention, if any :)
