comments.body:
:+1:
I was looking into replacing NLog with Serilog in our projects and this was one shortcoming of Serilog.
We have a kind of "audit" log beside our normal application log and the exact requirements described here:
- Non-buffered writes;
- Throwing when logging fails.

NLog has options to support both of these.

Thanks for the input @heavytread and @jods4 - good to know this is a desirable feature for some folks. Some early exploration was done in this space but there wasn't a lot of demand so it was put on hold.

There are a few design possibilities with pros and cons; with more time to think about it, I'm back to preferring:

``` csharp
var logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .AuditTo.File("audit.txt")
    .WriteTo.SomeOtherSink()
    .CreateLogger();
```

In this model, the `LoggerConfiguration` structures the internal pipeline so that `Safe*` is not applied to  any `Audit` sinks, but does still wrap regular `WriteTo` sinks so that events from the audit log can be (unreliably) mirrored to something like Seq for easy inspection.

While `AuditTo` would ultimately boil down to adding a regular `ILogEventSink`, the configuration object would be `LoggerAuditConfiguration` instead of `LoggerSinkConfiguration`, forcing sinks that intrinsically supported auditing to opt in by providing an additional extension method on this type. This would permit sinks like those based on `PeriodicBatchingSink` to configure an alternative internal implementation for auditing scenarios, as the batch/timer-based implementation is unlikely to provide audit-like guarantees.

In practice I think this'd all work fairly smoothly because nearly all auditing will rely on `File`, `RollingFile`, `EventLog` or one of a few other reliable-enough sinks.

In the situation where a single logger might be used across the whole app, but only a subset of events "audited", I think sub-loggers would work here:

``` csharp
var logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .AuditTo.Logger(lc => lc
        .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(Matching.WithProperty("IsAudited", true))
        .AuditTo.File("audit.txt"))
    .WriteTo.SomeOtherSink()
    .CreateLogger();
```

How does this proposal sound?

sounds good!

> In practice I think this'd all work fairly smoothly because nearly all auditing will rely on  File ,  RollingFile , 

Yes but you'd be amazed what this kind of config helped us caught with NLog. 
Sometimes there's a typo in the configured path, the ACL on the file or folder are incorrect, the disk is full, the file is locked by another process or the network share is not available...

Everything usually works smoothly but it's terrible when the day you need to look at a log (or worse an audit log) you notice you had a bad config and there's no log!
Thanks @jods4 I'll run with this then :+1:

Hi Nicholas. Yes, all of that sounds very clean and a lot less hacky than what I'd proposed. Forcing sinks to declare whether or not they support auditing sounds lot better than changing the batching behavior so that batching might not actually happen even when the sink developer is expecting it to.

@heavytread this is now available in the published `-dev` packages for Serilog, Serilog.Sinks.File and Serilog.Sinks.Seq. We've got a tracking issue #828 to cover Serilog.Sinks.RollingFile and the two configuration subsystems.

Is it likely you'll have a chance to try out what's currently in the `-dev` build? Some additional validation/feedback would be great :-)

Call me crazy, but that sounds like it really is starting to cross down the path of event sourcing and making Serilog an [event sourcing implementation](https://github.com/EventStore/EventStore) seems to overload its value as a logging platform.  That said, it would be interesting to see how the event sourcing practice and logging would best complement one another.

@normanhh3 you could say that :-) but event sourcing is definitely not the intent here. Another way of thinking about it is that audit events are almost like a super-critical level, `SoImportantThatINeedToMakeSureThisReachesDiskBeforeMovingOn`. Many ways to use it, I suppose.

Anyhow, this one shipped in 2.2 (IIRC) so the ticket here is out-of-date. Cheers!

There must be something I am fundamentally missing. Even when I'm using the Literate Console, I'm not getting the functionality I'm expecting. I'm using it like this:

`Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
                .WriteTo.LiterateConsole(Serilog.Events.LogEventLevel.Verbose).CreateLogger();`
            `Log.Verbose("Ah, there you are!"); // This won't write to the console`

I'm expecting the above log to log to the console. Am I misguided?

> Default Level - if no MinimumLevel is specified, then Information level events and higher will be processed.

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Configuration-Basics

Level in concrete sink make sense only if it is higher than "global".

@aensidhe, 
I thought I did specify the minimumlevel... 

`Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration() .WriteTo.LiterateConsole(Serilog.Events.LogEventLevel.Verbose).CreateLogger();`

Even using named params doesn't work:
`Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
                .WriteTo.LiterateConsole(restrictedToMinimumLevel: Serilog.Events.LogEventLevel.Verbose).CreateLogger();`
            `Log.Verbose("Ah, there you are!"); // This won't write to the console`

@nathvi try this:

```
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
.MinimumLevel.Verbose() /// global minimum level
.WriteTo.LiterateConsole()
.CreateLogger();
```

Quote from docs:

> Logger vs. sink minimums - it is important to realize that the logging level can only be raised for sinks, not lowered. So, if the logger's MinimumLevel is set to Information then a sink with Debug as its specified level will still only see Information level events. This is because the logger-level configuration controls which logging statements will result in the creation of events, while the sink-level configuration only filters these. To create a single logger with a more verbose level, use a separate LoggerConfiguration.
Yes, that works and makes sense. Thank you!

comments.body: Stephen does a good job of explaining the Producer/Consumer pattern implementation here: http://blog.stephencleary.com/2012/11/async-producerconsumer-queue-using.html

Hi @jezzsantos,

Nothing directly exists OoTB that I am aware of.  As you mentioned you could implement via the delegating sink or your own sink implementation.

Just out of interest, was the call to the Azure Queue an IO or a network latency issue? (to give you 5x improvement)

https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-periodicbatching should go some of the way towards it (it's what the other sinks use).

The difference from what you've suggested is that the queue used is strictly non-blocking (and thus unbounded) but otherwise should cover what you need, and has the benefit of allowing batched writes for fewer roundtrips.

(It'd be interesting to look at a fixed-length/blocking queue, but probably significant work.)

@merbla thanks for the confirmation.

I have started creating a sink like that described here, for general purpose use. Might be useful to community for anyone with slow sinks, that they can just plugin perhaps.

An Azure queue _should_ in theory be quick to write to (in terms of network latency), but it is still an HTTP across the network, and that's when in production in the cloud.
In development, with the azure emulator in the mix, it is a call to an underlying local SQL database, which evidently (from pperf testing) blasts the disk to 100% for us when we are doing many API calls during integration testing. Which slows everything down 5X.

Primarily for us, the 5X improvement we want to see is locally in the Azure Emulator. And that directly affects the speed of our integration and E2E testing feedback loop. Which is vital to us. Which is why we are going after it. We assume any improvement seen locally will equate to some improvement in production (at scale), so there is more value in it.

Besides which, since we are calling our logging on average about 50-100 times in a single REST API call, it makes sense to batch these logging requests in memory before writing to queue, so this optimization is long overdue for us anyhow.

Guys @merbla @nblumhardt , I have just finished refining and performance testing a `BufferedQueueSink : ILogEventSink` class that has the following characteristics:
- Can be inlined with any other IEventLogSink
- Implements the consumer/producer pattern, but that is buffered and bounded.
- Can be configured with any buffer size (default is 50) but can be anything. The buffer size controls how many log events can be submitted (produced) before the buffer postpones (asynchronously) any more incoming log events, and forces consumption of those [queued] log events before allowing any postponed log events to be consumed. (This is what makes it a useful rolling buffer). This buffering is to prevent memory footprint exceeding the available memory, in the case where the production rate may be quicker than the consumption rate. Exactly what you need if writing the log events is slower than the code producing the log events. The sink uses the `BufferBlock<T>` from the MS TPL library.
- Supports concurrent consumption, so that a [thread pool] thread will be used to consume log events while the thread that produces logs events returns. This is especially useful if your sink is expensive in time or I/O. The calling thread does not spend its time writing to the sink, it simply queues the log event in a buffered memory queue.
- In performance testing, it is demonstrated with this sink, that the logging thread spends less than 10ms producing 1000 log events, and then returns. Whilst the consuming thread takes about 30s to consume the 100 events and persist them to local db storage. Thats a couple orders of magnitude increase in performance for the logging thread than it would be if it were using the original sink to write to local storage directly. Particularly useful if you are utilizing extensive and heavy logging but don't want the code that is logging to be blocked writing too sinks.
- It is believed that this sink can help improve the performance of any sink that uses the calling thread to write to the sink. It does come at the cost of a thread pool thread (per instance of the sink).
- One improvement would be to dedicate a single thread to be used for all instances of this sink, wherever they are used.

The reasons and motivation for writing this sink is described in the opening post of this issue.

I am happy to share this implementation along with its unit tests and integration tests, as a standalone component with the community to use, if someone can simply guide me how best to do that. The code is less than 200 lines long (2 x classes).

Here is the gist of the code: https://gist.github.com/jezzsantos/44bf844b27bebafcb64d9947e1896649

Hey Jezz, sounds awesome! I haven't had a chance to check out the gist, but in terms of making this available what do you think of packaging this in something like `Serilog.Sinks.Async`?

One possible API is:

``` csharp
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .WriteTo.Async(wt => wt.File("log.txt"))
    .CreateLogger();
```

The `wt` arg would be a `LoggerSinkConfiguration`, meaning that _any_ existing sink could be adapted this way. Under the hood, the `Async()` extension method can use a second logging pipeline to achieve this pretty smoothly.

There's enough interest in this kind of thing that I can see potentially being part of Serilog in the long-term, but just standing up a personal repo that we can all help to shape during the development process would be the easiest/quickest way to get started.

What do you think?
I am happy to do as you suggest. wilco

Thanks here is my first crack at it. https://github.com/jezzsantos/Serilog.Sinks.Async

I am working on the Nuget and AppVeyor CI right now
Shall we move the discussion over there?
Awesome, sounds great.
CC @DmitryNaumov - Dmitry, thinking this could be a good option to provide the background file I/O we were talking about, would be great to have your thoughts. Cheers!

Hey @DmitryNaumov,
I am no expert at Dataflow, the sink we now have over at https://github.com/jezzsantos/Serilog.Sinks.Async is based on work described here: http://blog.stephencleary.com/2012/11/async-producerconsumer-queue-using.html whihc describes how the `BufferBlock<T>` behaves when the buffer reaches its limit (to prevent) memory overflow. 

As I understand it, when the buffer is full, the async producer call is async waited on until the consumer catches up. So, not blocked per-se, just async blocked.

Can we take this discussion over there: https://github.com/jezzsantos/Serilog.Sinks.Async?

I am actually witnessing problems with this implementation in our REST service, that I don't yet understand, and it would be good if we could collaborate on that, over there rather than on this closed thread?

@nathvi ah, I see, yes - the edit makes it much clearer :+1: . You're opening the log file twice and not closing it in between.

When you configure Serilog, you need to construct the logger only _once_, and re-use it throughout the program.

If you do, for some reason, need to close/reopen the logger, you can `Dispose()` it (if an instance) or `CloseAndFlush()` the static `Log` class. I would guess that's not what you're after though.

Thanks for the note.

Just to make sure we're on the same page, I've created a .NET 4.5 console app, installed the `Serilog.Sinks.Console` package, and slightly modified your example to:

``` csharp
var log = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .MinimumLevel.Verbose()
    .WriteTo.Logger(config => config
        .MinimumLevel.Verbose()
        .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(e => e.Level == LogEventLevel.Debug)
        .WriteTo.Console())
    .WriteTo.Logger(config => config
        .MinimumLevel.Verbose()
        .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(e => e.Level == LogEventLevel.Information)
        .WriteTo.Console())
    .CreateLogger();

log.Debug("This is debug");
log.Information("This is info");
```

Both events are written to the console. Changing it to:

``` csharp
var log = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .MinimumLevel.Debug()
    .WriteTo.Logger(config => config
        .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(e => e.Level == LogEventLevel.Debug)
        .WriteTo.Console())
    .WriteTo.Logger(config => config
        .Filter.ByIncludingOnly(e => e.Level == LogEventLevel.Information)
        .WriteTo.Console())
    .CreateLogger();
```

Also works as I expect. I think the problem is likely to be specific to the file - does the process writing the file have adequate permissions? You can verify this be enabling [SelfLog](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Debugging-and-Diagnostics).

In any case, am I correct to assume that the config you really want is this one?

``` csharp
var log = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .MinimumLevel.Debug()
    .WriteTo.File("c:\\...\\log.txt")
    .WriteTo.Seq("http://...:5341/", restrictedToMinimumLevel: LogEventLevel.Information)
    .CreateLogger();
```

Hope this helps,
Nick

comments.body:
Would this not contradict the statement in the docs: 

> Property names may be suffixed with an optional format, e.g. :000, to control how the property is rendered; these format strings behave exactly as their counterparts within the `string.Format()` syntax

For example, `string.Format("{0:3}", "Information")` does not return `"Inf"`

The expectation set out with all other string format specifiers would be overridden for the special case of specific strings for level when shortened, which is perhaps a more glaring inconsistency that we implemented with `{Level,3}`

This is the case I was thinking of too, when we originally looked at it.

The content after `:` is completely dependent on what type is being formatted, so though `:3` doesn't return a three-digit number when applied to `Int32`, it could if that was the designer's preference over `000`.

For levels, `u3` or `w3` (three uppercase, or three lowercase) is natural when compared against .NET's numeric hexadecimal formats; the only thing missing is a way to specify sentence-cased values, perhaps `s3` or `l3`. It's pretty uncommon to have short values with an inital cap and trailing lowercase, so maybe not something that needs to be accommodated.

That's true, however the docs would have to change to cover the fact that if you're formatting any string other than level, placing `:3` within the format will behave differently. This means the only place to know how it works is by looking at the docs, which makes me wonder if aligning the new feature with the `string.Format` functionality might add more confusion, given the subtle difference in its behaviour.

Agreed, `:3` looks odd. I was thinking we'd only initially support `:u3` and `:w3` for this reason (I can't see mixed-case abbreviated levels being particularly popular).

Figuring out how to format a fixed-width level still requires some documentation/Googling either way, so not sure if it is too much of a caveat. By the same token, formatting any other .NET type (date, numeric etc.) requires specific knowledge of its formatting syntax.

The quirk I think we should try to get away from is that no other .NET type uses the `,n` width specifier to modify the output, only to (potentially) apply whitespace padding. I'd initially thought this was a pretty nifty trick on our part, but in hindsight worry that it's a bit much magic. Though the syntax is clean, the semantics are different enough that knowledge of .NET's formatting conventions isn't enough for someone to discover this functionality directly.
PR'd above; to avoid the `:3` oddity, `:t3` will do the `Inf` title-case formatting, in addition to `u3` and `w3` for upper/lowercase.

Hi Nick

Just looking at the PR and its changes.

I was a bit confused in the instance of logging with {Level:t7}, based on the updated inline data tests:

``` c#
[InlineData(LogEventLevel.Warning, 8, " Warning")]
```

became

``` c#
[InlineData(LogEventLevel.Warning, 8, "Warning")]
```

Is the expectation of logging at `Debug` level with `{Level:t8}` for the output string to be 8 characters wide, with padding? Based on your update it appears that it will log out `Warning` with no padding, therefore not being fixed-width.

Hi Anthony,

No, the numeric part of the format is interpreted more like a "trim" than padding. I left the n+1 length tests in there, modified, to make the behavior clear, though the decision to go that way was arbitrary.

To get the padded result, `{Level,8:t7}` would result in `" Warning"` if desired.

It may make more sense to pad, I'm not sure though - the `,n` padding can also provide this so probably not an issue in practice. What do you think?

Cheers,
Nick

`{Level,8:t7}` seems like a DSL in its own right. I liked the idea that the number told you how wide to expect the output to be, irrespective of its content. There's also the choice to pad right in SeriLog IIRC? How would that be represented, if at all?

> {Level,8:t7} seems like a DSL in its own right

Or a _really_ funky emoticon ;)

Yes, it's pretty ugly, though I'd be surprised to spot this one in the wild. I can see this feature used for short level names, but `Information` is already getting pretty wide for use in a text log.

Right padding should be achieved with `,-n` (as in other .NET format strings) but I don't think we've implemented it in Serilog yet.

Ah sorry, to properly answer your question. Right pad:

```
"inf   "
```

Would look like:

```
{Level,-6:w3}
```

`8:t7` does look like some kind of cool monster. I think we're on to something!

I think seeing the examples actually makes it more coherent. We're packing a lot of configuration into a quite restrictive format, so something like `{Level,-6:w3}` is inevitable. This makes me wonder if this is the correct place for it, but aside from configuring it in code there's little else that can be done. I'm sure the community will be the first to complain should they disagree, but I think it's a useful feature and definitely one I'll be using.
:+1: thanks again for driving it! It's still pretty much my favourite 2.0 feature :-)

comments.body:
### Proposal 1

``` csharp
var evt = logger.CreateEvent(
    DateTimeOffset.Now, level, exception, "Some {Number}", 42);

evt.AddOrUpdateProperty(
    logger.CreateProperty("Ticks", 123));

evt.AddOrUpdateProperty(
    logger.CreateProperty("User", user, destructureObjects: true));

logger.Write(evt);
```
- `CreateEvent()` parses the message template and binds parameters (invoking destructuring policies etc. as needed)
- `CreateProperty()` just handles the scalar conversion/destructuring duties.

It's not an incredibly elegant interface, lots of long method names - but this kind of thing is only used in glue code, not typical application code.

#### Issues/questions

First, it's a breaking change for the `ILogger` interface. At this point very few 2.0-compatible packages will _implement_ `ILogger`, so it's the last opportunity to get this change in, I think. If we make this change we should also do #585.

The _Serilog.Extensions.Logging_ code above could not use `CreateEvent()` as proposed, since the binding logic generates warnings when template "holes" don't have corresponding values. Because of this, the standalone `MessageTemplateParser` would still be needed. A workaround to benefit from caching might just be to grab a copy of the one from the Serilog source, so maybe a non-issue.

Finally, it's worth noting that the names don't conflict on first character with anything in `ILogger`, but if we decided to add symmetric versions to `Log` then `Create***()` will have a first-char collision with `CloseAndFlush()`. This could be avoided by simply requiring callers to use `Log.Logger.Create***()`, we might come up with an alternative name, or given the infrequent use of both the factory methods and `CloseAndFlush()`, we might not care.

Hi Mike, this one is still causing me a bit of consternation. Sitting with @merbla  here discussing this, and thinking back to the original reason that `IScalarConversionPolicy` is not exposed...

The premise is that _sinks are responsible for formatting scalars_ is a pretty strong design principle in Serilog. 

E.g., if you have a `TimeSpan`, then the MSSQL sink should be free to format that as a SQL timespan, and a JSON-based sink might format it as ISO.

`Destructure.AsScalar()` exists to let more types through this pipeline, but the underlying mechanism (`IScalarConversionPolicy` etc.) probably shouldn't also take the role of providing string formatting.

What do you think? Given this whole concept any more consideration? Cheers!
Why are reflection types considered to be Scalar?

Just for the sake of history, this is the [PoC for transforming reflection types](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/commit/1e14bb41c5753add0c864b99ab8b473f787737ed) that I made while investigating this. I didn't attempt to turn it into a PR because my testing revealed that allowing reflection types to be destructured results in an `OutOfMemoryException`

Aaah right, thanks for the link, that makes the issue a bit clearer (I'd forgotten where the handler for this was plugged in).

Regarding why they're scalar, it was too easy to create explosively large object graphs during destructuring otherwise. Perhaps an `IDestructuringPolicy` would have been a better implementation option - `Type` could come through as a string, and `MemberInfo` would be a structure with `Name` and `DeclaringType` (suspect that was one of the earlier suggestions around this thread). `ParameterInfo` could get some similar special treatment.

Am I on track now? :-)
Raised a PR to internalize this interface until we're comfortable with a design (if one is required at all).

I'm really glad this has led to some great discussion!  From my take (as a newb but avid fan of Serilog :smile: ) my whole take is that there should be a mechanism whereby if configured I can always expect certain objects to look a certain way.  I appreciate delegating formatting to the sinks.  However, if I have a certain object, I would expect that object to always be formatted a certain way -- either at the sink level and/or before then anytime that object is rendered, or _both_. :)

If the sinks are formatting, they should also respect the wishes of the implementing application to also format it a certain way before they have their say in it, IMO!

Another thought, FWIW, when I first thought about this feature, I was thinking along the lines of a WPF `DataTemplate`, where you could basically create a template a generic template and no matter where in the application it was viewed, you could always expect it to look a certain way -- if that helps!

Maybe it's me that caused it, but there seems to be a few related issues going on here. I'm going to see if I can write down my understanding of them, and how they're related.

## The example given in this issue

@Mike-EEE created this issue with a suggestion to consider a `FormatterConfiguration` as a potential solution to the way `MethodBase` types are treated and ultimately rendered by most (all?) sinks. I say that because the only example given by @Mike-EEE involves `MethodBase` which is a _reflection type_. Maybe @Mike-EEE has different scenarios where formatting would be necessary, but this is only one we have so far.

Reflection types are: `System.Type`, `MethodBase`, `ParameterInfo`, etc. However, in Serilog, they are defined by [`ReflectionTypesScalarConversionPolicy`](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/32127146a394353eb3a26583b5a2ec5b0c404f25/src/Serilog/Policies/ReflectionTypesScalarConversionPolicy.cs) as derived from either `System.Type` OR `System.Reflection.MemberInfo`.

## What is a Scalar?

[Serilog wiki says](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Structured-Data):

> Scalars are .NET types that can be represented as atomic values; most value types like int fit this description, but so do some reference types like Uri and string
> ...
> Out of the box, Serilog recognises the following list as basic scalar types, regardless of any other policies applied:
> Booleans - bool
> Numerics - byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, float, double, decimal
> Strings - string, byte[]
> Temporals - DateTime, DateTimeOffset, TimeSpan
> Others - Guid, Uri
> Nullables - nullable versions of any of the types above

I note the absence of `Type` and `MemberInfo`. Most of these above make sense to me as _atomic_, except for perhaps `Uri` which can be broken apart further in useful ways. I can break apart `Uri` into pieces like `HostName` and `Query` (which I've often wanted to do - so that I can query and filter the logs more easily later). I can think of quite a few extremely useful ways to break apart `MethodBase` or even `Type` to make them more useful. Apparently, @Mike-EEE and @nblumhardt can think of various ways to break them apart too ;)

I think they should not be treated as `Scalar`.

# Now what?

I'm not sure yet. I feel like `Formatting` is not the right solution reflection types. As [@nblumhardt says](https://github.com/serilog/serilog/issues/723#issuecomment-215623341):

> sinks are responsible for formatting scalars is a pretty strong design principle in Serilog

Agreed. Makes sense.

I have a question now: what if _all_ types could be transformed early in the Serilog pipeline?

Ah yes @adamchester, I did indeed start out with `MethodBase`, but my intention/direction/ask here is for _any_ POCO object, whether it is scalar or not.  That is, a specified/configurable mechanism that is application-specific that allows an implementer to define the "look and feel" of any given object in the .NET universe.  Again I come back to the WPF DataTemplate concept.  That is very much the same spirit of the ask here.

> I have a question now: what if all types could be transformed early in the Serilog pipeline?

This is basically what I am after, yes. :)  Essentially, it should be (in order of priority):
1) Application-specific/defined formatting
2) Sink-specific/defined formatting.

If I as an application developer format a `MethodBase` into a string early in this pipeline, then this ultimately gets rendered as a scalar at the sink level.  Because I am deliberately/consciously setting this format/configuration, then I have explicitly given my "OK" on this override.  Hope this makes sense!

Thanks @Mike-EEE.

Do you think something like this makes sense?

``` csharp
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .Transform.ByType<Uri>(
        transformation: uri => new { Canonical = uri.ToString(), uri.Host, uri.Query })
    .Transform.ByType<Type>(
        predicate: typeof(Type).IsAssignableFrom,
        transformation: t => new { Name = t.Name, t.Namespace, })
    .Transform.ByType<MethodBase>(
        predicate: typeof(MethodBase).IsAssignableFrom,
        transformation: mi => new { DisplaySig = mi.ToString(), mi.ReflectedType, mi.DeclaringType })
    .WriteTo.Sink(new MySink())
    .CreateLogger();
```

It's close!  My concern here is that it looks like it's being destructured?  It's hard to see how the item will be rendered, unless it is known that the property order is the order in which objects are rendered.

Also, I have begun lately to use `Project` rather than `Transform` ... thanks to some nice code/guidance that I've spied upon by @nblumhardt lately. :D  

I also do like `Format` as it seems stronger to my scenarios, but I am being selfish and not considering others in this regard!

@Mike-EEE - so in your scenario, it might look more like:

``` csharp
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .Transform.ByType<MethodBase>(
        predicate: typeof(MethodBase).IsAssignableFrom,
        transformation: m => $"{m.DeclaringType.Name}.{m.Name}")
    .WriteTo.Sink(new MySink())
    .CreateLogger();
```

You have chosen to convert one scalar to another scalar early in the pipeline. From there onwards, all sinks and formatters have no choice but to respect your wishes, right?

Note I'm not sure about the naming of `.Transform.ByType<T>` - just trying to make a point at this stage.

Exactly!  Basically an application-specific override that is checked first, otherwise, behave as normal.  Much like. :smile: 

Yeah, I used `Transform` for the longest time in my framework (and honestly I am a little burned out on the word LOL), but now I use a much more terse `With` command, but `Project` is exactly what it is. :)
@Mike-EEE did you see #728 ?
Very cool!  Yes, that works, too. :smile:

+1 on the PR. I think the two separate issues are still interesting to track:
- [ ] Reflection types don't always fit "scalar" definition, should be transformable when `@Destructuring`
- [ ] Text-based sinks would benefit from some kind of additional formatting mechanism (this issue, I think)

The first is a, straightforward change; the second probably not so, even though the notion makes sense. If the PR unblocks you @Mike-EEE I think the second item will probably remain unaddressed for now, as it's non-trivial to put a coherent design together for it - or at least seems that way first thing on a Sunday morning :-)
Watching from the stands on this one. @Mike-EEE did you care "when" in the pipeline these operations occurred or just that is was respected by the end of the pipeline?

Regarding text-based formatting, I think it needs some more example scenarios. For some reason I thought [`ICustomFormatter`](https://msdn.microsoft.com/en-us/library/system.icustomformatter%28v=vs.110%29.aspx) was going to help, when [I was looking at MessageTemplates](https://github.com/adamchester/MessageTemplates/blob/master/FsMessageTemplates/MessageTemplates.fs#L636).

comments.body:
Loggers can write to other loggers - see https://github.com/serilog/serilog/wiki/Configuration-Basics#sub-loggers

So you can have your occasional UDP logger set up as another sink to which your main logger sends events.

Combine that with http://nblumhardt.com/2014/10/dynamically-changing-the-serilog-level/ and you can turn the UDP tap on or off as required (by changing its level to fatal or some more permissive level).  

I don't think there's a way to have the sink completely disabled  on demand.  If I had to do that today, and in a jiffy, I'd probably pipe it through a small RX observable where I could filter in there myself and have the RX pipeline end up back at the UDP logger.  

(side note: that's handy for use in something like LinqPad anyway where it knows how to dump RX observables.  If running via the command line you instead set up the Serilog pipeline to go to Seq instead of RX).

@IanYates Thanks for the pointers. Unfortunately the built in stuff won't really help. 

Once the logger is created via CreateLogger() it cannot be "modified". So whether the UDP logger is a sub logger or configured as part of the main logger they both have to be scaffolded at time of the logger construction.

And the serilog level is global so when you mess with that you may lose logs elsewhere depending on how the permissions have been set up.

I took your suggestion about Rx and did something similar for our implementation. As we have a configuration store I can detect changes in there and when a log request is invoked we spin up the new logger configuration before writing to it (based on the settings). In this way we can have various logging levels per sink as needed, never have to touch the global level. 

From a performance perspecitve in our web app we can still configure the logger "once" and store it globally and use for subsequent requests without the cost of spinning it up each time. We lock access to the log singleton and only rebuild it if we detect a configuration change eg. Turn UDP On, Turn Email Off etc.

Not ideal as I would still prefer to see the ILogger be able to be configured after it has been created, but it was probably done that way to keep things simple internally which is fair enough.

I'm going to hijack this because it's the first Google result for "unit testing Serilog". If you're interested in unit testing your Serilog log output you can use the [TestCorrelator sink](https://github.com/Microsoft/serilog-sinks-testcorrelator)!
@MitchBodmer Don't wanna be offensive, but why someone would want to test log output?

@Sigvaard no offense taken! It's a fine question.

**The short answer:**

To prevent regressions!

**The long answer:**

Often the nature/frequency/content of the log output your application produces is important enough that it's worthy of protecting with an automated regression suite. You may want to ensure that the right errors are produced by mission critical systems for alerting purposes, or just prevent yourself from overrunning a rate limited document database. In any case, having a way of checking that the log output you expect is produced can be very useful.

You could, of course, do something like writing to a file and then parsing that file to ensure it contains the elements you need. Unfortunately that method is often both arduous and fragile, requiring file IO in each test and breaking if the log format changes in a way that doesn't actually violate the business requirement.

Additionally if you've made the choice, as many Serilog users have, to use a global logger instead of passing an ILogger to every class that produces log output, you might face an additional challenge as you try to parallelize your tests. Since each class will be writing to the same logger, they will likely overwrite each other's logs and logger configurations leading to non-determinism in your test suite.

The sink above is a way of solving those problems, and providing you a way to get the fully structured log events from Serilog that we all love so much. That way you can more easily assert on properties of the event like level and timestamp and more intelligently look at the values of the properties you're interested in. No parsing required!
In my case, I need to test to verify that sensitive data is not being pushed to our log aggregator

The Serilog file/rolling file sinks support a single process only. For multi-process scenarios, using either separate filenames, or one of the non-file-based sinks, is necessary.

(Alternatively, it's possible to create a custom/forked file sink with different synchronisation behaviour if you want to go down that path.)

FYI:  The boost logger will not allow the same process to write into the same file, it always starts a new file.  It never tries to append to the end of an existing file that it did not create within the process.  IMHO:  That is the best design choice.  It is simple to implement and it solves all kinds of problems.

Maybe instead of doing it at the sink level you could write your own ILogger instead?  To keep things simple (for some definition of simple) you could log to an RX observable  (I myself just did this last week in LinqPad and it worked really well).

From the observable you could use some RX operators to do things like buffer or delay your observable stream of events and unleash the buffered/delayed stream when the main stream gets a log event with warning/error/fatal level.  After X events or Y seconds pass you could then close the tap on the buffered/delayed stream.

All the while you're still subscribing to your main observable and forwarding on those log events to another Serilog logger which is actually wired up to various sinks.

There's a bit of experimentation to be done with regards to enrichers (you'd need them to apply before log events hit the observable) but the general idea is fairly sound.

Of course if you're unfamiliar with RX then you could code the buffering by hand without too much effort but it'd be harder to change (X number of events, Y seconds of events, etc - easily composed with RX but harder with timers and manually managed lists).

The key thing here is that you can have one Serilog pipeline configured to write to another Serilog logger.  This is a handy extension point to use for your buffering.
See https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/serilog/TVZZDCtvwdE for another use case of loggers writing to other loggers

## Strawman

Being totally ignorant of your internal implementation of these format strings, as a user I'd like _something_ like this:

```
{SourceContext:<{0}> | }{Message}
```

... to output this, if context is set:

```
<SomeClassName> | Awesome message.
```

... and this, if context is **not** set:

```
Awesome message.
```

Note, no leading space.

Thanks @stajs. OCD is a valuable trait in an API designer, in my humble opinion :-)

I don't think Serilog's current output templates are going to be able to cover this - diverging too far from .NET standard format string compatibility will get hard to manage and will seem unpredictable to newcomers. Currently the format strings work identically to .NET's `{0} {1}` strings, with named "hole" support being the only twist.

However.... all of this is handled via `ITextFormatter`, a public interface that most sinks support (at least internally) in order to switch between human-readable and JSON output. The most common use of this is to write JSON to log files.

Would implementing an alternative language entirely for this task be reasonable? I.e. `HandlebarsTextFormatter` could be used as an output formatter and thus support all manner of conditional goodies. A simpler syntax implemented e.g. with Sprache might also work.

Currently you can plug this in as:

```
.WriteTo.Sink(new RollingFileSink(..., outputFormatter: new HandlebarsTextFormatter("{{SourceContext}} {{Message}}")))
```

In the long run a nicer way of plugging it in would be desirable, but to kick the tires and try out some concepts independently you (or someone keen) could publish this as a separate NuGet package today and get some feedback.

Just a thought, anyway!

comments.body: see https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-email/pull/13

Thanks for the report and PR, sorry to hear about the mail flood :-|

Since email is one of several sinks that would benefit from rate limiting, what do you think about going in a slightly different direction with something like:

``` csharp
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
  .WriteTo.Console() // etc.
  .WriteTo.Logger(l => l
    .Filter.PerMinuteInExcessOf(100)
    .WriteTo.Email(...))
  .CreateLogger();
```

It's less obvious/ergonomic, but keeps each sink from eventually taking on a dozen different configuration options. Would love to hear your thoughts.

A slightly hacky version of the method is here: https://gist.github.com/nblumhardt/d3baa1ea511242951e78

Clever approach - and I don't mean "clever" as in "obscure" or "tricky" as we so often mean in programming circles :)

I suppose emailing should be one of those rare things so it's probably limited to warnings or worse anyway, but since this is being applied generally, could it be useful to maintain multiple PerMinuteInExcessOf values for various levels of logging from verbose through to fatal?  That way error and  fatal could be set to perhaps 100, warnings at 10 and others at 1 or 2.  

I suppose someone could take this to the extra and use a Func<Message,GroupBucket> to really discriminate if it was so desired.  That's probably (and should be) rare but it could be used behind the scenes to implement the common simple API.

Okay I have thought deeply about it and discussed it with a colleage.

Your filter solution might be a clever implementation, but from my point of view, it is not very useful.

Consider the error log events e1...e1000 being generated.
My solution configured to max=3 mails will give you mails containing: e1, e2-e101,e102-e201. All others will be swallowed. I can trust the system that I really received e1..e201 without gaps.

The rate limiting solution from @nblumhardt will silently remove some messages from inbetween. If you want to analyse something from it, you never can be sure, there was something removed from inbetween. This gets worse times 10 with the suggestion from @IanYates to allow different rates for different error levels.

Something else: In my solution, if I want to get not more than 5 mails per hour, I simply put a 5 in right spot and I am done. If I want to archive the same thing using rate limiting, what rate do I have to choose? The best case is, you provide some kind of formula. But isnt the actual number dependant on the way the batching is implementes? 

I am going to test this next: From my observations, the first email only contains a single log event and after this, every mail contains 100 log events but what would happen, if I emit 2 errors and never ever emit anything again. will I receive the second email? In either way, this yields an interesting follow up question: If I allow only a really low rate of errors, will I either receive the second error mail way too late or will I receive many mails all with only one or two log lines? Both is not very desireable.

Last point is easy: Why is the rolling file sink allowed to have a parameter about how many files are okay while basically the same thing on the email sink is "too many configuration parameters"?

the rate limiting approach might be useful somewhere else.

Consider a class always emitting the timing of an executed operation but you really are not interested in every timing but you maybe want to see some timings now and then. There you could apply the rate limiting and would not need to change the actual emitting code.

okay i tested the batching part. It either batches 100 log events into one mail or it batches all log events from 30 seconds.
Even the lowest rate limiting would yield 120 mails/hour per server and process and also the lowest rate limiting would remove way to many events. I would basically get many thin mails instead of a low amout of full mails.

I hope, I got my point through by now.
I testest https://github.com/serilog/serilog-sinks-email/pull/13 to my best standards :smile: and we are running this now at our company as a kind of private fork.

Hi Fabian, thanks for all the follow-up!

> Why is the rolling file sink allowed to have a parameter about how many files are okay while basically the same thing on the email sink is "too many configuration parameters"?

Sorry about the lack of clarity in my statement there. I meant to emphasise "different". The rolling file sink is the only one that stores a set of rolling files, so it makes sense that its implementation should be there.

All sinks could potentially benefit from rate limiting - networks can be saturated, databases can be filed, etc. - so having a consistent way to represent the limit among various sinks would have the benefit of consistency/predictability.

I think you make some good points on how the limiting might best work - sliding vs hopping window - but I think that's orthogonal to the API (we could use either rate limiting algorithm in either option).

Whether per-minute or per-hour is appropriate is also a variable, I see how per-hour is more useful in your case.

If the sliding window is used, it might be possible to use fractional per-minute or per-hour values to gain some flexibility.

Great discussion, will try to make some time to dig in deeper. @serilog/core any thoughts?

I opened this issue in february together with a working pull request which would only require a click on the merge button. @nblumhardt had his own ideas about how to solve the issue and then .... nothing!

4 months have passed without any working solution for rate limiting in the nuget package. The risk to use the current package is not feasable and I am not sure, whether this will change or not. I am still using a private build of the email sink.

Did something happened in the meantime regarding rate limitation? what is the plan here?

Hi Fabian,

I'm sorry to hear you have to maintain a forked version of the sink. This does illustrate the problem we both face though: you may not want to keep one version of this code working - I am hesitant to maintain a separate rate limiting implementation in 50 or more different Serilog sinks that could benefit from it, as I did my best to explain above.

Before opening a PR it's usually a good idea to [propose your changes first](https://www.igvita.com/2011/12/19/dont-push-your-pull-requests/); otherwise, it can take some extra effort for everyone to get on the same page.

If you're still interested in solving this one, do you think the rate limiting algorithm from your proposal could be wrapped up in a sink-neutral API? I think it'd be a great addition to the Serilog toolkit if so. If not, let me know why - I didn't mean to shut down this discussion by closing the issue, I'm just trying to keep the tickets for the various sinks in the corresponding trackers. Both the PR thread, and the new issue thread above, are still open.

Cheers,
Nick

Here's the implementation of `ForContext`:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Pipeline/Logger.cs#L79

And here's the implementation of `Dispatch()`:

https://github.com/serilog/serilog/blob/dev/src/Serilog/Core/Pipeline/Logger.cs#L157

You see the call in there to `_sink.Emit()` - that will call the parent `Logger` passed into the constructor in `ForContext()`.

If `Dispatch()` is recursively overflowing the stack, it's possible `Emit()` has been optimised away somehow (though it's a surprising elision given the interface-based dispatch to `ILogEventSink.Emit()`).

This is most likely due to something resembling:

``` csharp
var logger = ...
for (var i = 0; i < 100; ++i)
{
    logger = logger.ForContext("X", "y");
}

logger.Information("Boom!");
```

Of course, the repeated reassignment may be a bit more subtle than that, involving `Log.Logger` and so-on.

I can't see this problem in the code you've supplied, but there's a chance that something elsewhere in the codebase is making the repeated assignments to `Log.Logger` and the deep Rx stack just happens to be the first place it hits the stack size limit.

Searching for any `ForContext()` calls that are assigned back to a long-lived logger would be a worthwhile next-step.

Cheers!
Any luck here @johnkattenhorn?
Yep, we (I) were chaining them together :-( Changed the implementation around by building a bunch of extensions to correctly achieve what I wanted.

comments.body:
Thanks for the note. I did consider something like this back when LogContext came onto the scene, but the current design won because it's clear the log context is not tied to the logger (it'd be strange to push something onto the context via an `ILogger`, log an event with a completely _different_ `ILogger`, and see the properties appear on it.

If you just want to push onto a single `ILogger` then `ForContext()` does this; if the goal is to affect multiple `ILoggers` then having the mechanism be external to all of them seems to make sense.

At this point I think it's safe to say the ship has sailed (there's a high bar for interface breaking changes), but interesting to hear about your scenario so thanks again for posting.

Ah, sorry Colin, I misread your original post and realise now you're talking about a suggestion for _m.e.Logging_, not Serilog.

It sounds like the design you've reached is a reasonable one; the static/ambient nature of contextual correlation doesn't mesh with interfaces so well to me, but it's more stylistic than substantial, and the testing scenario is a fair one.

Still not sure this is something Serilog can help with, but if you end up raising a discussion on the _Logging_ repo it'd be very interesting to follow along.

Where I thought Serilog could help is by vetting my idea :) I figured the people here probably have way more experience with logging frameworks in general than I do, both individually and collectively. My experience is about 90% with antique versions of log4net (the other 10% being various home-grown frameworks and jury-rigged solutions).

The main thing I don't like about my solution is that it's leaking out logging infrastructure details from a component that has nothing to do with logging. I'd be interested to get feedback on whether others think this is something general enough to be worth bringing up at the _Logging_ repo. It sounds like log4net has a similar concept and it would be nice to be able to normalize them.
Not sure there's a huge amount we can do to move this forward from here, so closing for the time being. Would be interesting to continue the discussion sometime, though. Cheers!

comments.body:
Hi Dmitry,

Thanks for the thoughtful post.

Would the design below (which mimics `WriteTo.Logger()` already in Serilog cover it?

``` csharp
var log = new LoggerConfiguration()
  .Enrich.WithThreadId()
  .WriteTo.AsyncLogger(al => al
    .WriteTo.Console())
  .CreateLogger();
```

The `AsyncLogger` sink could use TPL/threadpool/worker thread to shuttle messages to its connected sinks, without blocking the main logger.

I added `WithThreadId()` as a reminder that enrichers applied to the background logger would execute in their own context, so things like thread id and logging context may not appear as expected. Maybe one caveat of this design.

This'd probably make quite a nice _Serilog.Sinks.AsyncLogger_ package without needing any effort in the core right now.

I'd prefer something unintrusive over say, a per-sink wrapper that needs to be accounted for/configured throughout the API.

What do you think?
This is really interesting, I like the idea of wrapping the existing sync and offloading with `WriteTo.AsyncLogger`

@nblumhardt I've committed preliminary code in my [repo](https://github.com/DmitryNaumov/serilog/commit/2106f15bddccc289f24ad36baf13ed6e021cd40d) to give some food for discussion. Questions are:
-  Configuration. Extension method WriteAsyncTo doesn't please my eyes. But Logger(Sink)Configuration are doing great job incapsulating their state. 'Internal' doesn't work because configuration and sinks are in different assemblies. Any help/suggestions/ideas are welcome.
- Sink batching support. Imo, sinks should support batches on their lowest level. Otherwise writing to file or network wouldn't be as effective as it can be. It can be done via adding method to ILogEventSink, but it breaks contract, deriving from it or adding brand new separate interface for it. Want to hear your opinion.
- Imo makes no sense to have both PeriodicBatchingSink and DelegatingPeriodicBatchingSink. Delegation should be implemented out-of-the-box. Existing sinks like Seq should not derived from PBS, but be implemented in sync-way and use delegating capabilities of PBS or DBPS (which one will survive). It would keep async things in one place and simplifies sink development.
- PBS.EmitBatchAsync. Didn't understand why declare async contract to be called and waited from timer's thread? We're already 'in background', it just complicates things imo.
- And last (but I think I forget something) but not the least - can I use any mock library for tests?

Please share your thoughts on these issues, may be you totally disagree with idea of built-in async support.

Hi Dmitry, sorry about the slow reply (as usual for me it would seem :-))

- Seems like trade-offs one way or the other here
- Yes, I would add batching natively to sinks if I could go back in time I think; having said that, the batching algorithm tends to be sink-specific in some cases so not sure one solution would cover everything
- Also makes sense, but hard to go back now for this as the solution we have is pretty reaonable; perhaps designing chainable sinks as a separate package would help flesh out an alternative design?
- I'm fine with that; NSubstitute seems to be fairly friendly but if there's anything else in use that'd be fine too

HTH! :-)
